quote: "And flaying," it says, "the whole burnt offering, they shall divide it limb by limb, and the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire upon the altar, and shall pile up wood on the fire; and the sons of Aaron the priest shall lay on the divided limbs and the head and the fat and the wood which are upon the altar. But the entrails and the feet they shall wash with water, and the priest shall lay all upon the altar; it is a victim and a sacrifice, an odor of sweetness to the Lord." How the flesh of the Word of God, which here is named a "calf," is flayed, and how it is divided "limb by limb" by the priests, is worth observing. I think that that priest strips off the hide of the "calf" offered as a "whole burnt offering" and draws off the skin by which its limbs are covered, who strips from the Word of God the veil of the letter and lays bare its inner parts, which are the limbs of spiritual understanding; and these limbs of the inner Word he places not in some lowly place, but sets them on high and holy, that is, "upon the altar," when he opens the divine mysteries not to unworthy men who lead a lowly and earthly life, but to those who are the altar of God, in whom the divine fire ever burns and the flesh is ever consumed. Upon such as these, then, this "calf of the whole burnt offering," divided limb by limb, is placed. For he divides the "calf limb by limb" who can explain in order and discourse with fitting distinction what was the progress of one who "touched the fringe" of Christ, but of another who "washed his feet with tears and wiped them with the hairs of the head," and how much more excellent than these it is to have "anointed his head with myrrh"; and also what eminence he has who "reclined upon his breast." To discourse, then, on the causes of each of these, and to fit some things to beginners, other things to those who are already advancing in the faith of Christ, and yet other things to those who are already perfect in his knowledge and love — this is "to have divided the calf limb by limb." But also one who knows how to show what were the beginnings of the law, what progress too was made in the prophets, and what fullness of perfection is held in the Gospels; or who can teach with what "milk" of the word the "little ones" in Christ are to be fed, and with what "herb" of the word "those who are weak in the faith" are to be refreshed, and what also is that "solid and strong food" by which the athletes of Christ are to be fattened; whoever knows how to divide these single things by spiritual reasoning, such a teacher can be seen as that priest who "places upon the altar the whole burnt offering divided into limbs." He also adds "wood" to the altar, that the fire may be quickened and burn, who mingles his discourse not only concerning the corporeal virtues of Christ, but also concerning his divinity. For the divinity of Christ is from above, whither this fire hastens. Fittingly, therefore, the heavenly fire consumed all these things that were done in the body by the Savior, and restored them all to the nature of his divinity. Yet with wood applied this fire is kindled; for up to the wood was the passion of Christ in the flesh. But when he was hung upon the wood, the dispensation of the flesh was ended; for rising from the dead he ascended to heaven, whither the nature of fire shows its course. Whence the Apostle also said, that: "even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him." For the whole burnt offering of his flesh, offered through the wood of the cross, joined earthly things to heavenly and human things to divine. "The entrails" indeed "together with the feet" the word of the precept commands "to be washed with water," announcing the sacrament of baptism under a figurative proclamation. For he washes the "entrails" who purges the conscience; he washes the feet who receives the consummation of the sacrament and knows that "he who is clean has no need except to wash his feet," and that "no one can have a part with Jesus unless he wash his feet."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the offerings of the soul it describes as far inferior. This soul has neither a "bull-calf" nor a "sheep" nor a "kid" to offer to God; but it does not even find "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons". It has only "fine flour"; from it, it "offers unleavened loaves from the oven", from it a work made "in the pan" or "mixed with oil on the griddle". Whence it seems to me that the one here called "a soul" is to be understood as that man whom Paul names "the animal (natural) man"; who, even if he is not pressed by sins nor headlong toward vices, nevertheless does not have anything spiritual in him, anything that might figuratively be reckoned the flesh of the Word of God. For thus Paul the Apostle himself says of him that: "the animal (natural) man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. For it is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand, because it is spiritually discerned. But the spiritual man examines all things". This one, then, who is named "a soul", cannot offer all things, because he cannot examine all things; but he offers only "fine flour and unleavened loaves", that is, this common life — placed, for example, in agriculture or in seafaring or in some of the uses of common life; yet even he too offers an offering to God, although he is said "to offer" only "fine flour" merely "sprinkled with oil". For every soul needs the oil of the divine mercy, nor can anyone escape the present life unless the oil of the heavenly compassion be present to him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For just as flesh, if it be not sprinkled with salt, however great and choice it be, is corrupted, so also the soul, unless it be in some way salted with continual temptations, immediately is dissolved and grows slack. Whence it is clear that on this account it was said that "every sacrifice shall be salted with salt."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In the second place, the oblation "of the first fruits", that is, of the beginnings of the produce, is commanded. And this, if you remember well, the law commands to be done on the day of Pentecost. In which a "shadow" plainly was given to them, but for us the truth was reserved. For on the day of Pentecost, when the sacrifice of prayers had been offered, the Church received the first fruits of the coming "Holy Spirit" of the Apostles. And truly these were fresh, because it was new; whence they were even said to be "filled with new wine". "Roasted with fire". For fiery tongues settled upon each one. "And broken in the middle". For they were broken in the middle, when the letter was separated from the spirit. "And well cleansed". For the presence of the Holy Spirit cleanses all filth, granting remission of sins. The oil of mercy too is poured into this sacrifice, and the frankincense of sweetness, through which we are made "the good odor of Christ".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After this it speaks of the peace (salutary) offerings, which are offered from animals, that is, from "oxen" or "goats and sheep"; and nothing beyond these is admitted for immolation — not even the birds, which above had been admitted among the offerings to be offered. For this one, who offers the peace offerings, is without doubt already conscious of his own salvation; and therefore he who has arrived at salvation must of necessity offer things that are great and perfect. For thus the Apostle too says: "solid food, however, is for the perfect".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Thereupon the order of the sacrifices is directed to the offering of victims for sins, in which it is said a second time: "the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: whatever soul shall sin before the Lord unwillingly". Rightly does it say "soul" of the one whom it describes as sinning; for it would not have called it spirit, of which it would say that it would sin; but neither would it call this one a man, in whom, with sin intervening, the "image of God" in no way stands firm. It is not, then, the spirit that sins; for "the fruit of the spirit" — as the Apostle describes — "is love, joy, peace, patience", and the rest like these, which are also called "the fruits of life". Finally, elsewhere too he says: "he who sows in the flesh shall from the flesh reap corruption; and he who sows in the spirit shall from the spirit reap eternal life". Since, then, there is one who sows and another in whom it is sown, and it is sown either "in the flesh", when one sins, so that "corruption" be reaped, or "in the spirit", when one lives according to God, so that "eternal life" be reaped — it is established that it is the soul which sows either "in the flesh" or "in the spirit", and that it is the soul which can either rush into sin or be turned back from sin. For the body is its follower to whatever it may choose; and the spirit is its guide to virtue, if it be willing to follow it.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The discourse concerns the sacrifices which are offered by those who have sinned through ignorance or not by will. Hence also in what went before, when we were speaking of the high priest's sacrifice, we observed that it was not written of him that he had been in ignorance. But if anyone remembers well the things that were said, he can say to us that the sacrifice which we said the high priest offered "for sin" we set down as holding the figure of Christ. And it will not seem fitting that Christ, "who knew no sin", should be said to have offered a sacrifice "for sin", even though the matter is transacted through a mystery and the same one is set down both as high priest and as victim. See, therefore, whether we can meet this too in this way: that Christ indeed "did no sin", yet was made "sin for us"; while he who was in the form of God deigns to be in the form of a servant; while he who is immortal dies, and the impassible suffers, and the invisible is seen; and, because for us all either death or all the rest of frailty was brought upon the flesh from the condition of sin, he too, who "was made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man", without doubt "for sin", which he had taken up from us, because "he bore our sins", offered "the spotless bull-calf", that is, the uncontaminated flesh, "as a victim to God". But what do we make of what is joined in the sequel? For where it says: "if indeed the high priest who is anointed sins", there is added: "so that he makes the people to sin, he shall offer for his own sin". How then will it fit that through the flesh which Jesus took up from us, he himself, made sin, "made the people to sin"? Listen concerning this too, whether perchance we can answer with some consistency. The passion of Christ confers life on those who believe, but death on those who do not believe. For although through his cross there is salvation for the Gentiles and justification, yet for the Jews there is destruction and condemnation. For so it is written also in the Gospels: "behold, this one is born for the ruin and the resurrection of many". And in this way, through his own sin, that is, through the flesh driven to the cross, in which he had taken up our sins, he indeed freed us who believe from sin, but "the people who did not believe" he made to sin, for whom to the evil of unbelief there was added also the impiety of sacrilege. And in this way that high priest through his own sin "made the people to sin", while, being set in the flesh, he could both be seized and slain. For let us suppose, for example, that if "the Lord of majesty" had not come in the flesh, he would not have reproved the Jews, he would not have been grievous to them even to look upon, he could by no means have been seized nor delivered to death; without doubt "his blood" would never have come "upon them and their children". But because he came in the flesh and was made "sin for us" and could suffer these things, therefore he himself is said to have "made the people to sin", who made it possible for them to sin against him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For "on account of sins not voluntary" it is in general the "soul" that is commanded to offer, but after this the text proceeds through diverse and various persons; and it is commanded that, "if indeed it be the high priest who has transgressed and offers a sacrifice for sin, he should offer a bull-calf" as a whole burnt offering, but not by that same rite by which he offered the one for an offering. For of this one he shall place upon the altar of the whole burnt offerings "the fat and the two kidneys with their fat, and the fat that covers the inner parts", only these. "Of its blood" too, "dipping his finger, he sprinkles seven times before the Lord, and anoints from it the horns of the altar of incense. But the rest of the flesh, with the hide and the entrails and the dung, he commands to be burned with fire outside the camp, in a clean place". It must indeed be observed that in the sin of the high priest the lawgiver did not add that he had sinned through ignorance or unwillingly. For ignorance could not befall one who has been advanced in order that he might teach the rest.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But these things have been said in general; now, however, they are divided by kinds. "If the high priest", it says, "who has been anointed, should sin, so as to make the people sin, he shall offer for his own sin a bull-calf from the oxen, without blemish, to the Lord". Both terror and mercy are displayed together in the divine laws. Is nothing, then, after all, safe — not even the high priest? And what high priest? The very one who has been anointed, the very one who kindles the divine altars with the sacred fires, who immolates offerings and peace offerings to God; who intervenes as a certain mediating re-propitiator between God and men — not even he, I say, remains immune from the contagion of sin. But see the mercy of God, and know it more fully from Paul's teaching. For he himself, writing to the Hebrews, says: "for every high priest taken from among men is appointed for men to offer victims to God", and a little later he says: "the law appoints as priests men having weakness", so that they may be able to offer, as for their own weakness, so also for the weakness of the people. You see, then, the dispensation of the divine wisdom. It appointed as priests, not those who could in no way sin — otherwise they would not be men — but those who ought indeed to imitate him "who did no sin", yet "to offer victims first for their own, and then also for the people's transgressions". But what especially is to be admired in a priest of this kind? Not that he should not sin — which cannot be — but that he should acknowledge and understand his own sin. For he never amends who does not think that he has sinned. And at the same time, because he too can more easily pardon those who sin who is himself stung by the consciousness of some weakness of his own. But what is the oblation of the priest "for sin"? "A bull-calf", it says, "for a whole burnt offering". We find in the second place that a "bull-calf" is offered by the high priest "for a whole burnt offering", once for an offering, once "for sin". But the one that is offered for an offering is consumed "upon the altar" of the whole burnt offering. But the one that is offered "for sin" is commanded to be burned "outside the camp, with the hide and the entrails and the dung, in a clean place", only the fat and the kidneys being offered on the altar. Although to divide and distinguish these several matters is both beyond our powers and beyond your hearing, nevertheless we shall attempt to seek out for you some occasions for understanding and to bring them into the open. See, then, whether perhaps Jesus, whom Paul says "made peace" through his blood "not only for the things that are on earth, but also for the things that are in the heavens", is himself this bull-calf, who "in the heavens" indeed was offered not "for sin" but for an offering, but "on the earth", where sin "reigned from Adam until Moses", was offered "for sin". And this is to have suffered "outside the camp" — outside those, I think, the camps which Jacob had seen, the heavenly camps of the angels of God, of which it is written in Genesis: "and Jacob, looking up, saw the camps of God in array, and the angels of God met him, and Jacob said, when he saw them: these are the camps of God". Outside those heavenly camps, then, is this whole earthly place in which we dwell, in which Christ suffered in the flesh. But as for its saying that it is burned "with the dung and the entrails", see whether perhaps, by comparison with the heavenly bodies, this body of human nature is figuratively called dung. For it is earth and taken from earth. But that basket of dung too, which is put at the roots of the fig tree to be cut down, what else does it show but the mystery of the dispensation assumed in a body? Nor yet are the entrails said to be lacking to him. For although he bore the lowly "form of a servant", nevertheless "the fulness of the divinity dwelt in him". Although these things have been discussed boldly, nevertheless the hearing of the faithful ought always to be nourished toward greater things. The same things too are to be understood of the bull-calf of the synagogue.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But in the moral sense this high priest can be seen as that faculty of piety and religion which within us performs, as it were, a certain priesthood, through the prayers and supplications that we pour out to God. If this transgress in anything, it forthwith "makes sin" the whole people of good acts that is within us. For we do nothing of a right work when the guiding sense of good works has declined into what is depraved; and therefore for the amending of this, not any victim whatever, but the sacrifice of "the fatted calf" itself is required. Likewise too the fault of the synagogue — that is, the amending of all the virtues that are within us — is repaired not otherwise than by the mortification of Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It will now be a great task to pursue the diversities of victims and the rites and varieties of sacrifices, and one belonging to a work far other than that discourse which the common crowd receives in the general assembly. But that we may seem to touch upon some things in passing: almost every victim, indeed, which is offered has something of the form and image of Christ. For every victim is recapitulated in him, so much so that, after "he himself was offered", all the victims ceased which had preceded him in type and "shadow"; concerning which, as far as we could, we showed in what went before how the bull-calf offered by the high priest, whether as an offering or "for sin", held his form. But the "fat", which is offered in the offering, "covering the inward parts" and clinging to the kidneys, can be understood as that holy soul of his which veiled the "inward parts", that is, the secrets of his divinity, but clung to the "kidneys", that is, to the corporeal matter which had been chastely taken up from us; and, set in the middle between the flesh and God, to be sanctified upon the sacred altars and to be made bright by the divine fires, it imposes the nature of the flesh, to be preserved with itself unto the heavens. But that the little kidneys are delivered to the fires — who would doubt that they indicate that there were no motions of the generative parts in Christ? But that "of the blood of the victim the priest" is recorded "to sprinkle seven times before the Lord", evidently the power of the Holy Spirit, of sevenfold grace, is designated under a mystery. The four "horns of the altar", which are anointed "with blood", indicate that the passion of Christ is reported by the four Gospels. As for the caul of the liver which is offered — in the liver anger is slaughtered, in the caul the swift and impetuous force of fury is shown. But the rest of the blood, which "is poured out at the base of the altar", I think designates the form of that grace by which "in the last days", after "the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in", "all Israel" that is left, placed at the last as it were "at the base of the altar", will itself also receive the outpouring of the blood of Christ. But concerning the lambs and the kids, the turtledoves and the doves, and also the "fine flour sprinkled with oil" or baked "in unleavened loaves", as far as the matter could bear, it has been said above.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if there be a sin "of the whole synagogue", the synagogue is none the less commanded to offer "a bull-calf" as a whole burnt offering. But in the sin of the synagogue it is said: "if it should be ignorant, and the matter be hidden from the eyes of the synagogue, and it should do one of all the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done"; from which it is clear that "the whole synagogue" too can transgress through ignorance. And this the Lord also confirms in the gospels, when he says: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "But if a ruler", it says, "should sin, he shall offer a goat from the she-goats". This ruler can be seen as the power of reason which is within us. And if this should sin in us, and we should do something foolish, that sentence of the Savior is to be greatly feared by us, which says: "you are the salt of the earth. But if the salt should lose its savor, it is good for nothing, except to be cast out and trodden underfoot by men". This one too, then, has his own victim.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But "one soul", it says, "if it should sin, shall likewise offer a female goat", according to that substitution of victims which we mentioned above. But perhaps the hearers of the church may say: it was dealt with almost better among the ancients than with us, when, sacrifices being offered by diverse rites, pardon was granted to those who sinned. Among us there is only one pardon of sins, which is given at the beginning through the grace of the laver; after this no mercy is granted to the one who sins, nor any pardon. It befits indeed a Christian, "for whom Christ died", to be of stricter discipline. For them sheep, goats, oxen were slaughtered, and birds, and fine flour was sprinkled; for you the Son of God was slaughtered, and does it delight you to sin again? And yet, lest these things lift up your spirit not so much toward virtue as cast it down toward despair, you have heard how many are the sacrifices for sins in the law; hear now how many are the remissions of sins in the gospels. There is that first one, by which we are baptized "unto the remission of sins". The second remission is in the suffering of martyrdom. The third is that which is given through almsgiving; for the Savior says: "but nevertheless give the things that you have, and behold, all things are clean to you". The fourth remission of sins comes to us through this, that we too remit sins to our brothers; for thus the Lord and Savior himself says that: "if you remit to your brothers from the heart their sins, your Father too will remit to you your sins. But if you do not remit to your brothers from the heart, neither will your Father remit to you", and just as he taught us to say in the prayer: "remit to us our debts, as we too remit to our debtors". The fifth remission of sins is when "someone turns a sinner from the error of his way". For thus the divine Scripture says that "he who causes a sinner to be turned from the error of his way saves a soul from death, and covers a multitude of sins". A sixth remission too comes about through the abundance of love, as the Lord himself also says: "Amen, I say to you, her many sins are remitted to her, because she loved much", and the Apostle says: "because love covers a multitude of sins". There is still a seventh also, though hard and laborious — the remission of sins through penance, when the sinner washes "his bed with tears" and his "tears" become to him "bread day and night", when he is not ashamed to make known his sin to the priest of the Lord and to seek the remedy, according to him who says: "I said: I will declare against myself my injustice to the Lord, and you remitted the impiety of my heart". In which is fulfilled also that which the Apostle James says: "but if anyone is sick, let him call the elders of the church, and let them lay hands on him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the sick man, and if he be in sins, they will be remitted to him". And you therefore, when you come to the grace of baptism, have offered "a bull-calf", because you are baptized "into the death of Christ". But when you are led to martyrdom, you have offered "a goat", because you have slaughtered the devil, the author of sin. And when you have given alms and, with careful piety, have paid out toward the needy the affection of mercy, you have laden the sacred altar with fat kids. For if you "remit from the heart the sin to your brother" and, laying aside the swelling of anger, have gathered again within you a mild and simple mind, be confident that you have immolated a ram or offered a lamb in sacrifice. Furthermore, if, instructed by the divine readings, "meditating like a dove" and keeping vigil "in the law" of the Lord "day and night", you turn a sinner from his error and, his wickedness cast off, recall him to the simplicity of the dove, and by making him cleave to the saints cause him to imitate the fellowship of the turtledove, you have offered to the Lord "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons". But if that "love" which is "greater" than hope and faith should abound in your heart, so that you "love your neighbor" not only "as yourself", but as he showed who said: "no one has greater love than this, that he lay down his soul for his friends", know that you have offered loaves of fine flour "kneaded in the oil" of love, without any "leaven of malice and wickedness, in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth". But if you are in the bitterness of your weeping, worn out with grief, tears, and lamentation, if you have mortified your flesh and made it dry with fasts and much abstinence, and have said that "my bones are burned up like a frying-pan", then you have offered "the sacrifice of fine flour from the pan or from the griddle"; and in this way you will be found to offer more truly and more perfectly, according to the gospel, the sacrifices which Israel can no longer offer according to the law.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us see what is also to be thought concerning the things that have just now been read: "but if", it says, "one soul should sin unwillingly from the people of the land, by doing one of all the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done, and should transgress, and the sin which it sinned should become known to it, it shall bring its gift: it shall bring a female goat from the kids, without blemish, for the sin which it sinned". And after this it recounted the whole rite of the sacrifice, according to what we expounded above. Concerning the soul which, made under sin, it says offers, how it is to be thought, we have explained in the foregoing as far as we could; but what it added in this place, saying "a soul, if it should sin from the people of the land", does not seem to me idle. For who would doubt that the things which the law says are said to souls or to a people that are on the earth? What need, then, was there that to what it said, "one soul, if it should sin", it should add: "from the people of the land"? But it must be seen whether perhaps, for distinction from another people, which "is not of the land", this soul which "should sin" is said to be "of the people of the land". For this saying cannot suit him who said: "but our citizenship is in the heavens, whence too we await the Savior, the Lord Jesus". How, then, could I rightly call "of the people of the land" that soul which has nothing in common with the land, but is wholly in the heavens and dwells there, "where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God", whither too it "desires" to return "and to be with Christ: for it is much better; but to remain in the flesh he judges necessary for our sake"? This soul, then, which sins, is "of the people of the land", "doing one of all the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done". For a long time a certain astonishment held me stunned in this saying; for I do not see it said consistently that "a soul has sinned and done one of the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done". For if it is a commandment of the Lord, how ought it not to be done, since surely the commandments of the Lord are given precisely for this, that they be done? And how is the soul here said to have sinned which "did one of the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done"? And perhaps to some it will seem an error of expression made by the translators; but to me, inquiring more curiously, it has been found that all the translators rendered it alike, and therefore not an error of expression, but a sense of deeper understanding, is to be sought. As far, then, as it can occur to us, this seems to me the resolution. Certain commandments of the Lord were given that they should be done, certain that they should not be done. But as for those which ought to be done, human necessity demanded that there should be brought forth, inserted among them, those which ought not to be done. For example — to bring forth an illustration from these very sacrifices which we now have in hand — a lamb is commanded to be immolated at the Passover, not because God truly required the victim of a lamb year by year, but because it signified that "that Lamb which takes away the sin of the world" ought to be immolated. This, then, he willed to be done, that he did not will. For thus he says through Isaiah: "what to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord. I am full; the whole burnt offerings of rams and the fat of lambs and the blood of bulls and of goats I do not will". You have heard how he does not will "the victim of rams nor the fat of lambs"? Yet he gave the commandment as to how the victim either of bulls or of lambs ought to be offered. But he who understands the law spiritually seeks to offer these things spiritually. But if anyone offers according to the appearance of the carnal commandment, this is "one soul from the people of the land, which sinned unwillingly by doing one of all the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done, and transgressed", and therefore it adds in what follows: "and when the sin which it sinned shall have become known to it, it shall bring its offering before the Lord". For the soul ought to offer an offering when "it has become known to it" that God does not seek a carnal sacrifice, because "a sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit". "Its sin becomes known" to it, then, when it has learned from the Lord who says: "I prefer mercy to sacrifice", and when it has come to know how to immolate "the sacrifice of praise" in the church and to render "to the Most High its vows", through Christ our Lord, "to whom be praise and glory unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us now see what that soul also does which "hears the voice of one swearing an oath and is a witness", "or" which "sees" something "and is privy to it and does not disclose it", from which it too "has borne his sin" — without doubt his who either did something wickedly or swore. This also, according to the history, builds us up and teaches us never to pollute our consciences in another's sins, nor to lend consent to those who act wickedly. And I call it consent not only to act along with them, but also to keep silent about the things that have been done unlawfully. Do you wish to know that these things agree also with the Gospel precepts? The Lord himself says: "if you see your brother sin, reprove him between yourself and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not hear you, take with you two others or three. But if he does not hear even them, tell the church. But if he does not hear even the church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican". But the Gospel precept was given more perfectly in this, that it established the manner and discipline of disclosing the sin. For it does not wish you, if perchance you have seen your brother's sin, at once to fly out into public and everywhere to proclaim and divulge another's sins — which would surely be the mark not of one correcting, but rather of one defaming. "Alone", it says, "between yourself and him, rebuke him". For when he who sins sees the mystery kept for him, he too will keep the modesty of amendment; but if he sees himself defamed, he will at once turn to the shamelessness of denial; and you will not only not have amended the sin, but will even have doubled it. Learn, therefore, the order from the Gospels. First, it says, "alone, between yourself and him". Second, "take with you two others or three". Why "two or three"? "For in the mouth", it says, "of two or three witnesses shall every word stand". Since indeed in the third place it commanded the correction to be brought to the church, in the second it wishes "two or three" witnesses to be brought in. In their presence, if the one rebuked will not amend himself, then, when his sin has been brought to the church, he may be confuted by the witnesses previously brought in; for it frequently happens that one wishing to fulfill the Gospel command may seem a slanderer, if he brings a charge to the church and lacks witnesses. Lest, therefore, this happen, for that reason he commanded "two or three" witnesses to be brought in at the second meeting. Since, therefore, such is the command of the Gospel, and the law prescribes that, if one keeps silent, "he shall bear his sin", it is to be known that, if anyone either does not disclose the things which he sees in his neighbor's fault according to the rule given above, or, when called to testimony, does not speak the things that are true, he himself will take upon himself the sin which the one he conceals has committed, and the penalty of the deed will roll back upon the one privy to it. Sufficiently, therefore, in this chapter has the very text of the history built us up. Yet I think that that soul too, which reads what is written in the law of God: "the Lord has sworn and will not repent; you are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek", "hears the voice of one swearing an oath", as do the scribes and Pharisees, always meditating on these things, but they are silent and are unwilling to announce them to the people, lest they testify to the coming of Christ. Therefore for this reason they will bear the sin, in which, not announcing to the people the things that are true, they make Israel to sin.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these things another law is promulgated. "Whatever soul", it says, "touches any unclean thing, or the carcass of unclean beasts, and it is hidden from him, and he is defiled; or if he touches of the uncleanness of a man, of any uncleanness by which he may be defiled", and so forth. These things indeed are observed among the Jews quite unbecomingly and uselessly. For to what end is he held unclean who has touched, for example, a dead animal or the body of a deceased man? What if it be the body of a prophet? What if the body of a patriarch, or even of Abraham himself? What if he has touched even the bones, will he be unclean? What if he touches the bones of Elisha, which raise up the dead? Will he who touches be unclean, and do the bones of the prophet make unclean even that very one whom they raise from the dead? See how unfitting the Jewish understanding is. But let us first see what it is to touch, and what is the touch that makes unclean, and what indeed is the touch that makes clean. The Apostle says: "it is good for a man not to touch a woman". This touch is unclean; for this is that which the Lord said in the Gospel: "if anyone looks upon a woman to lust after her, he has already committed adultery with her in his heart". For the vice of concupiscence touched his heart, and his soul was made unclean. If, therefore, anyone touches something in this way, that is, either through lust for a woman, or through desire for money, or by any other craving of sin whatever, he has touched something unclean and is defiled. It behooves you, therefore, if you have touched anything of this kind, to know how you may offer a sacrifice, according to the things we recalled in what went before, so that you may be made clean. Do you wish me to show you "what" is "the soul which touched the unclean thing" and was made unclean, and again touched the clean thing and was made clean? She "who suffered an issue of blood and spent all her substance on physicians and could gain nothing" was brought down to this through the uncleanness of sin. For she had touched sin, and for that reason had received the "scourge" of the flesh. But after, full of faith, "she touched the fringe of Jesus, the flow of her blood stood still", and suddenly she was made clean who before had lived unclean for so long a time. And just as, when she had touched the Lord and Savior, he himself said: "who touched me? For I felt power go out from me" — that power, without doubt, which had healed the woman and made her clean — so it is to be understood that, if anyone touches sin, there goes out from that very sin a certain malignant power, which makes him who has touched it unclean; and this is truly to have touched the unclean thing. By a like reasoning it is to be said also concerning the "carcass" of a man, or the "carcass" of a clean or unclean beast. For he touches the "carcass" of a man who either follows or imitates someone dead in his sins. But if the differences of each are to be examined, let us review them one by one. The carcass of a man, as we said above, we can say to be that which the Apostle says to the Corinthians: "I wrote", he says, "to you in the epistle that you should not mingle with fornicators; not indeed with the fornicators of this world, or the covetous, or the rapacious, or those serving idols; otherwise you would have had to go out of this world. But now I have written to you that you should not mingle, if anyone named a brother is a fornicator, or covetous, or serving idols, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or rapacious — with such a one not even to take food". This, therefore, is to touch the "carcass" of a man: for one to offer himself as a companion, even in food, to one who, having been made a man in Christ, has again died in his sins. For that widow too, of whom the Apostle says, "who, living in delights, is dead while she lives", can be called the "carcass" of a man. But it must also be examined what the carcasses of animals are in the church. If any of the simpler sort, in that they have done nothing of prudence, also wallow in the filth of sins, if anyone follows or touches these with that touch which we expounded above, he has touched the "carcass" of animals. But that the church has animals also, hear how it says in the Psalms: "men and beasts you will save, O Lord". These, therefore, who bear zeal for the word of God and for a rational discipline, are called men; but those who live without such zeal and do not seek out the exercises of knowledge, yet are faithful, are called animals indeed, but clean. For just as there are certain men of God, so there are also certain sheep of God. For it is written that Moses was not a sheep of God, but "a man of God". And Elijah was not a sheep of God, but "a man of God"; for so he himself says: "if I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty". But do you wish to hear of the sheep of God? It is said through the prophet: "my sheep, my sheep are holy, says the Lord". And again the Savior says in the Gospel: "my sheep hear my voice". And I do not think he would have said of men that "men hear my voice". But let him who has "ears to hear" hear these things, how the sheep hear the voice, but the men hear his word. These, therefore, are animals clean indeed on account of Christ, but "carcasses" on account of sin. If anyone "touches" these, that is, if anyone follows another in sin, he will be unclean. And if anyone "touches the carcass" of a man of this kind, that is, of one who, living at first according to reason and exercising himself in the word of God, afterward fell into sin — if anyone follows or imitates him, he touches the "carcass" of a man and will be unclean. But if you touch also "what is caught by a wild beast", you will be unclean. What is the wild beast? Is it a lion or a wolf, which snatches away men or beasts? That, I believe, is the wild beast of which the Apostle Peter says: "your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour. Resist him, strong in faith". And again, of whom does the Apostle Paul say: "for after my departure there will enter in ravening wolves, not sparing the flock". If, therefore, you see one "caught" by these "wild beasts", do not follow him, do not touch him, lest you too be made unclean. There are, besides, also other unclean animals, whose carcass it forbids to be touched. The unclean animals are men who are outside Christ, in whom there is neither reason nor any religion. If, therefore, you see the "carcasses" of all these, that is, their sins, the lawgiver tells you not to touch them, not to defile yourself with them, not to handle them. And these are the uncleannesses which are rightly to be fled. But to shun the touch of a man, or of a dead body, to which rather a religious burial is to be given, these are Jewish and useless fables, "having indeed a form of piety, but denying the power thereof". The first law, therefore, was given concerning uncleannesses, if anyone "was a witness" of some "oath" or fault "and did not disclose it", and through this was himself in a manner made unclean by the fellowship of sin. The second law is that by which it is forbidden to touch "anything unclean and a carcass".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now a third law of this kind is promulgated: "and the soul", it says, "which swears, pronouncing with its lips to do evil or to do good, according to all things whatsoever he shall utter to a man with an oath, and it is hidden from him, and afterward he knows it, and has sinned in some one of these — let him pronounce the sin which he has sinned, and he shall bring for the things in which he has offended, to the Lord, for the sin by which he has sinned, a female of the sheep" and so forth. How indeed, "if I pronounce with my lips or swear to do good" and do not do it, I am guilty of sin, there is no difficulty in showing; but how, "if I swear or pronounce to do evil" and do not do it, I have sinned, it is difficult to assign in word. For it seems absurd, for example, that if in anger I say I am going to kill a man and do not do it, I should, lest I seem to perjure myself or to deceive, be compelled to fulfill the deed which I rashly and unlawfully promised. Let us seek, therefore, what the matter is in which, if we promise to do evil and do not do it, we sin; but if we do it, we are excused from sin, so that the truth of the precept may reasonably stand. As far as it seems to be understood in this place, to do evil is to oppose someone and not to indulge him, that he may do what he wishes. And so we too, when we come to God and vow to serve him in chastity, "pronounce with our lips" and "swear" that we "will chastise our flesh", or do evil to it, "and reduce it into servitude", that we may be able to save the spirit. For so also did he say that he had sworn, who says: "I have sworn, and have determined to keep all your precepts". Since, therefore, it is the voice of the flesh which says: "for I do not do what I will, but what I hate, that I do", without doubt it has been afflicted by the spirit and constrained; "for it resists and fights against the spirit", and, unless evil is done to it, that it may be afflicted and weakened, the spirit cannot say: "when I am weak, then am I strong". If anyone, therefore, "has sworn and pronounced to do evil" to this "flesh which resists and fights against the spirit", and to afflict and mortify it, and has not done it, he is guilty of sin, in that he swore to torment his flesh and to subject it to servitude, and did not do it. But by the same oath he also determines to do good to the spirit. For in that he does evil to the flesh, he does good to the spirit. If anyone, therefore, has sworn this and has not done it, he is made guilty of sin. But do you wish to know that good cannot be done to one of these, unless you do evil to the other? Hear also the Lord himself saying: "I will kill and I will make to live". What does God kill? The flesh, surely. And what does he make to live? The spirit, without doubt. And again in the sequel he says: "I will strike, and I will heal". What does he strike? The flesh. What does he heal? The spirit. To what do these things avail? That he may make you "mortified in the flesh, made alive in the spirit"; lest perchance you too "serve the law of God with the mind, but with the flesh", if it be not mortified, "the law of sin". If, therefore, you have promised this order and have not been able to keep it, hear what the order of the law prescribes: "if he has sinned", it says, "in some one of these, let him pronounce the sin which he has sinned". There is in this something a marvelous secret, that it orders one to "pronounce the sin". For indeed all the things we do are to be pronounced in every manner and brought forth into public. If "we do anything in secret", if we have committed anything in speech alone or even within the secrets of our thoughts, all must needs be published, all brought forth; and brought forth by him who is both the accuser and the instigator of sin. For he himself now instigates us to sin, he himself also, when we have sinned, accuses. If, therefore, in this life we forestall him and are our own accusers, we escape the malice of the devil, our enemy and accuser. For so also elsewhere the prophet says: "do you", he says, "tell your iniquities first, that you may be justified". Does he not evidently show the mystery of which we treat, when he says: "do you tell them first?" — that he may show you that you ought to forestall him who is ready to accuse. "Do you", therefore, he says, "tell them first", lest he forestall you; for if you tell them "first" and offer the sacrifice of repentance according to the things which we said above are to be offered, and hand over your flesh to destruction, "that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord", it will be said to you also that "you have received your evils in your life, but now rest here". But David too speaks in the same spirit in the Psalms and says: "I made known my iniquity, and I did not cover my sin. I said: I will pronounce against myself my injustice, and you forgave the impiety of my heart". You see, therefore, that "to pronounce the sin" merits the remission of sin. For the devil, forestalled in the accusation, will not be able to accuse us further, and, if we are our own accusers, it profits us unto salvation; but if we wait to be accused by the devil, that accusation turns to our punishment; for he will have companions in gehenna, whom he has convicted as companions of his crimes.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Not without cause is a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons, taken in the sacrifices: for they are of equal worth, and it is never said separately, a pair only of pigeons, but a pair of turtledoves, and two young pigeons. The dove is the Holy Spirit. But the Holy Spirit, when he speaks of great and more hidden mysteries, which many cannot receive, is signified by the name of the turtledove — that is, of that bird which dwells always on the ridges of the mountains and on the tops of the trees; but in the valleys, and in the things which reach even to men, the dove is taken.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE SONG OF SONGS, HOMILY 2

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But what shall we say concerning the sacrifice of the "ram" bought "at a price" and "at the price of a shekel of the sanctuary", which is commanded to be offered for the expiation of sin? He is going to be rich who can purge his offenses "at the price of a ram". What these riches are, let us seek. The most wise Solomon teaches us, saying: "the redemption of a man's soul is his own proper riches". Do you hear the words of wisdom, how with necessary properties it declares the force of each word? He speaks of riches suited to "the redemption of the soul", and riches not another's nor common, but "proper riches". By which he shows that there are certain "proper riches" and certain riches not proper. But this the Lord more evidently declared in the Gospels, when he says: "but if you have not been faithful in what is another's, who will give you what is your own?", showing that the riches of the present age are not our own proper, but another's. For they pass away and "pass by like a shadow". But those are the "proper riches" of which the prophet says: "and to you I will gather the riches of the nations". From these riches perhaps also "Abraham was made very rich in gold and silver and cattle" and all furnishings. Do you wish me to show you from what treasuries these riches come down? Hear the Apostle Paul saying of the Lord Jesus Christ: "in whom", he says, "are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden". But in the Gospels too the Lord says that: "the rich scribe brings forth from his treasures new things and old". Of these the Apostle Paul too says that: "in all things you have been made rich in him, in all speech and in all knowledge". From these riches, therefore, which are brought forth from "the treasures of wisdom and knowledge", this "ram" is to be bought by us, which ought to be offered for sins — those, namely, which are committed against the holy things — and it is to be bought at the reckoning of a "shekel of the sanctuary". We already said above that every victim bears a type and image of Christ, much more the ram, which was once substituted by God to be sacrificed in place of Isaac. "At a shekel of the sanctuary", therefore, Christ is to be procured by us, who may dissolve our sins. "The shekel of the sanctuary" holds the form of our faith. For if you offer faith as a price, from Christ, as from a spotless ram given as a victim, you will receive the remission of sins. I feel that in explaining, the greatness of the mysteries surpasses our strength. But although we are not able to discourse of all things, yet we feel that all things are filled with mysteries. And therefore let it suffice to have set down indications for the studious, by which, stirred up, they may arrive at things higher and deeper than these, and understand from which flocks the "bull-calf" is to be sought for a victim, from which sheep the "ram" is to be provided. "For I have", says Jesus, "also other sheep, which are not of this fold; and those too I must bring, that there may be one flock and one shepherd". Let them know also where the turtledoves, where the doves are to be sought. "Your eyes", it says, "are like doves upon the fullness of the waters" (to the "fullness of the waters", therefore, we must hasten, for in these the beauty of the bride is described), "and your neck", it says, "like a turtledove's". In the doves the eyes are praised. For as to what it said: "doves upon the fullness of the waters" — they report that this kind of bird, when it comes to the waters, because there it is wont to suffer the ambushes of the hawk, catches sight of the enemy coming from above, the shadow of the flying one seen in the waters, and by the sharpness of its eyes evades the treachery of the imminent danger. If you too can thus foresee the ambushes of the devil and beware of them, you have offered "doves" as a sacrifice to God. But let those to whom such things are a care seek out also this: from which fields "fine flour" ought to be offered. I judge that it is from the crops of that land which "makes one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold fruit". Let them seek out also — unless it seem more curious than it ought — by which grinders this fine flour is prepared for the sacrifices. And let it not escape them that there are "two who grind", of whom "one shall be taken and the other left". From that mill, therefore, which is to be taken, it will behoove one to offer "fine flour". But the "shekel of the sanctuary" too, which is said to be necessary for the price of the ram — see whence and how it is to be sought out. "Shekel" is the name of the Lord's money, and in many places of the Scriptures the Lord's money is mentioned by various names of appellation. But a certain kind is called "approved", and a certain kind "reprobate". Approved was that money which the householder, "about to go abroad, having called his servants, gave to each according to his own ability". Approved too was that money which is called a "denarius", which was agreed upon with the laborers and given "from the last even to the first". You ought, therefore, to know that there is also other money, reprobate. Hear the prophet saying: "your silver is reprobate". Since, therefore, there is a certain "approved" kind, and a certain "reprobate", therefore the Apostle says, as to "approved money-changers": "proving", he says, "all things, holding fast that which is good". For our Lord Jesus Christ alone is he who can teach you an art of this kind, through which you may know how to discern which money it is that holds the image of the true king, and which is counterfeit and, as is commonly said, struck outside the mint, which has indeed the name of the king, but does not hold the truth of the royal figure. For there are many who have the name of Christ, but do not have the truth of Christ. And on account of this the Apostle says: "for there must be heresies also, that the approved may be made manifest among you". Therefore for that reason also in the present reading the lawgiver, looking wholly to the mystical and spiritual sense, added that this "ram", which is procured for this, that it may be able to absolve sin, is to be procured not with any shekel whatever, that is, not with any money whatever, but with a "shekel of the sanctuary". But if he was not looking to a mystery, what reason did there seem to be that a bought ram should be offered as a victim, and at a fixed price? And it does not suffice to have named the money by "shekel", but he added also "of the holy shekel"? What if someone had in his flocks the best rams and worthy of divine sacrifices? Or what if someone were so poor that he could not have "a shekel of the sanctuary"? Is this the moderation of the lawgiver, that, unless one has a fixed sum of money, his sin cannot be absolved? Which openly, according to the letter indeed, seems absurd, but according to the spiritual understanding it is certain that no one receives the remission of sins unless he has brought whole, approved, and holy faith, through which he may be able to buy the "ram"; whose nature is such that it wipes away the sins of the believer. And this is the "shekel of the sanctuary", an approved, as we said, and sincere faith, that is, where no deceit of perfidy, no perversity of heretical cunning is mixed in, so that we, offering sincere faith, may be washed "by the precious blood of Christ, as of a spotless victim"; through whom is to God the Father almighty, with the Holy Spirit, "glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us now see what law is set forth in offering victims "for sin". "And the Lord spoke", it says, "to Moses, saying: if any soul is hidden and sins unwillingly against the holy things of the Lord, he shall offer for his offense to the Lord a spotless ram of the sheep, at the price of a silver shekel of the sanctuary, for that in which he offended. And what he has sinned against the holy things, he shall restore, and shall add a fifth to it, and shall give it to the priest; and the priest shall make entreaty for him with the ram of the offense, and it shall be forgiven him". In the foregoing laws, which were reported concerning the sacrifices for uncleanness, wherever it said something was to be offered — for example, a sheep or a kid — it added: "but if his hand does not suffice for a kid or a lamb, let him offer a pair of turtledoves or two young doves", and again: "but if it does not suffice even for this, let him offer fine flour". But in this law, where it discourses of the sin which is committed against "the holy things", it substituted no substitution of a lesser victim, a second or a third, but appointed only a "ram" to be offered; nor did it show that the sin which is committed against "the holy things" can be loosed otherwise than if one slaughters a "ram"; and not simply a ram, but a "ram" bought "at a price" and at a fixed "price": "at a shekel", it says, "of the sanctuary". What then? If someone is poor and does not have "a shekel of the sanctuary" wherewith he might purchase a "ram", will his sin not be loosed? Riches, therefore, must be sought by each one, that his sin may be able to be absolved. But if the Lord deigns either to open our eyes to see or the ears of your heart to hear, let us seek out what the meaning of the lawgiver, veiled in mysteries, intends. And first indeed let us see of what sort this very thing is that has been recited, according to the letter. It seems to speak of those in whose hands "holy things" have been committed, that is, the things which have been offered among the Lord's gifts — for example, vows and offerings which are offered in the churches of God for the use of the saints and the ministry of the priests, or which, for the need of the poor, are offered by devout and religious minds. If anyone withdraws any of these by any presumption whatever, the law decrees that, if he is reminded that he has sinned and of his own accord receives compunction of heart — for concerning him who is not compunct of his own accord, but is convicted by another's reproving, the remedy is more difficult — this one, therefore, who has of his own accord remembered his sin, "shall restore", it says, that very thing which he had withdrawn, "and shall add to it a fifth, and shall offer a ram for sin" bought "at the price of a shekel of the sanctuary". As for what it says: "he shall add to it a fifth", the simpler sort suppose it was said thus: that, for example, if five coins were withdrawn, one is added, so that for five he is seen to restore six. But those who have skill in the discipline of numbers reckon the number of this word far otherwise. For in the Greek it does not have that which simply makes "a fifth", but has that which we can indeed say "above a fifth", unless it were said that this is the term for a certain special number among them, by which it is indicated that for five, five others are to be given and one over; so that, for example, it is understood that one who has stolen five coins both restores those very five and five others, with one added over. Yet these things are not straightway to be understood of thefts or frauds, but that also, if anyone has taken money from the holy things for his own necessary uses and has brought delays in restoring it, he is bound by a law of this kind. And this law ought to build up the hearers even according to the letter. For the observance is very useful and necessary, especially to those who preside over ecclesiastical dispensations, that they may know that they must observe more cautiously and diligently with regard to the things offered for the use of the saints.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us too, to whom these things perhaps do not happen, see in what part the discourse of the law may build us up. And I today, though I am a sinner, yet because the dispensation of the Lord's word has been entrusted to me, seem to have the holy things of God committed to me. Nor now for the first time, but often already and long since, do we use this dispensation toward you. If, therefore, anyone of you has received from me the Lord's money and, as is wont to happen, having gone out of the church and been snatched away by the various occupations of the world, has given to oblivion the things he had heard, and has fulfilled no work from the word which he received, this is he who has not restored the money received from the holy things. Wherefore, even at hearing these things, let him call to memory that he has neglected the things which had lately been committed to him in the word of God. Let him, therefore, restore both this which he received and add to it a fifth in that manner which we said before, that is, so that there be twice five and one added over. Let us see, therefore, how these five are restored. The number five is frequently — indeed almost always — taken for the five senses. We ought, therefore, to know that these five can be restored to the holy things in this way: that, if perchance we have presumed to abuse them in secular acts and have expended their use in the things which we have done not according to God, we now restore these very five to holy acts and religious ministries, and add to them five others, which are the senses of the inner man; through which we either, made "clean of heart", "see God", or "have ears to hear" the things which Jesus teaches, or take in that "odor" of which the Apostle says: "for we are the good odor of Christ", or take also that taste of which the prophet says: "taste and see, for the Lord is sweet", or that touch of which John says, that "we have beheld with our eyes and our hands have handled of the word of life". But to all these we add one over, that we may refer all these things to the one God. And let these things be said concerning the restoring of those things which had been taken away from the holy things by any fault whatever.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
If, according to the faith of the divine law, these things which are read to us were spoken by the Lord to Moses, I think that, as being the words of God, they ought to be understood not according to the incapacity of the hearers but according to the majesty of the one speaking. "The Lord," it says, "spoke." What is "the Lord"? Let the Apostle answer you, and learn from him that "the Lord is spirit." But if the word of the Apostle does not suffice for you, hear the Lord himself saying in the Gospels that "God is spirit." If therefore both the Lord and God is "spirit," the things which the spirit speaks we ought to hear spiritually. But I say yet something more: that the things the Lord speaks are to be believed not only spiritual, but even spirit. This I will prove not by my own opinion, but from the Gospels; hear our Lord and Savior saying to his disciples: "the words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life." If therefore we have learned from the voice of the Savior himself that the words which he spoke to the Apostles "are spirit and life," we ought in no way to doubt that the things also which he spoke through Moses are to be believed "spirit and life."

But let us see what these things are, concerning which we ought now, as far as we can, to say something. "And the Lord spoke," it says, "to Moses, saying: whatever soul shall sin, and passing over shall pass over the commandments of the Lord, and shall lie to his neighbor concerning a deposit or a partnership or a robbery, or has done some harm to his neighbor, or has found something lost and lies about it, and swears unjustly about any one of all the things which a man may do, so as to sin in these; and it shall be, when he has sinned and offended, that he shall restore the robbery which he robbed, or the injury which he inflicted, or the deposit which was entrusted to him, or the lost thing which he found, of every matter concerning which he swore unjustly, and he shall restore the principal itself, and shall add a fifth part over and above; and to whomever it belongs, to him he shall render it, on the day when he is convicted." Thus far, for the present, the kinds of sin are set forth, but afterward the purgation of it is commanded through offerings. If any are weak and incapable of the deeper mystery, let them be edified from the letter, and let them know that, if anyone "passing over shall pass over the commandments of the Lord and shall have lied to his neighbor concerning a deposit or a partnership or a robbery," he is declared guilty of an enormous sin. But far be it from the Church of God that I should believe there to be anyone in this assembly of the saints who conducts himself so wretchedly as to deny the "deposit" of his neighbor, or to defile a "partnership" by fraud, or himself to plunder what belongs to another, or to receive things robbed from others and, if they are demanded of him, to swear against his conscience concerning these. Far be it, I say, that I should suppose these things of any of the faithful. For confidently I say concerning you that "you have not so learned Christ," nor have you "been so taught." But neither does the law itself prescribe these things to the holy and faithful. Do you wish to know that these things are not spoken to the holy and just? Hear the Apostle distinguishing: "for the just," he says, "the law is not laid down, but for the unjust and the insubordinate, for the wicked and the defiled, for parricides, matricides," and the like of these. Since therefore the Apostle says the "law" is "imposed" upon men of this kind, let the Church of God — which far be it that it should be stained with crimes of this sort — leave the letter to others and be more holily edified by the spirit.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us therefore now see what is the "deposit" which each of the faithful has received. I think that we have received both our own soul and our body as a deposit from God. And do you wish to see another, greater "deposit" which you have received from God? To your very soul God entrusted "his own image and likeness." This deposit, therefore, must be restored by you as whole as it is established to have been received by you. For if you are merciful, "as your Father in heaven is merciful," the image of God is in you and you preserve the "deposit" whole. If you are perfect, "as your Father also in heaven is perfect," the deposit of the image of God remains in you. And likewise all the rest: if you are devout, if you are just, if holy, if "pure in heart," and if all the things which are present in God by nature subsist in you by imitation, the "deposit" of the divine image is safe with you. But if on the contrary you act, and instead of merciful are cruel, instead of devout impious, instead of kind violent, instead of tranquil turbulent, instead of generous a plunderer, then, having cast away the image of God, you have taken up in yourself the image of the devil and have denied the good "deposit" entrusted to you from on high. Or was this not what the Apostle, under a mystery, was commanding to his chosen disciple Timothy, saying: "O Timothy, guard the good deposit"? I even add this, that we have received Christ the Lord as a "deposit" and have the Holy Spirit as a "deposit." We must therefore take heed that we do not use this holy deposit unholily and, when sins solicit us to consent to them, swear that we have not received a "deposit." For if indeed we have it within us, we cannot consent to sin. But also the rational sense itself, which is in me, has been entrusted to me, that I may use it for the understanding of divine things: talent, memory, judgment, reason, and all the movements which are within me seem to have been entrusted to me by God, that I may use them in those things which the divine law has prescribed. But if the talent, skillful and keen-sighted, be turned to evil arts, and we abuse the things of God in those things which God does not will, this is to forswear the "deposit" and to turn benefits into treachery.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us now see what also is to be understood by "partnership." Do you suppose there is anyone who ought to be admonished according to the letter, lest perchance in a matter of money, or in any other kind of partnership, he deceive his partner by fraud? Of the utmost misery is that soul into which this kind of fraud can still fall. Yet nevertheless, because there is much fragility in man, let us admonish concerning these things also, since not even the Apostle was reluctant to command them. For he says: "let no one overreach his brother in business, since God is the avenger of all these things." But now let us inquire what also is the "partnership of the spirit." Hear the Apostle speaking concerning these very things: "if there is any comfort of love, if any partnership of the spirit, if any bowels of compassion, fulfill my joy." You see how the Apostle Paul understood the law of "partnership." Hear also John, how by one and the same spirit he speaks forth. "And we have partnership," he says, "with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ." And likewise Peter says: "you have been made partakers," he says, "of the divine nature" — which is to say, partners. And again the Apostle Paul says: "for what partnership has light with darkness?" But if there is no "partnership of light with darkness," then light can have "partnership" with light. Therefore, if "partnership with the Father and the Son" and with the Holy Spirit has been given to us, we must take heed that we do not by sinning deny this holy and divine "partnership"; for if we do "the works of darkness," it is certain that we have denied the "partnership" of light. But the Apostle also calls us partners "of the saints," and no wonder; for if it is said that we have "partnership with the Father and the Son," how not also with the "saints" — not only those who "are on earth," but also those who are "in heaven"? For Christ also "by" his "blood pacified things earthly and things heavenly," that he might make things earthly partners of things heavenly. This he clearly indicates where he says that there is joy in heaven "over one sinner doing penance," and again when he says that "those who rise from the dead will be as the angels of God in heaven," and when anew he promises "the kingdoms of the heavens" to men. This "partnership," therefore, whoever separates himself from the union of these by his evil deeds and evil thoughts breaks and denies. After these things it is spoken concerning "robbery"; there are robbers who are evil, and there are also good ones; and the good indeed are those of whom the Savior says that "they seize the kingdom of the heavens." But there are also evil robbers, of whom the prophet says: "and the robbery of the poor is in your houses." The Apostle, however, pronounces abruptly, saying: "do not err, for neither adulterers nor the effeminate nor those who lie with males nor thieves nor the rapacious shall possess the kingdom of God." Yet there is also, according to the spiritual understanding, a way of seizing culpably, just as those seize praiseworthily "the kingdoms of the heavens." To speak, for example: if a man not yet purged from vices, not yet separated from profane and sordid deeds, wishes stealthily to thrust himself into the assembly of the holy and perfect and to hear the discourse in which perfect and mystical things are treated: such a man has not rightly seized the knowledge of secret and perfect things. For it behooves us to remember the precept of the Savior, in which he says that "no one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise both the wineskins will burst and the wine will perish," showing that to a soul not yet renewed, but persisting in the oldness of malice, the secrets of the new mysteries which the world came to know through Christ ought not to be committed.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then the lawgiver adds: "or if he has done any harm to his neighbor, or if he has found something lost." The law of the letter seems to command this, that, if anyone finds what another has lost and it is asked for, he restore it and let it "not perish for him." This too is a useful edification for the hearers. For many think it is without sin if they retain another's property which they have found, and they say: God gave it to me, to whom do I have to render it? Let them learn, therefore, that this sin is like robbery, if anyone does not return what he has found. Yet nevertheless, if the lawgiver had wished only this, which is thought according to the letter, to be understood, he could have said: if he finds what had perished, or what someone had lost. But now, when he says "he has found a perdition," he wished us to understand something more. Those who sin exceedingly are in the Scriptures called "perdition," as we read said in the prophet Ezekiel: "you have become perdition," he says, "and you shall not subsist unto eternal time." There is, therefore, one who by seeking too much "finds perdition," so that, for example, let us say: heretics, to construct and defend their dogmas, search and dispute much in the divine Scriptures, that they may "find perdition." For when they have sought many testimonies by which to buttress the things they perversely hold, they are to be said to have found perdition for themselves. But if perchance one of these, hearing in the church the word of God treated according to the catholic faith, comes to his senses and understands that what he had found is "perdition," "he shall restore," it says, "what he found."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Both this one, who "found perdition," and that one who found "robbery," and also he who "denied the deposit," and everyone whosoever in any part "has harmed the soul of his neighbor and has sworn unjustly": "he shall restore," it says, "the principal itself and shall add a fifth part over and above, and to him whose it is he shall render it," according, at least, to that exposition concerning the adding of the fifth parts which we have already given before. "And he shall offer," it says, "to the Lord a ram of the sheep without blemish, at a price, for that in which he offended; and the priest shall pray for him before the Lord, and it shall be remitted him for the one of all the things which he did and offended in it." We have said above what it is to offer a "ram," and this one bought "at the price of the holy shekel." Now it remains for us to state that difference — that there he placed "the price of the holy shekel," while here he says only "the price" and has designated neither the amount of the price nor the name of the money. For above, where the law was given for a sin which had been committed in "holy things," we said the "holy shekel" was named, and that "shekel" is the name of a coin, as elsewhere it is called "obol," elsewhere "drachma," elsewhere "mina" or "talent" or "small copper coin" or "denarius." Here, therefore, none of these is named, but only "a ram to be offered at a price" is spoken of. For it makes a difference to sin in holy things and to sin outside holy things. Do you wish to see this same distinction elsewhere too? — Hear how in the books of the Kingdoms the priest Eli says to his sons: "for if a man sins against a man, then the priest shall entreat for him; but if he sins against God, who shall entreat for him?" Similarly also John the Apostle says: "there is a sin unto death; I do not say concerning that, that one should pray." Since therefore there is a diversity of sins, we ought to learn from the spiritual law in which sins only a "ram" is to be bought, and in which one is to be purchased "with the holy shekel"; and let us also inquire who these are that sell the rams. I judge them to be those who dispense the rams for sacrifice, who are also those who sell the oil for the lamps of the virgins, concerning whom the prudent ones said to the foolish virgins: "go to those who sell and buy for yourselves." They sell, therefore, either oil for the lights or rams for the sacrifices — who else but the holy prophets and the Apostles, who, when I have sinned, show me and give me counsel how I ought to correct my errors and amend my sins? Isaiah sells me a "ram" for sacrificing for sin, when he says to me as it were from the person of God: "the whole burnt offerings of rams and the fat of lambs and the blood of bulls and of goats I do not want." And a little after he adds: "take away your wickednesses from your souls, from before your eyes; learn to do good, rescue him who suffers injury, judge for the orphan and do justice for the widow; and come, let us dispute, says the Lord. And though your sins be as scarlet, I will whiten them as snow; but though they be as crimson, I will make them white as wool." Daniel too sells me a "ram," when he says that: "there is no place for sacrificing in your sight, that we might find mercy. But in a contrite soul and a spirit of humility may we be received, as if in a multitude of fat lambs; so let our sacrifice be in your sight today." David too sells us the "ram" of sacrifice, when he says: "a sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit, a broken and humbled heart God does not despise." Since therefore each of the prophets, or even of the Apostles, has given counsel to those who transgress, by which they may be able to correct or amend their sin, they will rightly be seen to have sold rams to these for sacrifice. But what price do they take from those who purchase? That, I suppose, the zeal of reading, the vigils of hearing the words of God, and above all I think the most worthy price is obedience, concerning which the Lord says: "I prefer obedience to sacrifice, and a hearing of the word rather than whole burnt offerings."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these things it follows: "and the Lord spoke," it says, "to Moses, saying: command Aaron and his sons, saying: this is the law of the whole burnt offering. This whole burnt offering shall be in its burning upon the altar all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall burn upon it and shall not be extinguished. And the priest shall put on himself the linen tunic, and shall put on the linen undergarment about his body, and shall take away the victim which the fire has consumed, the whole burnt offering, from the altar, and shall place it beside the altar. And he shall strip himself of his robe and be clothed with another robe, and shall cast out the victim which has been burned outside the camp into a clean place. And the fire upon the altar shall burn and shall not be extinguished; and the priest shall burn wood upon it in the morning, and shall heap the whole burnt offering upon it, and shall place upon it the fat of the peace offering; and the fire shall burn always upon the altar and shall not be extinguished." Hear that there ought always to be "fire upon the altar" — you too, if you wish to be a priest of God, as it is written: "for all of you shall be priests of the Lord"; for to you also it is said: "a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a people for possession." If therefore you wish to exercise the priesthood of your soul, let the fire never depart from your altar. This is what the Lord also commanded in the Gospels, that "your loins be girded, and your lamps burning." Let therefore the "fire" of faith and the "lamp" of knowledge be always kindled for you.
