But even the very one who is born, whether of male or female sex, the Scripture pronounces concerning him that he is not "clean from filth, even if his life be of one day." And that you may know there is in this something great, I know not what, and such as has come into the mind of none of the saints, no one out of all the saints is found to have kept a feast day or a great banquet on the day of his birth; no one is found to have had gladness on the birthday of his son or daughter; only sinners rejoice over a nativity of this kind. For we find indeed in the Old Testament Pharaoh, king of Egypt, celebrating the day of his birth with festivity, and in the New Testament Herod. Yet both of them stained the very festivity of their birthday with the shedding of human blood. For the one beheaded "the chief of the bakers," the other the holy prophet John "in prison." But the saints not only do not keep a festivity on the day of their birth, but, filled with the Holy Spirit, they execrate this day. For neither would so great and such a prophet — I mean Jeremiah, who was "sanctified in the womb" of his mother and "consecrated a prophet unto the nations" — have set down anything emptily in books that were to remain forever, unless it contained something secret and full of vast mysteries, when he says: "Cursed be the day in which I was born, and the night in which they said: Behold a male. Cursed be he that told my father, saying: A male is born to thee. Let that man be glad like the cities which the Lord overthrew in fury, and repented not." Does it seem to you that the prophet could have imprecated things so grave and so burdensome, unless he knew there was something in that bodily nativity which both seemed worthy of curses of this kind, and on account of which the lawgiver would arraign so many uncleannesses, upon which he would consequently impose fitting purifications? But it is a long matter, and one for another time, to explain the testimonies which we have taken up from the prophet; because now it is set before us to discourse not on Jeremiah, but on the reading of Leviticus. But Job too, speaking not without the Holy Spirit, "cursed the day of his nativity, saying": "Cursed be the day in which I was born, and the night in which they said: Behold, a male. Let that night be darkness, and let not the Lord seek it again, neither let it come into the days of the year, nor be numbered among the days of the months." But if it does not seem to you that Job speaks these things by the divine and prophetic Spirit, consider from these things which follow; for he adds: "but let him curse it who cursed that day, in which he shall slay the great whale." You see, then, how in the Holy Spirit he foretold concerning "the great whale" which the Lord "was to slay," of which that "whale" of Jonah was a type. Whence the Lord too, who "was to slay" that whale, the devil, says: "For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the whale, so must the Son of man also be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth." But if it pleases you to hear what the other saints also thought concerning that nativity, hear David saying: "In iniquities," he says, "was I conceived, and in sins did my mother bear me," showing that whatever soul is born in the flesh is polluted with the filth "of iniquity and sin"; and that on this account was said what we have already mentioned above, that: "No one is clean from filth, not even if his life be of one day." To these things this too may be added, that it be inquired what is the cause that, whereas the baptism of the Church is given for the remission of sins, according to the observance of the Church baptism is given even to little children; when indeed, if there were nothing in little children that ought to pertain to remission and indulgence, the grace of baptism would seem superfluous. "Whatsoever woman," then, "shall have conceived seed and borne a male, she shall be unclean" "seven days," just as she also who, "according to the days of her purification," is separated from all clean things "for seven days." For she spends seven days "in unclean blood," but "in clean blood thirty and three days." But this is in the nativity of "a male"; for she spends double the days in the nativity of "a female." She begins, then, to be in clean blood from the eighth day, and she is in clean blood for thirty-three days, that is, three decads and three monads. And when she "who has borne" has begun to be in clean blood, then the infant is circumcised: "For on the eighth day," it says, "thou shalt circumcise the flesh of his foreskin." This is the law of the letter, but do you inquire what circumcision the Apostle preaches, which he commands us both to receive and to have. "For we are the circumcision," he says, "who serve God in the spirit." But also what he says in the Psalm: "The sinners are estranged from the womb," consider whether he does not say this concerning those who receive that circumcision by which the Apostle forbids us to be circumcised, and it is then that "the sinners are estranged from the womb," when they are circumcised not in the spirit but in the flesh. For "they who are circumcised in the law are fallen from grace." Therefore "the woman is said to be made "unclean" "who has borne a male with seed conceived"; but "she who shall have borne a female" will not only be unclean, but doubly unclean. For she is written to remain "twice seven days in uncleanness."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But meanwhile she "who has borne a male," "on the eighth day" both the one who is born is circumcised and she is made clean. It is a matter of great labor for these things to happen in this brevity of time, yet, that we may say something in passing, this week may be seen as the time of the present life; for in a week of days the world was completed. In which, so long as we are set in the flesh, we cannot be pure to the point of clarity, unless the eighth day come, that is, unless the time of the age to come be present. On which day, however, he who is a male and has acted manfully is at once purified in the very coming of the age to come, and at once the mother who bore him is made clean; for she will receive the flesh purged of vices out of the resurrection. But if it had nothing virile in itself against sin, but was slack and effeminate in its acts, whose sin is such that it "is not remitted either in this present age or in the age to come": this one passes both one and the other week in his uncleanness, and only at the beginning of the third week arising is he purified from the uncleanness which he contracted by bearing a female. But the victims which are commanded to be applied for uncleanness of this kind are distinguished in two ways. First "a lamb" is commanded to be offered, "a yearling without blemish for a whole burnt offering, and a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin." But a second victim is enjoined: "if," it says, "her hand find not what may suffice for a lamb, she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a whole burnt offering and the other for sin." Whence it also seems marvelous that Mary's offering did not have the first victim, that is, "a yearling lamb," but the second, as one whose "hand did not suffice" for the first. For thus it is written concerning her: there came, it says, her parents, "that they might offer" for him "a victim, according to that which is written in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons." But in this too is shown to be true that which is written, that Christ Jesus, "whereas he was rich, became poor." Therefore for this reason he both chose a poor mother, of whom he would be born, and a poor fatherland, of which it is said: "And thou, Bethlehem, art the least among the thousands of Judah," and the rest. But we are compelled to run through these things briefly and not to examine each thing that is written, since indeed we are hastening to treat also something of the laws of leprosy, which have been recited.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We find, then, that six kinds are set forth concerning the leprosy of men, which six kinds are described in this manner. For either "in the skin of the body there comes a scar and a whitish sign in the skin of his body, the contagion of leprosy." Or "the leprosy flowering shall flower, and shall cover all the skin with the contagion from the head even to his feet." Or the third kind: "in the skin of the flesh there comes an ulcer and it is healed; and in the very place of the ulcer there comes a white scar." Or "in the skin of the flesh there comes a burning of fire, and" after these things "the healed burning shall be shining white, or bright with redness." The fifth kind, "when in a man or a woman there comes on the head or in the beard the contagion of leprosy." But the last kind is written, "when in baldness or in forehead-baldness there comes the contagion of reddish leprosy," which is "leprosy flowering in the baldness or in the forehead-baldness." These things, that we may use brevity of exposition (since indeed it is now our purpose to admonish the hearers briefly from those things which have been recited, nor is there time to examine each single thing to the point of clarity), seem to me to be referred to each single kind of sins, and in these the stains of the soul which befall it from sins are to be beheld. It must be said, then, first, that by these are designated the sins which, set in this life, we commit; of which some can now be cured, but others cannot. But secondly it must be understood that concerning those very sins which pass over with us after this life it is signified that there are in them also certain things so fixed in souls that they cannot be abolished; but that there are others which can receive purgation according to the inspection and judgment of that high priest from whom hidden things cannot lie concealed, and who will dispense the souls of individuals according to this, that he shall have seen in them the stains of leprosy to be either expiable or inexpiable. To gather the differences of this matter from the present reading and to search out, one by one, according to the indication of this Scripture, the things which can move us — this off-the-cuff discourse, as I have already said above, does not permit. For scarcely could these things, digested into many volumes, be composed by those from whom the Lord has drawn away "the veil" over the reading of the Old Testament. We therefore, according to our powers, as much as it is fitting to bring forth into the open, will pursue, with the Apostle Paul opening for us the way of understanding, in which he says "that the law has a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things"; and according to this, that those things which seem to be written concerning oxen in the law he declares are to be attended to not concerning "oxen, for whom God has no care," but concerning the Apostles. In which, surely by consequent reasoning, we are taught that those things too which are written concerning leprosy are a "shadow" having in other things the image of the truth. Therefore let us apply first, if it seems good, the very "shadow" of Scripture, and then let us inquire concerning its truth. In the wounds of bodies, after they have been cured, there remains sometimes the sign of the wound itself, which is called a scar. For scarcely is there anyone who is so cured that no indication of the wound received seems to remain. Pass now from that "shadow of the law" to its truth, and behold how the soul which has received the wound of sin, even if it be cured, nevertheless has "a scar" remaining "in the place of the wound." Which "scar" is seen not only by God, but also by those who have received from him the grace by which they can discern the languors of the soul and distinguish which soul is so cured that it has cast off in every kind the trace of the wound inflicted, and which is indeed cured, but still bears in the very trace of the scar the indications of the old disease. But that there are certain wounds of the soul, Isaiah teaches, saying: "From the feet even to the head there is no wound nor bruise nor inflamed sore," speaking these things without doubt concerning the sins of the people, that there are some to whom a poultice of medicine can still be applied. But that others are sinners to such a degree that not even a cure can be applied to them, the same prophet designates in this manner: "There is," he says, "no poultice to apply, neither oil nor bandages." But that "contrition" and "a sore of pain through chastisement" are imposed on the soul for the sake of cure, Jeremiah teaches, saying: "Thus said the Lord: I have raised up contrition, thy sore is with pain, there is none that judges thy judgment, thou art cured with pain, there is no profit in thee. All thy friends have forgotten thee, nor will they now inquire concerning thee; because I have smitten thee with the wound of an enemy, with strong chastisement, for all thy iniquity, since thy sins are multiplied. Why criest thou out over thy contrition? Thy pain is violent, because of the multitude of thy iniquities thy sins have prevailed and have done these things to thee. Therefore all who devour thee shall be devoured, and all thine enemies shall devour their own flesh; and those who afflicted thee shall be in affliction, and all who devastated thee I will give over to plunder; for I will recall thy health, and from the pain of thy wound I will recall thee, said the Lord." Remember more diligently what you have heard from the prophet said concerning wounds and concerning scars and concerning swellings. For these things will be necessary to us for the exposition of the scars or wounds or other things of this kind which are mentioned in the inspections of leprosy. Yet we will add further what the same Jeremiah in another place mentions, in these words, concerning the wounds of the soul and the cures, in which nevertheless traces of the wounds have remained after the scar has closed over: "Behold, I will bring on its scar, and I will heal them together and manifest to them peace and faith; and I will turn the captivity of Judah and the captivity of Jerusalem." If, then, we have learned sufficiently from the prophet concerning the wounds and scars of souls and the cures and healings which are brought about with God as physician, behold now that soul concerning which God says that "I have brought on its scar." After wounds, without doubt, "he brings on a scar and health." "And I have healed them, and I will manifest to them peace and faith." If, then, after the knowledge and medicine of God, if after "the manifestation of peace and faith" which we have received through Christ, again in that scar some indication of the former sin should rise up, or some sign of the old error be renewed, then "there comes in the skin of" our "body the contagion of leprosy" to be inspected by the high priest, according to those things which the lawgiver has set forth.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the second kind of leprosy is, if "it shall have flowered," it says, "in the skin, so that it covers all the skin of the body from the head even to the feet, throughout all things whatsoever the priest shall have inspected." When, then, it shall have covered over "all the skin of the body," then the priest pronounces him to be "clean" from the contagion. But "on whatsoever day there shall appear in him living color," again "he is judged unclean" through this, that "living color has appeared in him" which he did not have before. Concerning this some even before me have said that "living color" indicates the reason of life which is in man; and while this reason is not yet set in the soul, if any of that sin be done, it is not reckoned, for the reason that he who transgresses seems not yet capable of reason; but when reason has found place and time in him, if he now does anything against reason, he is rightly seen to be culpable. But we, considering more diligently the things which are written, judge that these things are rather to be taken concerning those whose sense has been occupied or oppressed by frenzy or madness or in whatever way, and who act against reason. These, then, are called clean from leprosy, that is, immune from sin, because their act or motion has no sense. But if perchance "living color" of the body "shall appear in him," that is, if the health of his sense be repaired in him, and after these things he does anything against the reason of the right and the just, sin is said to be reckoned to him from that part in which "living color," that is, the sense of living reason in him, "appeared."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The third law concerning lepers is, "when in the skin of the body an ulcer is formed, and in the place of the ulcer a white scar with redness is found." But the cause of an ulcer is when in the body a filthy and noxious humor abounds. So then also in the soul are understood as ulcers those things which boil up from unclean desires or filthy thoughts. And if perchance these have been cured through the grace of faith and the remission of sins, and the soul has been made whole, nevertheless there remains "a scar," and that "scar" does not have a color like that of the body, but is "whiter," it is pronounced to be "leprosy." For a desire is so shining and clear that even to those who look further it shows the indications of the sin residing in it, and perhaps of such a "sin" as is "unto death"; and therefore it is described not only to be "a white scar," but also "reddish." But as to his saying that the scar itself "appears lower," it is certain that a stain of sin of this kind makes the soul lowly and cast down.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The fourth was the law, where it is said that "if in the skin there comes a burning of fire," and after these things, "when the burning has been healed, it itself becomes shining and white with redness, or certainly whitish, and the appearance of it is lower than the rest of the skin": and this he says is "the leprosy which has flowered in the burning." See, then, whether "a burning" is not in every soul whatsoever that receives "the fiery darts of the evil one"; or whether everyone who burns in carnal love is not "scorched by fire." These, then, are the "burnings" and kindlings of "fire." But also he suffers "a burning" who is set ablaze by desire of human glory, and who is inflamed by the heats of anger or fury. But if perchance the soul be cured of these wounds through faith, and after health received, despising him who said: "Behold, thou art now made whole, sin no more, lest something worse befall thee," it begins to bring forth the fruit of the old vice from the scar that had closed over, and the scar is not made even with the skin of the rest of the body, but is "lower" and still retains that color which it had at the time of leprosy: his "leprosy has flowered again in the burning," and therefore he is judged "unclean" by the priest.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The fifth kind of leprosy is when "a contagion is formed on the head or in the beard of a man or a woman, so that the appearance of the contagion itself is lower than the skin of the body; and this is the leprosy of the head or of the beard." See, then, whether it can happen that "leprosy of the head" be thought to be in him who has not "Christ as his head," but some other — for example, Epicurus, who preaches pleasure as the highest good; does not both the head and the beard of such a man seem to you unclean? But also he who, whereas he ought to be a man and to act as one perfect, if perchance he is easily and as a boy overcome by sin, he too must be said to have "leprosy of the beard," because, whereas he ought to overcome the evil one and to proceed with priestly honor, which is designated in the beard, hindered by the vices of adolescence, he suffers "leprosy of the beard." But that in the Scriptures the soul is indicated as a woman which can not so much bring forth the seed of the word as receive it, has often been said; and this soul is designated to have "leprosy" "on the head," if it has the man, who is "the head of the woman," that is, the teacher, polluted and unclean, following either Marcion or Valentinus or someone of that kind.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now the sixth and last kind of leprosy is set down, which "comes in baldness or forehead-baldness"; which things, as far as they are in themselves, are clean. For thus also the law says: "If any one's," it says, "hairs of the head have fallen off, he is bald, he is clean. But if they have fallen off from his forehead, he is forehead-bald, he is clean." And these things are suitably referred to the soul, so that, when it casts off and lays aside those things which are dead by their own nature, it is said to be clean. But after this, if those things which had first been purified shall be seen to sprout up again, filthier and lower than the dignity of purity requires, they will render the soul unclean and leprous.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: From this now, generally, concerning every leper in whom there shall have been "the contagion of leprosy" and it shall appear "lower than the rest of the skin" — for every vice of the soul is lower than its remaining virtues — the law, which "is spiritual," decrees certain such things: "Let his garments," it says, "be unstitched, and his head uncovered, and his mouth covered over." By which it designates that he who is leprous in soul, that is, who is fixed fast with sins, ought not to sew coverings upon himself and to cover over the baseness of sin. For just as he whose "garments are unstitched" bears the baseness of his body naked and uncovered, so ought he who is hedged about with some sins to cover his evils and disgraceful deeds with no sewn-on words, with no veils of excuses; so that he may not become "a whited sepulchre, which outwardly indeed appears beautiful to men, but within is full of the bones of the dead and of all uncleanness." The divine law wills, then, that the sinner not only not sew on "garments," but also not cover "the head," so that, if there is any sin of the head, that is, if anything has been committed against God, if there has been sin against the faith, not even these things be held covered over, but be made public to all, that by the intervention and chastisement of all he may be amended and merit pardon. Yet this leper is commanded to cover only his "mouth": what is this, that he is enjoined to have all the parts of the body naked, and only the "mouth" he is commanded to cover? Is it not plain and set in the open that to him who is in the leprosy of sin speech is closed, the "mouth" is closed to him, so that the confidence of speech and the authority of teaching are shut out? For "to the sinner God said: Why dost thou declare my righteous acts, and takest up my covenant through thy mouth?" Let the sinner, then, have his "mouth" closed, because he who has not taught himself cannot teach another; and therefore he who by acting evilly has lost the freedom of speaking is commanded to cover his "mouth."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "He shall be unclean," it says, "and shall sit separated outside, his dwelling shall be outside the camp." It is clear that every "unclean" one is cast out from the assembly of the good and separated from the company and camps of the saints; and therefore it says that: "his dwelling shall be outside the camp."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if perchance he shall have been made clean, he does not indeed come of his own accord and by himself to the priest, but is offered, it says, by another, nor does he enter into the camp. For neither was it fitting that "on the same day on which he was made clean," before those things which were suitable were done for him, "he should enter into the camp." On account of which "the priest," it says, "shall go out to him outside the camp." For always to him who cannot yet "enter into the camp" there "goes out" that one who can "go out outside the camp," who says: "I went out from God and came into this world." "The priest goes out," then, "to him" and considers whether he now receives health, whether he is being purged from the contagion of leprosy.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But when the priest shall have seen him, he commands that "there be taken two living hens for him who is being made clean, and cedar wood and twisted scarlet and hyssop." It seems to me that here too these "two hens" have a certain likeness of the two goats, of which one is offered to the Lord and the other is sent forth "into the wilderness"; for so here also, of the two hens, one is immolated and the other is let go "into the field." He, then, who is being purged of leprosy gives here too some part which is cast away "into the wilderness"; but the other part is offered to the Lord for him. Yet not yet does this one, who is being purged of leprosy and offers the hens, offer at the altar even that very hen which is offered for him to the Lord, as "turtledoves or doves." For not yet "on the same day" is he who is being purged of leprosy made worthy of the divine altar. On account of which the lawgiver commands that "on the same day on which he is purged, two hens be taken" for his purification. But I think that here too the meaning of that hen is latently held, through whom the purification of the sinner is effected, concerning which it is written: "How often would I have gathered thy children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and thou wouldest not!" Yet he who is purified has need also to be purified through "cedar wood." For it is impossible that the leprosy of sin be able to be purged without the "wood" of the cross, unless there be applied also the "wood" in which the Savior, as the Apostle Paul says, "stripped off the principalities and powers, triumphing over them in the wood." Yet there is joined to the cleansing of this leprosy also "twisted scarlet," and there is associated also "hyssop." The "twisted scarlet" contains the figure of the sacred blood, which was wrung out from his side through the wound of the "lance." "And hyssop." Physicians report that this kind of herb has a nature such that it dilutes and cleanses out, if any of those filths from the corruption of a noxious humor have settled in the breast of men. Whence also necessarily in the cleansing out of sins the figure of this kind of plant has been taken up. But that scarlet has often been taken up for the aids of salvation, we find recounted in the divine volumes, as in the childbearing of Tamar, when, it says, "one first put forth his hand. But the midwife, taking scarlet, bound it on his hand, saying: This one shall come out first." But also Rahab the harlot, when she had received the spies and received from them a pact of safety, they too said to her: "And thou shalt set as a sign a little scarlet cord, and shalt bind it in that window, through which thou didst let us down."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Yet observe also this, that the priest himself is not said to immolate the hen; for not yet is this one, who was a leper, worthy that the priest himself immolate for him. On account of which neither is the blood of the hen offered at the altar, but it says that "the hen shall be slain in an earthen vessel, in which vessel living water has been put," so that both water may be taken up for purification and the fullness of the mystery be completed in "water and blood," which is said "to have gone out from the side" of the Savior, and no less in what John sets down in his epistle and says, that purification is made "in water and blood and spirit." Whence here too I see all these things fulfilled. For there is the "spirit" of that hen which is slain, and the "living water" which is in the vessel, and the "blood" which is poured out over it; not that we should think the grace of baptism is to be repeated through these things, but that every purification of sins, even this which is sought through repentance, has need of the aid of him from whose side "water" proceeded "and blood."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: See, then, how both the "living hen and the cedar wood and the twisted scarlet and the hyssop are dipped in the blood of the young bird and in living water," so that from this, sprinkled and purified from the "water and blood" in which that "hen" too was dipped which is sent forth "into the field," and sprinkled "seven times toward the Lord," he who is being purified may be made clean from all the uncleanness by which he had been possessed from the contagion of leprosy.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But note also this, how, whereas above he had said: "This is the law of the leper; on the day on which he shall have been made clean," now he adds to all these things and says: "and he shall be clean." For if the leprosy having once been cast off he "has been made clean," how shall he still "be clean"? But see that, even if anyone be made clean from sin and be no longer in the act of sin, nevertheless the very traces of the crime committed need purification, both that which we have expounded and, no less, others which are commanded in what follows. For we have observed that to this — that it is written concerning leprosy: "on the day on which he shall have been made clean" — after these things, among the other things which are commanded, it is said a third time: "and he shall be clean," and again at the last it is written: "and he shall be cleansed." Whence it seems to me that there are certain differences even in the purification itself, and, so to say, certain advances of the purgations. For it can be said even of him who ceases from sin: "and he shall be clean," but not immediately will he so be seen as "clean" that he has attained to the summit of purity. Finally he adds to those things which he had said, "on whatsoever day he shall have been made clean": "and the living hen," it says, "shall be sent forth into the field, and he who is being purified shall wash his garments"; but after these things, "he shall shave," it says, "every hair"; and he adds: "and he shall be washed in water"; and after these things is added: "and he shall be clean." For neither is it enough that in the sprinkling he had said: "he shall be clean," unless he had also added these things. This one, then, who is being purified from leprosy, had filthy garments until now, even after the sprinkling, and now he is commanded to "wash" them. Yet these garments do not seem to me to have been in all respects of evil weaving: otherwise he would command them rather to be cast away than washed. In which is shown that his manner of life had neither been in all respects alien from God, nor purely and wholly kept in the Lord. For he would not wash the garments, unless they had been filthy, nor again would he use them once washed, if they had been of a weaving alien in all respects. But as to his being commanded to "shave off every hair," I think that everything whatsoever of dead work that has sprung up in the soul set in sins — for this is now what the hairs are called — he is commanded to cast off. For the sinner, everything that has been born in him whether in counsel or in word or in work, it is expedient, if he truly wishes to be purified, that he shave off and cast away, nor suffer anything to remain. But the holy one ought to keep every hair, and, if it is possible, "iron ought not to go up upon his head," lest it be able to cut off anything of his wise thoughts or words or works. Thence, finally, it is that of Samuel too it is said that "iron did not go up upon his head"; but also of all the Nazarites, who are the righteous, because the righteous man, as it is written, "in all things whatsoever he shall do, they shall prosper, and his leaves shall not fall." Hence also of the disciples of the Lord even "the hairs of the head" are said "to be numbered," that is, all their acts, all their words, all their thoughts are kept with God, because they are righteous, because they are holy. But of the sinners every work, every word, every thought must be cut off. And this is what is said: "that every hair of his body be shaved, and then he shall be clean." But observe also this, that it is not enough for him after purification either to have "washed his garments" or to have "shaved every hair," unless he has also "been washed in water." For he ought to cast off all filths, all uncleanness, not only from his garments, but also from his own body, so that no stain of the extinguished leprosy remain in him. A third time, then, now purified, he is thus at last made worthy "to enter the camp" of the Lord;

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Yet he is not immediately permitted to enter his own house, but it is said that he "remain outside his own house for seven days, and shave every hair of his head and beard and eyebrows"; as though it had not been enough that he had first "shaved every hair," now it is added that he "shave every hair of his head and beard and eyebrows." For the same thing seemed to have been said in that he had said "every hair was to be shaved." But this repetition does not seem to me to be empty. For he wills, after the sinner shall have been made clean, after he shall have received through repentance the remission of sins, to admonish him concerning the purgation "of the head and of the beard and of the eyebrows," as if he were saying to him: "Behold, thou art now made whole," see that thou contract no further guilt of the head. For "the sin of the head" is to think otherwise concerning the divine doctrines than the faith of the Church holds. But in the beard, that he remember that he has laid aside the sins of virile age and be converted and become as an infant. But in the eyebrows he casts down arrogance and bends to the humility of Christ the ill-raised eyebrow. A second time, then, in this manner "every hair of the body is shaved." And just as these things are doubled, so also it does not suffice to have "washed the garments" once in the first purification, but a second time it is enjoined, "that he wash his garments and his body with water," and then a fourth time is added: "and he shall be clean."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But these things happen when he is indeed set within the camp, yet still "outside his own house." For it says after seven days: "on the eighth day he shall take to himself two lambs." Now not another "takes," but he himself "takes to himself." "Two lambs," it says, "without blemish, and one yearling ewe without blemish, and three tenths of fine flour sprinkled with oil, and one cyathus of oil," so that after these things, purified by a fifth purification, he may be brought to completion. Of these "two lambs," then, one indeed is immolated and is said to be "for the trespass": "in the place," it says, "in which he is slain for sin, and where the whole burnt offerings are made, in the holy place." Behold, now he is made worthy to offer sacrifice, who was able to arrive at the fifth purification, and his victim becomes "the holy of holies." But the other lamb is made "a whole burnt offering," in which also "the priest is said to make propitiation for him, that he may be purged." Therefore the first "lamb," which is "for the trespass," seems to me to hold the form of that very virtue which he took up who was in sins, through which he was able to drive away from himself the affection for sinning and to bear penitence for his old evils; but the second "lamb" to hold the figure of that virtue now recovered, through which, all vices being cast off and driven far away, he offered himself whole and wholly to God and stood forth worthy of the divine altars. But the "ewe" which is taken up after the lambs, as far as we are able to conjecture in places so difficult, I think designates the fecundity of him who is converted from sin and has offered himself wholly to God, by which, after all things, he makes use of the offspring of good works and abounds in the fruits of innocence. Into three parts, then, the reasoning of this purification, that is, of conversion from sin, is divided. The first is the victim by which sins are loosed; the second is that by which the soul is converted to God; the third is that of fecundity and of the fruits which he who is said to be converted shows forth in the works of piety. And because these victims are three, therefore he subjoins also that "three measures of the tenth of fine flour" are to be taken up, that everywhere we may understand that purification cannot be made without the mystery of the Trinity. But see that here, in the fifth purification, meal is not taken up, but now this one who is being purified from sins has "fine flour"; "fine flour" is ascribed to him, whence he may now have clean bread, and this is "sprinkled with oil." But also his "oil" is divided to two uses; one, with which "the fine flour is sprinkled," the other, of which the priest takes "the whole measure of the cyathus," as it says. In which, as I perceive, both his bread is made rich for mercy, and the oil, by which the true light and the fire of knowledge are kindled, "is placed upon his head through the hands of the priest." For thus it says: "And the priest," it says, "who makes him clean, shall set him in the sight of the Lord, at the door of the tabernacle of testimony." See that it belongs to the priest to "set" him who is converted from sin, that he may be able to be stable and no longer to waver nor "to be moved by every wind of doctrine." He sets him, then, not only within the camp, but "at the very door of the tabernacle of testimony before the Lord."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And after, according to those things which were said above, the victims are offered for purification, he applies, it says, also "the cyathus of oil" and separates it "before the Lord." "And the priest," it says, "shall take of the blood, and shall put it upon the tip of his right ear and upon the extremity of his right hand and upon the extremity of his right foot." And after these things, it says, "the priest shall take" not the cyathus of oil itself, but "of" it, and "shall pour it out," it says, "into his own left hand, and the priest shall dip his finger in the oil which is in his left hand, and shall sprinkle it seven times before the Lord"; and again: "of that which remains in his left hand, he shall put it upon the right ear of him who is being purified, and upon the extremity of his right hand and upon the extremity of his right foot"; and after these things: "that which shall have been left of the oil, the priest shall put," it says, "from his hand upon the head of him who is being purified." You see how it belongs to the last and highest purification that the ear be purified, that the hearing may be kept pure and clean, and the right hand, that our works may be clean and nothing unclean and filthy be mingled with them. But also the "feet" are to be purified, that they may be directed only to good work and no longer incur the lapses of youth. But "seven times the priest sprinkles toward the Lord of the oil." For after all things which were celebrated for the purified one, after he was converted and reconciled to God, after the victims immolated, it was in the order of things that he should also invite upon him the sevenfold power of the Holy Spirit, according to him who had said: "Render unto me the gladness of thy salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit." Or certainly, since the Lord in the Gospel testifies that the hearts of sinners are besieged by "seven demons," fittingly "seven times before the Lord the priest sprinkles" in the purification, so that the expulsion of the "seven evil spirits" from the heart of the purified one may be declared "by the oil shaken off seven times with the fingers." Thus, then, to those converted from sin purification indeed is given through all those things which we have said above, but the gift of the grace of the spirit is designated through the image of "oil," so that he who is converted from sin may be able not only to obtain purgation, but also to be filled with the Holy Spirit, whereby he may be able both to receive back the former "robe and ring" and, reconciled in all things to the father, to be restored into the place of a son, through our Lord Jesus Christ himself, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The Day of Atonement is needed by all who have sinned, and therefore among the solemnities of the law, which contain the figures of the heavenly mysteries, there is held a certain solemnity which is called the Day of Atonement. This, then, which has now been read out, is the legislation of that very solemnity which, as we have said, is called the Day of Atonement. But let us see first what the content of the letter itself intends, so that, while you pray — provided that you so beseech the Lord that you may deserve to be heard — we may be able to receive the grace of the Spirit, through which we may have strength to explain the mysteries which are contained in the law. "Two sons of Aaron died, Nadab and Abihu, when they offered strange fire at the altar of the Lord." It was necessary that Aaron should be instructed by heavenly teaching in what manner he ought to approach the altar, and by what rite of supplications he might make God propitious, so that he too might not incur those things which his sons had incurred by approaching the altar of God incautiously and improperly, offering "strange fire" and not that which had been divinely given. Therefore, then, concerning these things the law spoke beforehand in this manner: "and the Lord spoke to Moses, after the two sons of Aaron died while they offered strange fire before the Lord, and they died. And the Lord said to Moses: speak to Aaron your brother, that he enter not at every hour into the interior holy place, which is within the veil before the sight of the propitiatory, which is above the ark of testimony, and he shall not die." From which it is shown that, if he should "enter the holy place at every hour" unprepared, not clothed in the priestly garments, nor with the appointed victims prepared, nor with God first made propitious, he shall die. And justly indeed, as one who has not done those things which it is fitting to do before one approaches the altar of God. This word touches all of us, it pertains to all, what the law here speaks; for it has commanded that we should know how we ought to approach the altar of God. For there is an altar upon which we offer our prayers to God, so that we may know how we ought to offer, namely that we should put off the "filthy garments", which is the uncleanness of the flesh, the vices of morals, the defilements of lusts. Or do you not know that to you too, that is, to the whole church of God and to the people of believers, the priesthood has been given? Hear how Peter says of the faithful: "a chosen" he says "race, royal, priestly, a holy nation, a people for acquisition." You have therefore the priesthood, because you are a "priestly nation", and therefore you "ought to offer to God the victim of praise", the victim of prayers, the victim of mercy, the victim of chastity, the victim of righteousness, the victim of holiness. But that you may offer these worthily, you have need of garments that are clean and set apart from the common garments of the rest of men, and you have as necessary the divine fire, not some fire "strange" to God, but that which is given by God to men, of which the Son of God says: "I came to send fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it be kindled." For if we use not this, but another fire and one contrary to this, that fire of him who "transforms himself as an angel of light", we shall without doubt suffer the same things which "Nadab and Abihu" suffered. Therefore the divine command has commanded that Aaron be instructed "not to enter the holy place at every hour" to the altar, but only when he has first done those things which are commanded to be done, lest perchance he die.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But first of all let us show how these things which are written concerning the sacrifices the Apostle says are "figures" and "forms", whose truth is shown in other things, lest perchance the hearers should think that we presume and violently bend the law of God to another sense than that in which it is written — that is, if no Apostolic authority in these things which we assert should go before. Paul therefore, writing to the Hebrews, namely to those who indeed read the law and had these things meditated upon and well known, but had need of understanding as to how one ought to think concerning the sacrifices, says in this manner: "for Jesus entered not into the holy place made with hands, the copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, that he might now appear before the face of God for us." And again he says of the victims: "for this he did once, by offering himself as a victim." But why do we seek testimonies concerning these things one by one? If anyone should review the whole epistle itself written to the Hebrews, and especially that passage where he compares the high priest of the law with the high priest of the promise, of whom it is written: "you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek", he will find how this whole passage of the Apostle shows those things which are written in the law to be "copies" and "forms" of living and true things. It behooves us therefore to seek a high priest who "once in the year", that is, throughout all this present age, offered a sacrifice to God, clothed in a garment whose quality, with the Lord's help, we shall show. "He shall be clothed" it says "with a sanctified linen tunic." Linen arises from the earth; therefore the true high priest Christ is clothed with a "sanctified linen tunic" when he takes on the nature of an earthly body; for it is said of the body that "it is earth and into earth it shall go." Therefore my Lord and Savior, wishing to raise up again this which had gone "into earth", took on an earthly body, that he might carry it, lifted up from the earth, to heaven. And this, which is written in the law, that the high priest be clothed with a "linen tunic", holds the figure of this mystery. But that which he added, "sanctified", is not to be heard idly. For the "tunic" of Christ's flesh was "sanctified"; for it was not conceived from the seed of a man, but generated from the Holy Spirit. "And let there be" it says "linen breeches upon his body." The "breeches" are a garment with which the private parts of the body are wont to be covered and bound up. If therefore you consider that our Savior indeed took on a body and, placed in a body, performed human acts, that is, of eating and drinking and other such things, but did not perform this one work alone which pertains to the private parts of the body, and that his flesh lay open neither to marriage nor to the procreation of children, you will find in what manner he had the sanctified "linen breeches", so that it may truly be said of him that: "our less honorable parts have more abundant honor." Consider, however, also the very garb of the high priest, that what by nature seems less honorable in him, when the linen breeches are put on and bound with a girdle, it is fitting to say of him even according to the letter that: "our less honorable parts have more abundant honorableness." So therefore also everyone who, living in chastity, imitates Christ, ignorant of this one thing alone among human acts, he too is clothed with "sanctified linen breeches" and has surrounded his "less honorable" parts with "more abundant honorableness". Therefore he is clothed with a "sanctified linen tunic" and there are "linen breeches" upon his body. But lest perchance these "breeches", with which the private parts are covered, should slip loose and flow down and reveal and uncover the shamefulness — "for you shall not" it says "make steps to the altar, lest perchance your shamefulness be revealed in them" — lest therefore "your shamefulness be revealed" by the breeches flowing down, "let the breeches", it says, "be bound with a girdle." At a certain time, expounding John the Baptist and elsewhere Jeremiah — since Jeremiah indeed was said to have had a girdle, but John a leathern girdle about his loins — we sufficiently showed how through these things it is declared as an indication that that part of the body was in such men so dead that neither "Levi" nor anyone else was believed to have been "in their loins", but only chastity and pure modesty. Therefore the high priest "is girded with a linen girdle and places a linen turban upon his head", all of linen. What is called the "turban" is a certain ornament which is placed upon the head, which the high priest uses in offering the victims, or the other priests. But each one of us too ought to adorn his head with priestly adornments. For since "the head of every man is Christ", whoever so acts that from his acts he confers glory upon Christ, has adorned his "head, which is Christ". The adornment of the head can be understood in us in another way also. Since indeed that which is in us first and highest and the head of all is the mind, one will cultivate his head to the dignity of the high priest, if he adorns his mind with the disciplines of wisdom. These, therefore, are the things with which the high priest is commanded to be clothed, and "so" at length "to enter the holy place", lest, not having these, he die.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now indeed concerning the victims, some are commanded to be the high priest's own, but others are "to be taken from the people". His own is said to be the "bull-calf", which among animals is more precious and stronger; and the second animal, the "ram", which among sheep is without doubt more precious. But from the people the gifts are commanded to be offered: a "ram" from the leaders and "two goats" from the people; one that is to be sent away "into the wilderness", which is also named "the scapegoat", and one that is to be offered to the Lord. If the whole people of God were holy and all were blessed, there would not be made two lots over the goats, and one indeed bear the lot to be sent away "into the wilderness", but the other to be offered "to the Lord", but there would be one lot and one victim to the Lord alone. But now, since in the multitude of those who approach the Lord there are some who are the Lord's, but others who ought to be sent "to the wilderness", that is, who deserve to be cast off and separated from the victim of the Lord: therefore the part of the victim which is offered by the people, that is, one single goat, is immolated to the Lord, but the other is cast off and sent away "into the wilderness" and is named "the scapegoat". Yet the lot falls upon both, and that one indeed which is sent "into the wilderness" is said to "bear upon itself the sins of the sons of Israel and their injustices and their iniquities". For it is not that "goat" which is made "the Lord's lot", but that one whose lot it is to be sent away "into the wilderness", that is said to bear them away, according to that, I believe, which is written: "I gave Egypt as your exchange, and Ethiopia, and Soënen for you, from the time that you became honorable in my sight." Therefore the sins of those who have done penance, and of those who have forsaken malice, are taken upon their own heads by those who have been made in the lot of that goat which is sent away "into the wilderness", who have made themselves worthy of such a ministry or of a lot of this kind. And, as it were on the contrary, that also which was said will be fitted to these: "to him who has, it shall be given." For just as to him who has righteous deeds, more is added to him, so also to him who has sins to such a degree that he is found "in the lot of the scapegoat", of that one which is sent forth "into the wilderness", there shall be added to him those things which are wiped away from the saints, so that in them too may be fulfilled that which is written: "but from him who has not, even that which he has shall be taken from him", that it may be added to him "who has many minas" of sins. But since he who is "in the lot of the Lord" bears his hope not in the present age but in the future, and he whose "lot is the Lord" "dies daily": therefore he indeed upon whom "the lot of the Lord" has fallen is slaughtered and dies, that by his blood he may purify the people of God; but that one who has fallen into the contrary lot is not worthy to die, because he who is "in the lot of the Lord" "is not of this world", but that one "is of this world" and "the world loves that which is its own". Therefore he is not killed, nor is he worthy to be slaughtered at the altar of God, nor does his blood deserve to be poured out "at the base of the altar".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But that which we say concerning the lot, let not the hearer take it as though some such lot is meant as is wont to be conducted among men by chance and not by judgment. "The Lord's lot" is to be taken as though one should say the choice of the Lord or the portion of the Lord, and again the lot of that one which is sent "into the wilderness" is to be taken as that portion which, for its own unworthiness, is spurned and cast off by the Lord. For indeed the very word "scapegoat" contains the signification of one cast off and rejected. From which we can also understand this, for example: an evil thought ascends into your heart, a desire of another man's wife or of a neighbor's possession; understand at once that this is of "the lot of the scapegoat", cast it off immediately and expel it from your heart. How do you cast it off? If you have with you the hand of the "ready man", that is, if divine reading is in your hands and the precepts of God are held before your eyes, then truly you will be found "ready" to cast off and drive back those things which are of the foreign lot. But also if anger ascends into your heart, if jealousy, if envy, if malice "to supplant a brother", be "ready" to cast them off and to expel and send them "into the wilderness". But if there ascends into your heart "to think the things which are of God", concerning mercy, concerning righteousness, concerning piety, concerning peace, these are of "the Lord's lot", these are offered at the altar, these the high priest receives, and in these he reconciles God to you. Therefore, then, he too who "casts out" that one in which "the lot of the scapegoat" is, that is, evil thoughts, evil desires, is not a slothful man nor one occupied with worldly business, but is "ready" and prompt and vigilant; who, even if he should seem to become soiled by the fact that he has touched something unclean, will "wash his garments" at once and "will be clean". Which we can understand, as far as it pertains to each one of us, that according to the moral sense "the ready man" is the very reason which is within us, through which there is for us discernment of good and evil, which, even if it seems to become soiled while it examines and handles the very things which are evil, yet if it casts them off and expels them from the heart and drives them far away, then, as it were purified and cleansed by better thoughts, the rational mind will be seen to be "clean". Nor indeed should you marvel that we have drawn to the person of the Savior also this one who casts out the goat and expels it "into the wilderness", because he is said to "wash his garments" and "be made clean" on account of that which we read said in the prophet concerning the Lord, as we said above: "and I saw Jesus the great priest clothed in filthy garments". But if indeed this is piously understood to be said on account of the assumption of the flesh, here too, in the washing of the garments, the same figure can be preserved.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Yet since the word of God is rich and, according to the judgment of Solomon, is to be "inscribed upon the heart" not simply, but doubly and "triply," let us try even now to add some things to those which were spoken a while ago according to our strength, that we may show how, "in a type of things to come," here too one goat was offered to the Lord as a victim and the other was sent away "alive." Hear in the Gospels Pilate saying to the priests and the people of the Jews: "Which of the two do you wish that I release to you, Jesus who is called Christ, or Barabbas?" Then all the people cried out that he should release "Barabbas," but hand Jesus over to death. Behold, you have the goat which was sent away "alive into the wilderness," bearing with itself the sins of the people that cried out and said: "Crucify, crucify!" This, then, is the goat sent away "alive into the wilderness," and the other is the goat that was offered to the Lord as a victim to make propitiation for sins, and made true propitiation for the peoples who believe in him. And if you should also inquire this — who it is that led this goat "into the wilderness," so that it might be proved in him also that he was washed and made clean — Pilate himself can be taken as the "man made ready." For he was the judge of that very nation, who by his sentence sent him out "into the wilderness." But hear how he was washed and made clean. When he said to the people, "Do you wish that I release to you Jesus, who is called Christ?" and all the people had cried out, saying, "If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar," then, it says, "Pilate called for water and washed his hands before the people, saying: I am clean from the blood of this man; see you to it." So then he will be seen, with his hands washed, to have been made clean.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us see after these things what the things are which the high priest does: "and he shall take" it says "a censer full of coals of fire from the altar which is before the Lord". We read also in Isaiah that the prophet is purged by fire through "one of the seraphim, which was sent to him, when it took with tongs one coal from those which were upon the altar, and touched the lips of the prophet and said": "behold, I have taken away your iniquities". To me these things seem to be mystical and to indicate this, that to each one, according to that in which he sins, if he is worthy to be purified, coals are applied to his members. For since the prophet here says: "I have unclean lips, and I dwell also in the midst of a people having unclean lips", therefore the "coal taken up with the tongs" by the seraph purges his lips, in which alone he professes himself not to be clean. From which it is shown that only as far as the word was his sin found, but that in deed or work he had sinned in nothing; otherwise he would have said that I have an unclean body, or I have unclean eyes, if he had sinned in desiring the things of others, and he would have said: I have unclean hands, if he had polluted them with wicked works. But now, since perhaps in speech alone he was conscious to himself of that fault of which the Lord says: "that even for an idle word you shall render account in the day of judgment", because it is difficult even for the perfect to avoid the fault of speech, therefore the prophet too needed only the purging of the lips. But we, if each one should return to his own conscience, I know not whether we can excuse any member of the body which does not need the fire. And the prophet indeed, since he was clean from all things, therefore deserved that "one of the seraphim should be sent to him" to purge his lips alone. But we — I fear lest we deserve the fire not for single members, but for the whole body. For when the eyes are wanton either through illicit desires or through diabolical spectacles, what else do they gather for themselves but fire? When the ears are not turned away from vain hearing and the disparagements of neighbors, when the hands are by no means restrained from slaughter and from robberies and plunderings, when "the feet are swift to shed blood", and when we hand over the body not to the Lord but to fornication, what else do we hand over but the whole body "into gehenna"? But when these things are said, they are held in contempt. Why? Because faith is lacking. Otherwise, if it were said to you today that the judge of the age wishes tomorrow to burn you alive, and, having heard these things, if there were free to you the space of one day, how much would you do? How and to whom would you run about? How humble, how mourning and squalid would you wander? Would you not pour out all your money upon those by whose intercession you believed you could escape? Would you not make all that you possess the redemption of your soul? But if anyone should try to delay or hinder you, would you not say: let all perish for my safety and let nothing remain, only that I may live? Why would you do this? Because you would not doubt about that, whereas about this you do doubt. And therefore the Lord well says: "do you think, when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith upon the earth?". And why do I speak of certain and undoubted dangers? Only if a case is to be pleaded before an earthly judge, which seems to have some fear from the laws, is not the watch kept with all vigils, are not the services of advocates and patrons prepared, even if the danger be doubtful or even only the fear of a mark of disgrace or the reckoning of a loss? Why do we not believe that we shall all stand "before the tribunal of Christ, that each one may carry back the proper things of the body, according as he has done, whether good or evil"? If we believed these things wholly, there would be for us, according to that which is written, "the redemption of a man's soul his riches". But whence can we either feel or believe or understand these things, when we do not even assemble to hear these very things? For which of you, when the Scriptures are read out, lends an ear? God threatens through the prophet, and indeed in great wrath: "I will send a famine upon the earth, not a famine of bread nor a thirst of water, but a famine of hearing the word of God". But now God has not sent "famine" upon his church nor "thirst for hearing the word of God". For we have "the living bread which came down from heaven", we have "the living water leaping up into eternal life". Why do we in the time of fruitfulness kill ourselves with hunger and thirst? It belongs to a slothful and idle soul to suffer want in the abundance of all things. Have you not heard from the divine Scriptures that "there is a struggle" among men "of the flesh against the spirit and of the spirit against the flesh"? And do you not know that, if you nourish the flesh alone and foster it with frequent softness and a continual flow of delights, it will necessarily grow insolent "against the spirit" and become "stronger" than it? And if this happen, without doubt it, having reduced the spirit into its dominion, will compel it to obey its laws and vices. But if you come frequently to church, apply your ear to the divine letters, take the explanation of the heavenly commandments, then, just as the flesh by foods and delights, so the spirit will grow strong by the divine words and senses, and, made more robust, will compel the flesh to obey it and to comply with its laws. Therefore the nourishments of the spirit are divine reading, assiduous prayers, the word of teaching. By these foods it is nourished, by these it grows strong, by these it is made victorious. Because you do not do this, do not complain of the infirmity of the flesh, do not say that we wish but cannot; we wish to live continently, but we are deceived by the fragility of the flesh and are assailed by its goads. You give goads to your flesh, you arm it against your spirit and make it powerful, when you sate it with meats, flood it with too much wine, caress it with every softness and nourish it to enticements. Or do you not know that this building of the church cannot be constructed from leprous stones? Hear what the Apostle says: "a little leaven corrupts the whole lump. Purge out therefore the old leaven, that you may be a new mixture". But let us return to what was proposed.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And he shall take" it says "a censer full of coals". Not all are purged by that fire which is taken "from the altar". Aaron is purged by that fire, and Isaiah, and any who are like them; but others, who are not such, among whom I reckon even myself, we shall be purged by another fire — I fear lest by that of which it is written: "a river of fire ran before him". That "fire" is not "from the altar". The fire which is "from the altar" is the fire of the Lord; but that which is outside the altar is not the Lord's, but is the proper fire of each one of those who sin, of which it is said: "their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished". That "fire" therefore is of those very ones who kindled it, as also elsewhere it is written: "walk in your fire and in the flame which you have kindled for yourselves". But to Isaiah not his own fire is applied, but the fire of the altar, which will "purge around" his "lips", and to this one, of whom it is said: "and he shall take a censer full of coals of fire from the altar which is before the Lord, and shall fill his hands with the finely-composed incense". This indeed our Lord did more fully. For he "filled his hands with the fine incense", of which it is written: "let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight". He "filled" therefore "his hands" with the holy works which he wrought for the human race. But why is it called "the incense of composition"? Because there is not one kind of works, but from righteousness and from piety, from continence, from prudence and from all virtues of this kind is composed that by which God is pleased. But also that which he added, "fine", we understand not idly. For he does not wish that he who tends toward perfection understand the word of God grossly and carnally, but in these things seek out the fine and subtle sense, so that, if perchance he hear it written: "you shall not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treads", he may understand these things not of oxen — "for neither is God concerned about oxen" — but as said of the Apostles. But also if anyone can expound the reason concerning the providence of God, which is most fine and most subtle, that one is said to "fill his hand with fine incense". Which therefore of us is so prompt and "ready" that, when the high priest is about to enter into the "holy of holies", he offers "the fine incense of composition"? For it is necessary that we each offer something to the tabernacle of God, something also to the priestly garments, but something too which through the hands of the high priest may ascend to God himself through "an odor of sweetness". Therefore our high priest, the Lord and Savior, opens his hands and wishes to receive from each one of us "the fine incense of composition"; it is necessary for us to seek out the kinds of incense. "Frankincense" must be sought by us, and not just any frankincense, but the clear kind. The high priest does not wish to receive from you anything obscure or filthy; he seeks the clear. But he also demands from you "galbanum", whose nature is such that by the vehemence of its odor it drives away noxious serpents. He seeks also "stacte"; for he wishes our words or works to be strained and refined. He seeks also "onyx", with which as with a kind of shield his animal is covered and remains unharmed. So he wishes you too to be protected with "the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the fiery darts of the evil one". Yet all these things he wishes to be composed by you, nothing disordered, nothing restless, nothing unseemly, but he wishes this, "that all our things be done in a composed and honorable manner". Therefore even now our true "high priest" Christ stands and wishes "his hands" to be filled "with the fine composed incense", and from each church which is under heaven he considers what is offered, how wholly and diligently it composes its "incense", how "fine" it makes it, that is, how each one of us orders his works and how he examines the sense and words of the Scriptures with spiritual explanation. Nor are the ministries of the angels lacking from offices of this kind; "for the angels of God ascend and descend to the Son of Man", they search out and act carefully as to what they may find in each one of us which they may offer to God. They see and scrutinize the mind of each one of us, whether it has anything such, whether it thinks anything so holy that it may deserve to be offered to God. They gaze and consider whether any of us, from those things which are said in the church, "is pricked in heart" and turns his mind to penance, whether, having heard these things, he thinks to "correct his ways" and "to forget the past and to prepare himself for the future", at least according to that most impious Ahab, of whom the Lord says: "have you seen how the heart of Ahab was pricked?". But in all these things, what shall I say of those who neither hear these things with their ears nor receive them in their heart? What hope of compunction in them, what suspicion of conversion, what way of amendment? For if we doubt even about those who hear, what do we hope for concerning those who hear not at all? But let us use the words of the Lord and say: "let those who have ears of hearing, hear", and let those who hear know that it is written that "when you are converted and groan, then you shall be saved and shall know where you were". And if "you first tell your sins", I will hear you as a holy people. Have you heard how, even if you were a sinner, only if you are converted and desist from sin, you are now called holy? Nothing therefore is to be despaired of for those who are pricked in heart and are converted to the Lord; for the malice of transgressions does not surpass the goodness of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Therefore the high priest "takes a censer full of coals of fire from the altar which is before the Lord, and fills his hand with the fine incense of composition and carries it into the interior of the veil". Let us understand first what the history designates, and then let us inquire what the spiritual sense holds. Twofold is the house of the tabernacle of testimony or of the temple of the Lord. The first is that in which is the "altar of the whole burnt offerings", which is stirred up with perpetual fires, in which house it is lawful for the priests alone to stand and to celebrate the rites and ministries of the sacrifices, and to neither the Levites nor anyone else besides is access granted. But the second house is the interior one, separated from this only by a "veil". Within which veil are the "ark of the testament" and the "propitiatory", upon which the "two cherubim" are set, and the "altar of incense" is placed. Into this house "once in the year" whoever was first, the high priest, having first offered the victims of atonement of which we have expounded above, would enter, having both hands filled, one with the "censer of coals" and the other with the "incense of composition", so that, when he had entered, at once, the incense being placed upon the coals, the "smoke" might ascend and fill the whole house, so that a "cloud" of incense might veil the sight of the holy things which the entry of the high priest had revealed. If the ancient custom of the sacrifices has been made clear to you, let us see what these things also contain according to the mystical reason. You have heard of two houses, one as it were visible and open to the priests, the other as it were invisible and inaccessible: except the one high priest alone, the rest are outside. This first house I think can be understood to be this in which we now are, placed in the flesh, the church, in which the priests minister "at the altar of the whole burnt offerings", that fire being kindled of which Jesus said: "I came to send fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it be kindled". And I do not wish you to marvel that this house lies open to the priests alone. For all, whoever have been anointed with the ointment of the sacred chrism, have been made priests, as Peter too says to the whole church: "but you are a chosen race, royal, priestly, a holy nation". You are therefore a "priestly race" and therefore you approach the holy things. But each one of us too has in himself his own whole burnt offering, and he himself kindles the altar of his own whole burnt offering, that it may always burn. If I renounce all that I possess and take up my cross and follow Christ, I have offered a whole burnt offering at the altar of God; or "if I hand over my body that I may burn, having charity", and attain the glory of martyrdom, I have offered myself as a whole burnt offering at the altar of God. If I love my brothers so that "I lay down my soul for my brothers", if "I contend for righteousness, for truth, even unto death", I have offered a whole burnt offering at the altar of God. If I "mortify" my "members" from every desire of the flesh, if "the world is crucified to me and I to the world", I have offered a whole burnt offering at the altar of God and I myself am made the priest of my own victim. In this way therefore the priesthood is carried out in the first house and the victims are offered, and from this house the high priest, clothed with sanctified garments, sets forth and enters into the interior of the veil, as we have already above set down the words of Paul saying: "not into the holy place made with hands, but into heaven itself Jesus penetrated" it says, "and appears before the face of God for us". Therefore the place of heaven and the very seat of God is designated through the figure and image of the interior house. But behold with wonder the order of the sacred things. The high priest, entering into the holy of holies, carries with him fire from this altar and takes "incense" from this house. But also the garments with which he is clothed he took from this place. Do you think my Lord, the true high priest, will deign to receive from me too some part of "the fine incense of composition", which he may carry with him to the Father? Do you think he finds in me some little spark and my whole burnt offering burning, so that he may deign from it to "fill his censer with coals" and in these to offer to God the Father "an odor of sweetness"? Blessed is he in whom he has found the coals of his whole burnt offering so living and so fiery that he judges them fit to be placed upon the "altar of incense". Blessed is he in whose heart he has found a sense so subtle, so fine and so spiritual, and so composed with the diverse sweetness of the virtues, that he may deign to "fill his hands" from it and to offer to God the Father the sweet odor of his understanding. But on the contrary, unhappy is the soul whose fire of faith is extinguished and whose heat of charity grows cold; to whom, when our heavenly high priest has come seeking from it living and burning coals upon which he may offer incense to the Father, he finds in it dry ashes and cold embers. Such are all who withdraw themselves and make themselves far from the word of God, lest, hearing the divine discourses, they be kindled to faith, grow warm to charity, be set afire to mercy. Do you wish that I show you how from the words of the Holy Spirit fire goes forth and kindles the hearts of believers? Hear David saying in the psalm: "the word of the Lord set him on fire". And again it is written in the Gospel, after the Lord had spoken to Cleopas: "was not our heart" it says "burning within us, when he opened to us the Scriptures?". Whence therefore will you burn? Whence will "coals of fire" be found in you, who are never set on fire by the word of the Lord, never inflamed by the words of the Holy Spirit? Hear also elsewhere David himself saying: "my heart grew warm within me, and in my meditation a fire blazes forth". Whence do you grow warm? Whence is fire kindled in you, who never meditate on the divine words — nay, what is more unhappy, you grow warm at the spectacles of the circus, you grow warm at the contests of horses, at the struggle of athletes? And that fire is not from the altar of the Lord, but is that which is called "strange fire", and you heard a little above that those who offered "strange fire before the Lord were extinguished". You grow warm also when wrath fills you and when fury inflames you, you burn at times and are tossed by the fires of carnal love and most shameful lust. But all that is "strange fire" and contrary to God; and whoever kindles it will without doubt bear the lot of Nadab and Abihu.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The divine word therefore says: "and he shall place incense upon the fire in the sight of the Lord, and the smoke of the incense shall cover the propitiatory which is over the testimonies, and he shall not die. And he shall take of the blood of the bull-calf and shall sprinkle with his finger upon the propitiatory toward the east". The rite indeed of atonement for men among the ancients, which was made to God, he has taught how it should be celebrated; but you, who have come to Christ, the true high priest, who by his blood made God propitious to you and reconciled you to the Father, do not cling to the blood of the flesh; but learn rather the blood of the Word, and hear him saying to you: "this is my blood, which shall be poured out for you for the remission of sins". He who is imbued with the mysteries knows both the flesh and the blood of the Word of God. Let us not therefore linger in these things which are both known to those who know and cannot lie open to those who are ignorant. But that he "sprinkles toward the east", do not take it idly. From the east atonement comes to you; for thence is the man whose "name is East", who was made "the mediator of God and men". You are invited therefore by this always to look "toward the east", whence rises for you the "sun of righteousness", whence light is born for you; so that you may never "walk in darkness" nor that last day catch you in darkness; lest the night and gloom of ignorance steal upon you, but that you may always dwell in the light of knowledge, always have the day of faith, always obtain the light of charity and peace.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these things the Scripture adds: "and there shall not be" it says "a man, when the high priest enters within the interior veil in the tabernacle of testimony". How "shall there not be a man"? I understand it thus, that he who has been able to follow Christ and to penetrate with him the interior tabernacle and to ascend the heights of the heavens, shall now "not be a man", but according to his own word shall be "as an angel of God". Or perhaps even that word will be fulfilled concerning him which the Lord himself said: "I said, you are gods and sons of the Most High, all of you". Whether therefore, made spiritual, he becomes one spirit with the Lord, or through the glory of the resurrection passes into the order of angels, rightly he will now "not be a man"; but each one himself provides this for himself, that he either exceed the appellation of man or be reckoned within the condition of this word.
