For if man, made "in the beginning", had kept that which the Scripture says to him: "behold, I have placed before your eyes death and life, choose life", if he had done this, never indeed would the mortal condition have held the human race. But since, forsaking life, he followed death, he was made man; and not only man, but also earth, on account of which he is said also "to return into earth". I inquire, however, what this death is, which he says: "I have placed before your eyes". For concerning life there is no doubt that God indicates himself, who said: "I am the truth and the life". What therefore is this death contrary to life, which God "placed before" our "eyes"? I think it is said concerning that one of whom Paul says: "the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed". This therefore is the "enemy", the devil, who indeed was first placed "before the eyes", but "shall be destroyed last". But he had been placed "before the eyes" not that we should follow him, but that we should avoid him. Whence I also judge that the human soul in itself can be called neither mortal nor immortal. But if it attains life, it will be immortal from participation in life (for death does not fall upon life); but if, turning itself away from life, it draws participation in death, it makes itself to be mortal. And therefore the prophet says: "the soul which sins, it itself shall die", although we understand its death not as the destruction of its substance, but that this very thing, that it is estranged and exiled from God, who is the true life, is to be believed to be death for it. Let there be therefore "no participation of righteousness with iniquity", "no fellowship of light to darkness, no concord of Christ with Belial". If we have chosen life, we shall live always, "death shall not have dominion over us", and there shall be fulfilled in us the word of the Lord who said: "he who believes in me, even though he die, shall live". Let us therefore choose life, let us choose light, that "we may walk honorably in the day", so that we too, following Jesus within the veil of the interior tabernacle, may now be not as mortal men, but as immortal angels, when our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who is "the way and the truth and the life", shall have "destroyed the last enemy, death", "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages! Amen".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us see who this is who receives that one whose "lot has become the scapegoat's", that he may cast him "into the wilderness". "A man" it says "ready shall receive the goat which has come into his lot, upon whom the lot of the scapegoat has fallen, and shall lead him away into the wilderness." The end of this lot is the "wilderness", that is, a deserted place, deserted of virtues, deserted of God, deserted of righteousness, deserted of Christ, deserted of every good. And so upon each of us too awaits one lot of the two. For either, acting well, we are "the Lord's lot", or, acting badly, our lot leads us "to the wilderness". Do you wish that I show you evidently how those two lots are always at work and each one of us becomes either "the Lord's lot" or "the scapegoat's" or "the wilderness'"? Consider in the Gospels that "rich man" living "splendidly" and luxuriously, and "Lazarus lying at his gate full of sores and desiring to be filled with the crumbs which fell from the rich man's table", of whom the end of each is designated: "Lazarus died" it says "and was carried away by the angels into the bosom of Abraham. But likewise also the rich man, and he was carried away into the place of torment." You notice evidently the places of each lot, distinct. See also who they are who carry away; "angels", it says, who are always "ready" to carry away. For they are ministers of God appointed for this very thing, to fulfill the lot which you have prepared for yourself. For if you have lived well, if you have "broken your bread to the hungry from the soul", clothed the naked, "judged a right judgment", resisted the unjust against his injustice, and have not placed your counsel with those who prepare snares for the innocent, you will make your "lot the Lord". But if you serve lust, if you are "a lover of pleasure more than of God", if you "love the world", if you have not hated malice, you have made your "lot the scapegoat's", that you may be carried away "into the wilderness" by the hands of the minister of God who is appointed for this very thing by God; and therefore he is called "ready", because he blushes at the person of no one, neither of the rich, nor of the powerful, nor of the king, nor of the priest. But do you wish to know that the things which are said pertain to us? These animals which receive those lots are not unclean nor foreign to the altars of God, but are clean and such as are wont to be offered in sacrifices; so that you may know that these hold the figure not of those who are outside the faith, but of those who are in the faith; for the goat is a clean animal and consecrated to the divine altars. And you therefore, through the grace of baptism, have been consecrated to the altars of God and have been made a clean animal. But if you do not keep that command of the Lord which he said: "behold, you have been made whole; now sin no more, lest something worse befall you", but, when you were clean, have again stained yourself with the defilement of sin and have declined from virtue to lust, from purity to uncleanness, by your own fault, though you were a clean animal, you have handed yourself over "to the lot of the scapegoat and the wilderness".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Perhaps in another way also "the man ready" and clean, who "leads away that one whose lot has come, into the wilderness", and by that very act by which he leads him out, as one who has touched something unclean, is said to "wash his garments" at evening and to be clean — perhaps even our Lord and Savior himself may be understood, in that part in which he took on the "garments" of our nature, that is, of flesh and blood, which he "washed at evening"; on account of which also the prophet had long ago said of him: "and I saw Jesus the great priest, clothed in filthy garments, and the devil standing at his right hand, that he might contradict him." Therefore he "washed his robe in wine" — that is, in his own blood — "at evening", and was made "clean". And thence perhaps it was that after the resurrection he said to Mary, who wished to hold his feet: "do not touch me." But do you wish to see yet another form of the two lots? Consider those two who at the time of his cross "hung as robbers, one at his right and one at his left"; and see that one who confessed the Lord was made "the Lord's lot" and was carried away without delay "to paradise", but that other one, "blaspheming", was made "the scapegoat's lot", who would be carried away "into the wilderness" of hell. But also in that which is said, that "he affixed to his cross the contrary principalities and powers and triumphed over them", he fulfilled "the lot of the scapegoat" in these, and as "a man ready" he "led them away into the wilderness". Finally, in the Gospel also the Lord says: "that when the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, it goes through deserted places seeking rest and finds it not." So therefore our Savior too can be understood as "a man ready", who made his Church indeed "the Lord's lot" and consecrated it to the divine altar, but made "the scapegoat's lot" the contrary powers, "the spirits of wickedness and the rulers of this world of these shadows", whom, as the Apostle says, "with power he led as captives, triumphing over them in himself". "He led them as captives." Whither did he "lead them", unless "to the wilderness", to deserted places? For just as to that one who confessed he opened the gates of paradise by saying: "today you shall be with me in paradise", and through this gave to all who believe and confess an entrance for entering, which formerly, when Adam sinned, he had shut up — for who else could move aside "the flaming, turning sword which was set to guard the tree of life" and the doors of paradise? Who else could bend the "cherubim" watching with ever-wakeful guard, unless he alone to whom "all power in heaven and on earth has been given"? — so, I say, as none other but he himself could do these things, thus "the principalities and powers" and "the rulers of the world", which the Apostle enumerates, none other could "triumph over" and lead away "into the wilderness" of hell except he alone who said: "be confident, I have overcome the world." Therefore it was necessary that my Lord and Savior not only be born a man among men, but also descend to the lower regions, that he might lead down "the lot of the scapegoat", as "a man ready", "into the wilderness" of hell, and, returning thence with the work accomplished, ascend to the Father, and there more fully be purified at that heavenly altar, so that he might endow the pledge of our flesh, which he had carried up with himself, with perpetual purity. This therefore is the true Day of Atonement, when God was made propitious to men; as the Apostle also says: "since God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself"; and again he says of Christ: "making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things which are in heaven or the things which are on earth". It is commanded therefore in the law that on the day of atonement all the people should "humble" their "soul". How the people "humbles" its "soul", he himself says: "the days will come" it says "when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then they shall fast in those days". Many feast days therefore are kept according to the law. There is a certain solemn day in the "first month", there is also another in the "second". But even in the "first month" there is one solemnity of the Passover, another of the unleavened bread, although the solemnity of "the unleavened bread" seems joined to "the Passover"; for the beginning of the unleavened bread is joined to the end of the Passover. But the Passover is called that day alone on which "the lamb" is killed, but the rest are called the days of the unleavened bread; for thus he says: "you shall make the solemnity of the unleavened bread for seven days". This therefore is the first solemnity. After these, "when" it says "you have reaped your harvest, and have gathered the produce from your field, you shall make a feast day of the first of your fruits". This day is after seven weeks of the Passover, that is, Pentecost, when it is also commanded to be said: "and you shall cleanse the holy things from my house". After these, in the seventh month other solemnities are kept. On the "first day of the month" the new moon of the trumpets, as it says in the Psalm: "sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month". But on the "tenth day of the seventh month" is this solemnity of atonement. "On this" day alone the high priest is clothed with all the priestly garments, then he is clothed with "manifestation and truth", then he enters into those inaccessible places, whither it is permitted to approach only "once in the year", that is, into the "holy of holies". For "once in the year" the high priest, leaving the people, enters into that place where is the "propitiatory" and above the "propitiatory" the "cherubim", where is also the "ark of testimony" and the "altar of incense", whither it is lawful for no one to enter except the high priest alone. If therefore I consider my true "high priest" the Lord "Jesus" Christ, how, placed in the flesh, he was with the people throughout the whole year, that year of which he himself says: "he sent me to evangelize the poor and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of remission", I observe how "once in" that "year", on the day of atonement, he enters into the "holy of holies", that is, when, the dispensation being fulfilled, he "penetrates the heavens" and enters to the Father, that he may make him propitious to the human race and entreat for all who believe in him. This atonement of his, by which he makes the Father propitious to men, the Apostle John, knowing it, says: "these things I say, little children, that we may not sin. But even if we have sinned, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he himself is the atonement for our sins". But Paul likewise makes mention of this atonement, when he says of Christ: "whom God set forth as a propitiatory in his own blood through faith". Therefore the Day of Atonement remains for us until the sun sets, that is, until the world receives its end. For we stand "before the doors" awaiting our high priest who tarries within the "holy of holies", that is, "with the Father", and entreats "for the sins" of those "who await him", not entreating for the sins of all. For he does not entreat for those who come into the lot of that goat which is sent forth "into the desert". He entreats only for those "who are the Lord's lot", who await him "before the doors", who "depart not from the temple, being free for fasting and prayers". Or do you think, you who scarcely on feast days come to church and are not intent on hearing the divine words nor give effort to fulfilling the commandments, that "the Lord's lot" can come upon you? Yet we desire that, having heard even these things, you may give effort not only to hear the words of God in church, but also to be exercised in your homes and to "meditate on the law of the Lord day and night"; for there too Christ is, and everywhere he is present to those who seek him. For therefore it is commanded in the law that we "meditate" on it when we go on the way, and when we sit in the house, and when we lie in bed, and when we rise up; and this is truly to "await before the doors" the "high priest" who tarries within the "holy of holies" and to be made into "the Lord's lot".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
We indeed, who are of the Church, rightly receive Moses and read his writings, understanding this about him: that he is a prophet, and that, by God's revealing to him, he wrote down in symbols and figures and allegorical forms the mysteries to come, which we teach to have been fulfilled in their own time. But whoever does not receive in him a meaning of this kind, whether he be one of the Jews or even one of our own, cannot show him to be a prophet at all; for how will he prove him a prophet, whose letters he asserts to be commonplace, aware of nothing future and containing no hidden mystery? And so, as this man who thinks in this way reads these things, the divine word rebukes him and says: "Do you suppose you understand what you read?" There is, then, the law, and all the things that are in the law, according to the Apostle's judgment, "imposed until the time of correction"; and just as those whose craft it is to make figures out of bronze and to cast statues, before they produce the true work of bronze or of silver or of gold, first form a model of clay after the likeness of the image to come — which model is indeed necessary, but only until the principal work is completed; and when that work has been finished for the sake of which the model of clay had been formed, its use is no longer sought — something of this sort understand also in those things which were either written or done "in a type" and figure of things to come in the law and the prophets. For the very craftsman and author of all things came, and transferred "the law, which had the shadow of the good things to come," to "the very image of the realities." But lest perhaps the things we say seem hard to be proved to you, examine them one by one. Formerly there was Jerusalem, that great royal city, where a most famous temple had been built to God. But after he came who was the true temple of God and said of the temple of his body, "Destroy this temple," and who began to open the mysteries of the "heavenly Jerusalem": that earthly one was destroyed, where the "heavenly" one appeared, and in that temple there did not remain "stone upon stone," from the time that the flesh of Christ became the true temple of God. Formerly there was a high priest purifying the people "with the blood of bulls and goats"; but from the time the true high priest came, who by his own blood should sanctify believers, that former high priest is nowhere, nor has any place been left to him. Formerly there was an altar, and sacrifices were celebrated; but when the true lamb came, who "offered himself as a victim to God," all those things, as set in place for a time, ceased. Does it not then seem to you that, according to the figure which we set forth above, they were as it were forms fashioned out of clay, through which the images of the truth were expressed? And so, finally, the divine dispensation took care that both the city itself and the temple and all those things should alike be overthrown; lest perhaps one still "a little one and a suckling in the faith," if he saw those things standing firm, while he gazes astonished at the rite of the sacrifices and the order of the ministrations, should be carried away by the very sight of the diverse forms. But God, providing for our weakness and willing to multiply his Church, caused all those things to be overthrown and utterly removed, so that, without any hesitation, once those had ceased, we might believe these to be true, for which the type had gone before in those.

Hence now some things must also be said by us to those who think that, according to the command of the law, the fast of the Jews too must be fasted by them; and first of all I will use the words of Paul, who says that, if anyone wishes to keep some one thing of the observances of the law, "he is bound to perform the whole law." Whoever therefore observes these fasts, let him also go up "three times in the year" to Jerusalem, that "he may appear before the temple of the Lord," that he may present himself to the priest; let him seek out the altar, which has been turned to dust; let him offer victims with no high priest standing by. For it is written that the people, fasting, should offer "two goats" as a sacrifice, over which lots must be cast, so that one of these should become "the Lord's lot" and be offered as a victim to the Lord, but of the other the lot should be that it be sent away "alive into the wilderness," the one that also has upon itself the sins of the people. All these things you must fulfill accordingly, you who wish to observe the fast according to the precept of the law; concerning which things a discussion was indeed made by us, as far as we could, in the earlier debate.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Ours, therefore — that is, we who do not "serve the shadow and the copy," but the truth — this is the Day of Atonement for us, on which the remission of sins has been given to us, when "Christ our Passover has been sacrificed." How then, having come to know the truth, "do we turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements of this world, to which you wish to be enslaved anew from the beginning, observing days and months and seasons and years?" Hear how the prophet too rejects a fast of this kind and says: "This is not the fast I have chosen, says the Lord, nor a day for a man to humble his soul." You, if you wish to fast according to Christ and "to humble your soul," every time of the whole year lies open to you; nay rather, have all the days of your whole life "for humbling your soul," if indeed you "have learned" from the Lord our Savior "that he is meek and humble of heart." When, then, is there for you no day of humiliation, you who follow Christ, who is "humble of heart" and the master of humility? You, therefore, if you wish to fast, fast according to the precept of the Gospel, and observe in your fasts the evangelical laws, in which the Savior commands concerning fasts in this manner: "But you, if you fast, anoint your head and wash your face." And if you inquire how you should "wash your face," the Apostle Paul teaches how you may "with unveiled face behold the glory of the Lord, transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord." "Anoint" also "your head," but take care that it be not with the oil of sin: for "let not the oil of the sinner make fat your head." But "anoint your head" with the oil of exultation, with the "oil of gladness," with the oil of mercy, so that, according to the command of wisdom, "mercy and faith may not forsake you." For this reason also the Apostle Paul, wishing to draw us away from these visible and earthly things and to lift up our minds and senses to the heavenly, cries out and says: "If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth." Does he not openly say to you: do not seek Jerusalem on the earth, nor the observances of the law, nor the fast of the Jews, but the fast of Christ? For, fasting, you ought to approach your high priest Christ, who assuredly is not to be sought on the earth, but in the heavens, and through him you ought to offer a victim to God. Do you wish me to show you still further what kind of fast you ought to fast? Fast from every sin, take no food of malice, partake of no feasts of pleasure, grow warm with no wine of luxury. Fast from evil deeds, abstain from evil words, hold yourself back from the worst thoughts. Do not touch the stolen loaves of perverse doctrine. Do not covet the deceitful foods of philosophy, which would seduce you from the truth. Such a fast is pleasing to God. But "to abstain from foods which God has created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful," and to do this together with those who crucified Christ, cannot be acceptable to God. The Pharisees too were once indignant at the Lord, because his disciples did not fast. To whom he replied that: "the sons of the bridegroom cannot fast, as long as the bridegroom is with them." Let those, then, fast who have lost the bridegroom; we, having the bridegroom with us, cannot fast. Yet we do not say this in order to loosen the reins of Christian abstinence; for we have the days of Lent consecrated to fasts, we have the fourth and sixth day of the week, on which we solemnly fast. There is indeed for the Christian the liberty of fasting through all time, not by the superstition of observance, but by the virtue of self-restraint. For how is chastity kept uncorrupted among them unless it is supported by the tighter aids of self-restraint? How do they devote effort to the Scriptures, how do they apply themselves to knowledge and wisdom? Is it not through the self-restraint of the belly and the throat? How does anyone "make himself a eunuch for the kingdom of heaven," unless he cuts back the abundance of foods, unless he employs abstinence as his handmaid? This, then, is the Christian's reason for fasting. But there is still another, a religious one, whose praise is proclaimed even in the writings of certain of the Apostles. For we find in a certain little book a saying of the Apostles: "Blessed is he who also fasts for this, that he may feed the poor." This man's fast is very acceptable with God and truly worthy enough; for he imitates him "who laid down his soul for his brethren." Why, then, do we mix new garments with old rags? Why do we put new wine into old wineskins? "The old things have passed away: behold, all things have been made new," through Christ our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The troubling utterance is the following: "The soul of all flesh is the blood" — behold an extremely difficult passage, which has shaken those who did not understand it! … According to my measure of understanding, and with prayer for help in the knowledge of the Divine utterances … I have observed that incorporeal things are given the same names as corporeal things, and thus corporeal things are related to the outer man, while those bearing the same names as the corporeal are related to the inner man. Scripture says that in man there are two. … Therefore in each of us there are two men. Why does the Holy Scripture say that the soul of all flesh is the blood? This is a difficult question. Just as the outer man is homonymous with the inner one, so also with respect to the parts of the body. One may say that each part of the body of the outer man is homonymous with the corresponding part of the inner man. … And so, everything that is in the sentient flesh you can find also in the inner man. Do not doubt, then, also concerning the blood, homonymous with the sentient blood, which, like the other parts of the body, the inner man has. It is precisely this blood of which the soul of the sinner is deprived.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Recently there was recited in the ears of the Church the word of God saying: "Be holy, for I too am holy, the Lord your God". What this name "holy" intends for itself, and what it signifies in the divine Scriptures, must be inquired into more diligently, so that, when we have learned the force of the word, we may also be able to fulfill its work. Let us therefore gather from the divine Scriptures those things over which we find the word "holy" said, and we discover that not only human beings, but even dumb animals are called "holy"; we find also that "vessels" of the ministry are called "holy", and that vestments are said to be "holy", and no less the places which are set within cities or suburbs and assigned to the priests. Among the dumb animals indeed, the "firstborn" of oxen or of flocks are commanded by the law to be sanctified to the Lord, and it is said: do not, it says, perform any work with them, since they are sanctified to the Lord. Concerning vessels, however, when in the tabernacle of testimony the vessels of the ministry, the "censers" or "bowls" or the rest of this kind, are called "holy" "vessels". Concerning vestments too, when the "robe" of the high priest Aaron and the "linen tunic" and the rest of the vestments of this kind are said to be "holy". If therefore we consider in what sense all these have been named "holy", we shall perceive how we too ought to give effort, that we may be able to be holy. A firstborn ox has been born to me: it is not permitted to me to employ it for common work; for it is consecrated to the Lord, and therefore it is called holy. We understand therefore from this dumb animal how the law, that which it wills to be holy, commands to serve no other but the Lord alone. Again, the "cups" or "bowls" which it calls holy are those which are never commanded to go out from the temple, but always to be in the holy places, nor to serve any human uses whatsoever. Similarly also the "vestments" which are named "holy" are not commanded to serve for use within the house of the high priest, but to be in the temple and never at all to be carried out from there, but to be consecrated to this alone, that the high priest ministering to God with them may be clothed, and that they may always be in the temple; while for the other common uses he uses common garments. Similarly also with these "cups and bowls" which are called "holy", it is not permitted to use them for human and common uses, but only for the divine ministries. But if you have understood how an animal or a vessel or a vestment is called holy, understand consequently that by these observances and laws a human being too is called holy. For if anyone has devoted himself to God, if anyone has entangled himself in no worldly affairs, "that he may please him to whom he has proved himself"; if anyone is separated and set apart from the rest of human beings who live carnally and are bound to mundane affairs, not "seeking the things that are upon the earth, but those which are in the heavens", that one is rightly called holy. For as long as he is mingled with the "crowds" and is tossed about in the multitude of those who are fluctuating, and is not free for God alone, set apart from the common throng, he cannot be holy. For concerning those what shall we say, who hasten with the crowds of the gentiles to the spectacles and defile their own sight and hearing with shameless words and deeds? It is not ours to pronounce concerning such. For they themselves can perceive and see what portion they have chosen for themselves. You therefore, who hear these things, to whom the divine law is recited, whom the very word of God itself addresses, saying: "Be holy, for I too am holy, the Lord your God", understand wisely the things that are said, so that you may be blessed when you have done them. For this is what is said to you: "Separate yourself" from every one, not only every man, but even "from a brother walking disorderly and not according to" the apostolic "traditions". "Be separated", indeed, "you who carry the vessels of the Lord, and go out from the midst of them, says the Lord". "Separate yourself" from earthly deeds, "separate yourself" from the concupiscence of the world: "for everything that is in the world", according to the Apostle, "is the concupiscence of the flesh and the concupiscence of the eyes, which is not from God". When therefore you have separated yourself from all these things, devote yourself to God as a firstborn calf; let sin not work through you, nor let malice impose a yoke upon you, but be set aside and set apart, given over only to priestly uses like a firstborn animal. Be set apart and severed, like holy "bowls" and holy "censers" free only for the uses of the temple and for the ministry of God. Separate yourself and set yourself aside from all pollution of sin, and be set aside and set apart within the temple of God like the holy garments of the high priest. For that man is set apart and separated within the temple of God, "who meditates in the law of God day and night" and who "greatly desires his commandments". "Be holy" therefore, "says the Lord, for I too am holy". What is: "for I too am holy"? Just as I, he says, am set apart and far separated from all things that are adored or worshiped whether on earth or in heaven; just as I exceed every creature and am set apart from all things that have been made by me: so also be you set apart from all who are not holy nor dedicated to God. But we say that one is set apart not by places, but by deeds, and not by regions, but by manners of life. Finally, the very word which in the Greek language is spoken, ἅγιος, signifies as it were to be outside the earth. For whoever shall have consecrated himself to God will rightly be seen to be outside the earth and outside the world; for he too is able to say, walking upon the earth: "we have our manner of life in the heavens". Solomon also in the Proverbs says: "it is a snare for a strong man hastily to sanctify something of his own; for after he has vowed it, it comes about that he repents". And this indeed is what he says, lest perhaps anyone, "when he gathers fruit from the threshing floor or wine from the presses", and has said: I wish to offer only so much to the Church, or to supply only so much for the use of the poor or of pilgrims; if afterward he presumes to take something for his own uses out of that measure which he vowed, he has now not presumed upon his own fruits, but has violated the holy things of God. And therefore "it is a snare for the strong man to sanctify something", that is, to vow it to God and afterward, led by repentance, to recall to his own uses those things which he had consecrated. But even if we consecrate and offer ourselves to God, or also if we vow others, let us observe this "snare", lest perhaps, after we have vowed ourselves to God, we again be subjected to human uses or deeds. Now each one vows himself, for example, as the Nazirites used to do, consecrating themselves to the temple of God for three or four or however many years it pleased, so that they might always be free there, observing those things which are written concerning the Nazirites; that they should nourish the hair of the head, and "no iron should go up upon their head" throughout the whole time of their vow, that they should not touch wine nor anything "from the vine", and whatever else the profession of the vow had embraced. But someone also vows another to God, as Hannah did with Samuel; for before he was born, she offered him to God, saying: "and I will give him to the Lord, given all the days of his life". From all which it is clear how each one of us, who wishes to be holy, ought to consecrate himself to God and to be occupied besides with no affairs or deeds which pertain in no way to God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The second commandment is like it, since it is the love of a human being who was made according to the image of God, and perhaps also according to his likeness. But in the exposition of the commandment which is set down concerning the love of one's neighbor, these things also must be said. For, according to what is said in the tenth Psalm, "he who loves iniquity hates his own soul", and according to what is said in Proverbs, "he who rejects discipline hates himself", it is manifest that no one who loves iniquity loves his neighbor as himself, since he does not even love himself; and no one who rejects discipline loves his neighbor as himself, seeing that he does not love his very self either. And thus it comes about that he who "loves iniquity", and "hates his own soul", cannot keep the second commandment. Likewise also "he who rejects discipline" loves some sin; and therefore he too who rejects any word of God's discipline "hates his own soul".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these things it is written: "keep", it says, "my precepts and do them, I am the Lord", and to these it added: "a man, a man, if he shall have cursed his father or his mother, let him die"; and after many things which it commanded, to which it also appended the penalties of transgression, it adds in the conclusion: "and keep all my precepts and my justifications and my judgments". Whence it seems to me consequent to inquire what is indicated in these single terms. For my part, according to what I have been able to observe, a "precept" or "commandment" is that which, for example, in the decalogue is said: "you shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery"; for this only is enjoined, and the penalty of the deed is not appended. But now indeed the same things are repeated, but with penalties added; for it is said: "a man, a man, whoever shall have committed adultery with the wife of a man and the wife of his neighbor, by death let him die, he who commits adultery and she who is committed adultery with. And if anyone shall have slept with the wife of his father, he has uncovered the shame of his father, by death let them die, both are guilty". Concerning these, however, precepts had already been given in the former passages, but what penalty awaited the one not observing them had not been appended. Now therefore the same things are repeated and the penalty of each single sin is decreed; and therefore these are rightly called justifications and "judgments", by which he who sins is judged to receive what is just. But observe the order of divine wisdom; it did not straightway establish the penalties together with the first precepts. For it wills that you should keep the precepts of the Father not from fear of punishment, but from love of piety; but if you have despised them, the punishment is now enjoined not so much upon a man as upon a despiser. First, therefore, you are summoned by kindness as a son: "for I have said: you are gods, and sons of the Most High, all of you". But if you are unwilling to be an obedient son, you are struck as a despiser, like a slave. After these things it says: "and if anyone shall have slept with his daughter-in-law, by death let them both die, they have done impiety, they are guilty". And these laws or these precepts he had given above without penalties; for he had said: "the shame of your daughter-in-law you shall not lay bare, since she is the wife of your son, you shall not reveal her shame", and all that follows. And this passage he appended in a like manner there without punishments, but here with various kinds of punishments. In which place I recall that word which the blessed Apostle Paul, writing to the Hebrews, says: "anyone making void the law of Moses dies without any mercy under two or three witnesses; of how much greater punishments will he be thought worthy, who shall have trodden underfoot the Son of God and reckoned the blood of the testament polluted, in which he was sanctified, and done contumely to the Spirit of grace?". But for what cause I have made mention of this scripture, listen. According to the law the adulterer or "adulteress by death used to die", nor could they say: we seek repentance and we implore pardon. There was no place for tears, nor was any faculty of amendment conceded, but it was necessary in every way that he be punished who had incurred the law. And this was observed also in each and every crime to which the penalty of death was appended. Among Christians, however, if adultery has been committed, it is not commanded that the "adulterer or adulteress" be punished with bodily destruction, nor is power given to the bishop of the Church to condemn the adulterer to present death, as then according to the law was done by the elders of the people. What then? Shall we say that the law of Moses is cruel which commands the "adulterer or adulteress" to be punished, and that the gospel of Christ, through indulgence, dissolves its hearers into what is worse? It is not so. For this reason we set forth above the word of Paul saying: "by how much more is he worthy of worse punishments who shall have trodden underfoot the Son of God" and so forth. Hear therefore how neither then was the law cruel, nor now does the gospel seem dissolute on account of the largess of pardon, but in both the kindness of God is maintained by a different dispensation. This, that according to the law, for example, the "adulterer or adulteress" was punished with present death: on account of this very thing, that he bore the penalty of his sin and paid the worthy punishments of the crime committed, what will there be after this that threatens vengeance to their souls, if they have transgressed in nothing else, if there is no other sin which condemns them, but they committed this alone and only then, when they were punished and bore the punishment of the law for this? "The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing"; for they received back their sin and the penalty of the crime is consumed. And therefore this kind of precept is found to be not cruel, as the heretics assert, accusing the law of God and denying that anything of humanity is contained in it, but full of mercy, for the reason that through it the people would be purged from their sins rather than condemned. But now the penalty is not inflicted upon the body, nor does the purgation of sin come about through bodily punishment, but through repentance; whether one bears this worthily, so as to be able to merit pardon for it, see to it. For there are many who neither are inclined to this nor seek the refuge of repentance, but, when they have fallen, are unwilling to rise up any further; for they delight to wallow in that mire in which they have stuck. We, nevertheless, do not forget that precept in which it is said: "with what measure you shall have measured, with the same it will be measured back to you". For we say also to God: "you have given us the bread of tears, and have given us to drink in tears in measure". There are therefore those "sins" which are said to be "unto death"; whence it is also consequent that, as often as anyone commits such a sin, so often does he die. For that there are many deaths of sin the Apostle Paul also signifies, when he says: "who has snatched us from so many deaths and will snatch us; in whom we hope that he will still snatch us". What deaths then does he here commemorate as many, except those of sins? For if he were not saying this concerning the deaths of sins, Paul would seem, according to his own opinion, to be going to remain immortal from this common death, who says: "he has snatched us from so many deaths and will snatch us; in whom we hope that he will still snatch us". For if he both "has snatched" and "will snatch", there will never be a time when he dies, whom the Lord will always "snatch". And therefore, according to those things which we have discussed, it must be seen whether perhaps it is even somewhat graver for us, who are by no means punished with this death for a common sin, than for those whom the sentence of the law condemned bodily; because for us vengeance is stored up for the future, while for them the paid punishments of their deed used to absolve them. But even if there is anyone who perhaps has been overtaken in sins of this kind, being now admonished by the word of God let him flee for aid to repentance, so that, if he has committed it once, he may not do it a second time, or, if he has already been overtaken a second time or even a third, he may add no further. For with a just judge there is a moderation of the penalty, not only according to the quality, but also according to the quantity.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But when we wish to examine the very letter of the words as given by Matthew, "He that speaks evil of father or mother, let him die the death," consider whether it was taken from the place where it was written, "Whoso strikes his father or mother, let him die the death; and he that speaks evil of father or mother, let him die the death." For such are the exact words taken from the law with regard to the two commandments; but Matthew has quoted them in part and in an abridged form, and not in the very words.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 11.9

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Among the other sins therefore which are punished with death, the divine law reports that also "he who shall have cursed his father or mother, by death let him die". The name of father is a great mystery, and the name of mother is a hidden reverence. Your father according to the spirit is God; your mother is the "heavenly Jerusalem". Learn these things from prophetic and apostolic testimonies. This same Moses writes in the canticle: "is not this same one your father who acquired you and possessed you?". But the Apostle says concerning the "heavenly Jerusalem" that: "she is free", he says, "who is the mother of us all". First, therefore, your father is God, who begot your spirit, who also says: "I have begotten sons and exalted them". But James the Apostle also says: "let us obey the father of spirits and we shall live". Secondly, your father is the father of the flesh, by whose ministry you were born in the flesh and came into this world, who carried you "in his loins"; as it is said of Levi that: "he was still in the loins of Abraham, when Melchizedek met him", "returning from the slaughter of the kings, and he blessed him, and received tithes from him". Because therefore the name of father is so sacred and so venerable, for that reason "he who shall have cursed his father or mother, by death let him die". Similar things are to be reckoned also concerning the mother, by whose labor, by whose care, by whose ministry you were both born and nourished. And you ought, according to the Apostle, to render an equal thanks to your parents. For if you dishonor your carnal father, the contumely of this returns to the "father of spirits"; and if you do injury to your carnal mother, the injury overflows to that "mother, the heavenly Jerusalem". So too a slave, if he is irreverent to his master, hurls contumely through this bodily master upon the "Lord of majesty"; for that Lord imposed his own name upon this carnal master. And therefore in no manner is a contention to be had against father or mother, not even in word, nor contradiction to be stirred up. He is a father, she is a mother; as seems good to them, let them act, let them do, let them say; they themselves shall know. However much of obedience we render, we do not yet repay the return of the grace by which we were begotten, by which we were carried, by which we drew in the light, by which we were nourished, perhaps also educated and instructed in honorable arts. And by them perhaps as authors we came to know God and came to the Church of God and heard the word of the divine law. On account of all these things, therefore, "whoever shall have cursed his father or mother, by death let him die". But if these things are decreed concerning bodily parents, what will they do who provoke God the Father with cursing voices? who deny that he is the founder of the world, or who, understanding with unworthy senses the "heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all", drag the prophetic sayings to the condition of some earthly city? It is good therefore to take care that we never venerate either the carnal father or the heavenly one with less than worthy honor, and likewise the mother; to observe also every commandment which commends to us modesty and chastity, so that neither in the present life may we be liable to death according to the law, nor according to the spiritual law may the future penalty of eternal fire await us; from which may our Lord Jesus Christ grant to us all to flee and escape, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Everyone who is a priest among men is small and slight in comparison with that priest of whom God said: "you are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek". But he is the "great priest" who is able "to penetrate the heavens" and to pass beyond the whole of creation and to ascend to him who "dwells in light inaccessible", the God and Father of the universe. For this reason the one too who among the Jews was called the "great priest" did indeed enter into the holy places, but ones made by hand, built of stones; he did not ascend into heaven nor was he able to stand before the "Father of lights". But because he was fulfilling the shadow and image of these things, therefore also he bore the name of "great priest" by way of shadow and image. Whence the Jews too, precisely through that by which they ought to have been nearest to the faith — because among them a certain foreshadowing and image of the truth had shone beforehand — while they thought the types were the truth, rejected the truth itself as though it were a lie. But we, who receive the "great priest", ought to understand how he himself is truly the "great priest". Truly he is the "great priest", who forgives sins not "by the blood of bulls and goats" but "by his own blood". Since therefore we have come to know who the "great priest" is, and we confess that the things which are written in the law about the "great priest" are written about the Savior — whom the treatise above showed to be truly the "great priest" — let us now see what those things are which the law writes about him in the prophetic spirit.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And the great priest" it says "from among his brethren, upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured and who has his hands perfected to put on the holy vestments, shall not take the mitre from his head, shall not rend his garments, and shall not go in to any dead soul; in his father or in his mother he shall not be defiled, and he shall not go out from the holy places and shall not pollute the name which is hallowed, the name of God upon him, because the holy oil of the anointing of his God is upon him; I am the Lord. He shall take to wife a virgin of his own kindred. But a widow and one cast out and one defiled and a harlot, these he shall not take; but he shall take to wife a virgin of his own kindred; and he shall not defile his seed among his people; I am the Lord, who sanctify him". Among the Jews too there was indeed an image of this observance, and the things which the law appointed were kept by the high priests of the Jews; but even if everything was diligently observed and even if all the things which the law commanded were fulfilled, not even so could all this observance make a great priest. For how can he be called a "great priest" who is able to sin? And that all the great priests too were under sin, we readily perceive from this very thing, that the law commands "that the priest should offer a victim first for his own sins, and afterwards also for the sins of the people". How then is he "great" who is set under sin? But my great priest Jesus is "great" for this reason, because "he did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth", and because "the prince of this world came to him and found nothing in him". Therefore also Gabriel the archangel, announcing his birth, says: "he shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High". Sin makes a man small and slight, virtue renders him eminent and great. For just as sickness of the body makes a man's body meager and slight, but health makes it flourishing and strong, so understand that sickness of sin makes the soul too lowly and small, but the health of the inner man and the works of virtue make it great and eminent, and the more it grows in virtues, the more it renders the greatness of itself extensive. Thus do I understand that which is written of Jesus: that "he advanced in wisdom and in stature and in grace with God and men". For who among men is there who does not "advance in stature" in boyhood, that this should be written of Jesus as though it were something remarkable? To you I say this, who hear in a bodily way that Jesus "advanced in stature". Understand therefore that "he advanced in the stature" of the soul, and his soul became great because of the great and enormous works which he did. Indeed the Apostle too, knowing that this stature is to be understood of the inner man, writes thus: "until we all meet in the perfect man, in the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ". For to grow according to the body and to become great is not in our power. For the body takes the material of its quantity from its generative origin, so as to become either great or slight; but the soul has in us the causes and the freedom of choice, so as to be either great or small. If therefore the soul be "little" and small, it can even "be scandalized"; for so it is written in the gospel: that "it is better to be cast headlong into the deep of the sea than to scandalize one of these little ones". He who is great is not "scandalized", but he who is "little". He who is great, whatever he sees, whatever he suffers, does not turn aside from the faith. But he who is "little" in mind and small, seeks occasions how he may "be scandalized", how he may seem to be tripped up in the faith. Therefore, in fine, we must take counsel most of all for those who are small in faith, nor ought we to expend as much care about the great and strong as about the "little ones" and beginners. For the strong man "bears all things, endures all things, and never falls". But with the "little ones" and the "weak in faith" it must be watched that they be not tripped up by occasion of us and fall back from the faith and fall away from salvation. Or show me from the Scriptures where anyone a sinner or of little merit has been called "great". Nowhere, I think, will you find it. But hear who they are who are called "great". Of Isaac it is said that "he advanced greatly, until he became great, great exceedingly". Moses was called "great" and John the Baptist was called "great", but now Jesus is called "great", and after him no one henceforth has been called "great". For before he was present who is truly "great", the saints, of whom we made mention above, were called "great" in comparison with the rest of men. But when he himself came, who was truly "great" not from comparison with the rest but by his own greatness — of whom also it is written that "he exulted as a giant to run his course" — thereafter no one henceforth has been called "great". This, then, is he of whom it is written: "the great priest from among his brethren". Which "brethren"? Those of whom he said, when he had risen from the dead: "go to my brethren and say to them: I ascend to my Father and to your Father and to my God and to your God". But if you wish to learn the brethren of Jesus also from the ancient writings, read the twenty-first psalm, where in the person of Christ it is said: "I will declare your name to my brethren, in the midst of the church I will praise you". "From among his brethren" therefore is Jesus "great", from those who had earlier been called "great"; and just as he is "shepherd of shepherds" and "high priest of high priests" and "Lord of those who rule" and "King of kings", so also he is great among the great; and therefore it added: "great from among his brethren".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But after these things: "upon whom" it says "the oil of anointing has been poured, upon his head". Do not seek on earth that "oil" which is poured "upon the head" of the "great priest" that he may become Christ; but if it seems good, learn from the prophet David what this "oil" is: "you have loved" he says "righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows". This, then, is the "oil of gladness" which, "poured upon his head", made him Christ. But it adds still further to his praises: "who has his hands perfected" it says. To what man, I ask, is it fitting that this be said? In what mortal can we find "perfect hands"? Even if this be Aaron, of whom mention seems to be made, how will he be thought to have had "perfected hands", with which "he fashioned the calf", with which he carved an idol? Even if you bring forward Moses himself, how will he seem to have had "perfected hands", who did not glorify the Lord "at the water of contradiction"? For which fault he is even commanded to depart from life. But if you wish to name some other of the saints, there meets you the word of Scripture which says that "there is no man upon earth who does good and does not sin". Rightly then does Jesus alone have "perfected hands", who alone "did no sin", that is, who has the perfect and whole works of his hands. And therefore of him it is rightly said: "who has his hands perfected, to be clothed with the holy things". For this is he who is truly "clothed with the holy things", not those which were "in type", but those very things which are truly "holy". But if you wish to hear of his more exalted garments, receive the prophetic words: "clothed" it says "with light as with a garment, the deep as a garment is his clothing". This is the habit of my great high priest, by which it is signified that he is clothed with the profound light of knowledge and wisdom, which are truly "holy" garments. "He shall not" it says "take the mitre from his head". We have already said before that the "mitre" is a kind of covering which, set upon the head, affords adornment to the high priest. This "great high priest" of mine therefore never lays aside the adornment of his sacred head. But what the "head of Christ" is, learn from the Apostle, who says: "but the head of Christ is God". Rightly therefore he never lays aside this adornment of his head, which is "God", because "the Father is" always "in the Son, as the Son" is always "in the Father". "And he shall not rend his garments". Truly this is he who "shall not rend his garments", but will always keep them clean, always whole, always chaste.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And he shall not go in to any dead soul". What is a "dead soul"? One that is dead; the prophet says: "the soul that sins, it shall die". Upon this dead soul, then, Christ does not come, because he is "wisdom", and wisdom does not enter into a malevolent soul. For that soul is dead, because in whom malice is present, sin also is present. "And sin, when it is consummated" it says "begets death". And on account of this Jesus "does not enter in to a dead soul". But if the soul lives, that is, if it has not in itself a mortal sin, then Christ, who is "life", comes to the living soul; because just as "light cannot be with darkness nor righteousness with iniquity", so neither can life be with death. And therefore if anyone is conscious to himself that he has within him a mortal sin and has not cast it from himself through the repentance of fullest satisfaction, let him not hope that Christ "enters in to" his "soul", who "does not enter in to any dead soul", because he is the "great priest".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "In his father and in his mother he shall not be defiled". This passage of Scripture is most difficult to explain, but if by your prayers you entreat God the Father of the Word to deign to enlighten us, by his own gift it will be able to be explained. Everyone who enters this world is said to be brought into being in a certain defilement. On account of which Scripture also says: "no one is clean from filth, not even if his life be of one day". This very thing, then — that he is placed "in the womb" of his mother and that he takes the material of his body from the origin of the paternal seed — can be said to be "defiled in father and mother". Or do you not know that, when a male child has been made forty days old, he is offered at the altar, that he may there be purified, as one who was polluted in the very conception, whether of the paternal seed or of the maternal womb? Every man, therefore, "is polluted in father and in mother", but Jesus my Lord alone entered clean into this generation, "he was not polluted in his mother". For he entered "an undefiled body". For it was he who had also long ago said through Solomon: "but rather, since I was good, I came to an undefiled body". "He was not" therefore "defiled in his mother", nor even "in his father". For Joseph furnished nothing in his generation except ministry and affection; whence Scripture granted him the appellation of father for his faithful ministry. For thus Mary herself says in the gospel: "behold, I and your father have been seeking you sorrowing". So then this alone is the "great priest" who "was defiled neither in father nor in mother". But let us see whether we can still find something more sublime and worthy of the dignity of so great a high priest. The true Father of all is said to be God. But the Apostle says our "mother" is "the heavenly Jerusalem". All therefore who sin "are defiled in the father" by whom they were created. For whether we have done anything impious or spoken it or thought it against God, when we have not believed God, "we have been defiled in the father". But would that it had then been done only through unbelief, and had ceased after we believed! So then we are also "defiled in the mother", if, believing God, we either injure the church or defile the liberty of our "heavenly mother" by the unworthy servitude of sin.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But our Lord Jesus Christ alone, "who knows no sin", "was defiled neither in father nor in mother" and "did not go out from the holy places". There were indeed some things to be set before the Jews in the passages above, to which they could not respond, but omitting those, what do they for the present tell us on this discourse, either they themselves or those who wish the law to be understood according to their sense: if these things are not referred to our high priest and Savior, how will it be proved according to the letter that "the great priest did not go out from the holy places", who nevertheless even took a wife, as is said below, "a virgin of his own kindred"? If "he does not go out from the holy places", if he goes forth nowhere, how or for what uses is he commanded to "take a wife"? For it must not be supposed that he could remain within the holy places with a wife. But let those suppose these things to whom "Jewish fables" are pleasing. But we have a "great priest" "after the order of Melchizedek", Christ Jesus, "never going out from the holy places"; for he is always in the holy places and remains always holy in his words, holy in his acts, holy in all his wishes, and he alone is the one who is never found outside the holy places. For he who sins "goes out from the holy places", and as many times as anyone sins, so many times is he made to be outside the holy places. But Christ, "who never sinned", "never went out from the holy places". But you too, who follow Christ and are his imitator, if you remain in the word of God, if "you meditate on his law day and night", if you are exercised in his commandments, you are always in the holy places and never depart from there. For the holy things are not to be sought in a place, but in acts and life and morals. If these are according to God and are held according to the precept of God, even if you are in your house, even if in the marketplace — and why do I say in the marketplace? — even if you be found in the theater serving the word of God, do not doubt that you are in the holy places. Or does it not seem to you that Paul, when he entered the theater or when he entered the "Areopagus" and preached Christ to the Athenians, was in the holy places? But also when he walked among the altars and idols of the Athenians, where he found written: "to the unknown God" and from this word took the beginning of his preaching of Christ, even there, "surveying" the "altars" of the gentiles, he was set in the holy places, because he was pondering holy things. But also whoever guards himself, after receiving the grace of God, lest he fall "into homicide, into adultery, into theft, into false testimony" and other things like these, but remains clean from every contagion of sin, this man "did not go out from the holy places", and did not defile the sanctification of his God in himself, because the holy "oil of anointing" of his God is upon him. That "oil" of which it is written in Exodus — how can it according to the letter properly be called the oil of God, which was compounded by the perfumer's art by an unguent-maker? But if you wish to see the oil of God, hear whom the prophet says to have been anointed with the oil of God, him without doubt of whom he says: "therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows". This, then, is the "great priest" who alone was anointed with the oil of God and in whom the "oil of the anointing" of God remained always holy.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But what is added after these things? "He shall take to wife a virgin of his own kindred, but a widow and one cast out and a harlot he shall not take, but he shall take a virgin of his own kindred; and he shall not defile his seed among his people; I am the Lord, who sanctify him". Since therefore the order of the whole exposition has been recalled to the true "great priest", Christ, let us now see also what ought to be understood about his nuptials. Paul the Apostle says: "but I wish to present you all as a chaste virgin to one husband, to Christ. But I fear lest, as the serpent seduced Eve by his craftiness, your senses be corrupted from the simplicity which is in Christ". Paul therefore wishes to "present all the Corinthians as a chaste virgin to Christ"; which assuredly he would never wish, unless he saw it to be possible. Whence perhaps it may seem wonderful how these, who came to the faith of Christ corrupted by diverse sins, are all together called a "chaste virgin"; a virgin so holy, so chaste, that she deserves even to be joined to the nuptials of Christ. But since we cannot refer these things to the integrity of the flesh, it is certain that they pertain to the integrity of the soul, whose — according to the very judgment of Paul — "the simplicity of the faith which is in Christ" has been called her virginity; and through this, because, when the sophistries of the philosophers or the Jewish superstitions ceased, Christ took the church to himself in simple faith, "he took to wife a virgin of his own kindred". For her faith is not corrupted by the philosophic sense nor by the ambition of circumcision, but she remained in the simplicity of confession as in virginal integrity. For so also he had long ago promised through the prophet, saying: "I will betroth you to myself in faith". "Everyone" therefore, according to the Apostle, "who is in Christ is a new creature". And as the same Apostle says: "that he might present to himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she might be holy and immaculate". How then does he make her, who is wrinkled, to be without "wrinkle", except that he "renews" her according to that which is written: "for even if our man who is without is corrupted, yet he who is within is renewed from day to day"? A "widow" indeed "and a harlot and one cast out Christ does not take", nor does such a soul enter the bridal chamber of the bridegroom. For he who "has entered there not having the wedding garment" will endure that which you know is written in the gospel. "A virgin" therefore he will take, "a widow he will not take nor a harlot nor one cast out or defiled". Why Christ should not take "a harlot" and a "rejected" soul "and a polluted" one into marriage, it is no labor to expound; but why a "widow" should not be received must be more diligently considered. Paul the Apostle, writing to the Romans, calls "the law the husband of the soul", and declares "that she, when the husband is dead, is loosed from the law of the husband, so that she is no longer an adulteress, if she has married Christ". But if it should happen that the law of the soul itself dies to it — that is, that the soul departs from the law and yet does not bind itself with the disciplines of a chaster wedlock, and, departing from the law, does not take up the yoke of the evangelical teaching: this soul will not be able to "marry Christ", having sought the wantonness of liberty, not the cultivation of a virginal and simple faith. This "great priest", therefore, "will take a virgin wife of his own kindred". It can also for this reason seem to be said "of his own kindred", because the soul of Christ was from the kindred and from the substance of all human souls. It can also, according to this — that he calls those who believe in him brethren — be said to be "of his own kindred", the soul which is joined to him in faith as in nuptials. Yet I do not want this to escape us, that the Hebrews deny they have it written, what we find among the Seventy translators: "of his own kindred". And rightly do they not have it written. For the nearness of God has been taken away from them, the adoption of sons has been taken away and transferred to the church of Christ. They therefore do not have it written that they are "of the kindred" of Christ, just as they did not deserve to be. But we who have this written and read it, let us indeed rejoice at the condescension of God, but let us carefully and anxiously take care lest our life and acts and morals at any time make us degenerate, lest this very thing be brought unto our condemnation, that, "when we are the kindred of Christ", we serve unworthy and foul and diabolical acts. "He who has" therefore "a bride is a bridegroom". You hear how Christ is called "bridegroom", but his "bride" is said to be the soul which is proved uncorrupted and virgin by the simplicity of faith and the purity of acts. For the Lord says also through Jeremiah the prophet: "have you not called me as Lord and Father and prince of your virginity?".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "But a widow and one cast out and one defiled he shall not take". If any of us has sinned, he is "cast out"; even if he is not cast out by the bishop, whether because it lies hidden or because he is sometimes judged unto grace, he is nevertheless "cast out" by the very consciousness of sin. Nor does the grace of man avail, when Christ does not receive such a soul into marriage as "cast out". Therefore "neither a widow", as we said above, "will he take, nor one cast out nor one polluted". She is called "polluted" who, even if she has not completely committed the sin, yet by this very thing that she thought it, that she wished it, that she desired it, even if she did not carry it out, is "polluted" and is not chosen by the "great high priest". For he requires an exceedingly pure, exceedingly clean and sincere soul, which he may join to himself, because "he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit". Whence also this is shown, that there are differences of sins, and that he who has sinned "a sin unto death" is "cast out", but he who does not "sin unto death" but something lesser, is "polluted". But the bride of Christ can be neither "cast out" nor "polluted", but a "virgin" undefiled, uncorrupted, clean. For remember the word of the Apostle which we set forth a little before, saying: "that he might present to himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she might be holy and immaculate".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But also "a harlot he shall not take". What is a "harlot" soul? One that receives to itself "lovers", of whom the prophet says: "you have played the harlot after your lovers". Who are these "lovers" who enter in to the harlot soul, except the adverse powers and demons, who conceive desire of her beauty? For the soul was created beautiful by God and exceedingly comely. Hear how God himself says: "let us make man according to our image and likeness". See of what comeliness, of what beauty the soul is; it has the "image and likeness" of God. When the adverse powers behold this beauty, that is, "the devil and his angels", they covet its form; and because they cannot become its bridegrooms, they desire to play the harlot with it. If therefore you receive, O man, into the bedchamber of your soul the adulterer "devil", your soul has played the harlot with the devil. If you receive "his angels", if diverse spirits that persuade you to sin, your soul has played the harlot with them; if the spirit of anger, if of envy, if of pride, if of unchastity has entered in to your soul and you have received it, have consented to it as it speaks in your heart, have taken delight in the things which it suggests to you according to its own mind, you have played the harlot with it. "A harlot" therefore "the great priest shall not take, and he shall not defile his seed among his people". What is this "seed" which he does not want to be "defiled"? In the gospels it is written that "he who sows, sows the word". He does not want, therefore, "the word" of God "to be defiled" by those "who sow". But who are "those who sow"? Those who put forth the word of God in the church. Let teachers therefore hear, lest perhaps they entrust the words of God to a "defiled" soul, to a "harlot" soul, to an unfaithful soul, lest perhaps they cast "what is holy to the dogs and pearls before swine", but let them choose clean souls, "virgins" "in the simplicity of the faith which is in Christ", let them commit to them the secret mysteries, let them speak forth to them the word of God and the hidden things of faith, that in them "Christ may be formed" through faith. Or do you not know that from this seed of the word of God which is sown, Christ is born in the heart of the hearers? For the Apostle too says this: "until Christ be formed in us". The soul therefore conceives from this seed of the word and forms the conceived word within itself, until it brings forth the spirit of the fear of God. For thus through the prophet the souls of the saints say: "from your fear, O Lord, we have conceived in the womb and have been in labor and have brought forth; we have made the spirit of your salvation upon the earth". This is the childbearing of holy souls, this the conception, these are the holy nuptials which are fitting and suited to the great high priest Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Moreover, blameless priests served the Godhead by offering blameless sacrifices, while those who were blemished and offered blemished sacrifices and whom Moses described in Leviticus were separated from the altar. And who else is the blameless priest offering a blameless sacrifice than the person who holds fast to his confession and fulfills every requirement the account of martyrdom demands? He is the one we have spoken of before.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He who is "perfect" is taught by God himself concerning the meaning of the festivals, and he does not need a man as his teacher for learning these things, but he learns from God, if anyone is able to grasp the voice of God. But he who is not such a one, but of lower rank, learns from him who has learned from God. There is, then, this twofold manner of teaching concerning the festivals. There is the one by which the prophetic mind, illumined through the Spirit, is taught — which, so to speak, is learned more by the gaze of the mind than by the sound of a voice, through which the truth itself, and not the shadow and image of the truth, is recognized. But those who cannot grasp the very brightness of God, nor behold the whole radiance of the truth with the fixed keenness of the mind, hear about the festivals in second place from those who learned first; and while the very property of direct inspection gave to those the truth of things, to these only hearing conveys the shadow of the truth. Conscious of this mystery, the Apostle said of the Jews that "they serve the shadow and the copy of heavenly things". For Moses is described as having seen the "heavenly things" themselves, but as having handed on to the people the types and images of the things which he had seen; for thus the divine utterance says to him: "See", it says, "that you make all things according to the form which was shown to you on the mountain". Such, then, is what has also been recited in this passage, that the Lord spoke to Moses concerning the festivals. And after these things: "And Moses declared", it says, "the feast days of the Lord God to the children of Israel". But now that the discourse concerning these things is finished, let us see what Moses is taught after them.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: First, concerning the "lamp" and the "lampstand" and the "oil" which is poured into it; second, concerning the "table" and the "shewbread" and their number and those who ought to use them. Let us therefore direct our mind more diligently to the things that are written, and let us pray that the grace of the Lord be granted us for discerning these things, so that in the letters which we read we may recognize what is the will of the Holy Spirit. "Command", it says, "the children of Israel, and let them bring you clean oil pressed from olives for the light, that a lamp may burn always outside the veil in the tabernacle of testimony, and Aaron and his sons shall kindle it from evening until morning before the Lord without ceasing, an everlasting statute throughout your generations. On the clean lampstand you shall kindle the lamps before the Lord until morning". He names a "clean lampstand"; he commands the "lamps" to be kindled by the high priest, and he prescribes that their "light" be supplied from the "oil" which is given by the people. And so, unless the people supply "oil", without doubt the "lamp" will be extinguished and there will be no "light" among the holy things. According to the letter, then, this was the sequence: that the people should contribute "clean oil pressed from olives", so that from it the "light of the lamp" might be supplied; "and Aaron kindled the lamps from evening until morning", providing fuel for the light with the nourishment of the oil which the people had contributed.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But "since the law is spiritual", let us ask of the Lord — if indeed "we have turned to the Lord" — that "the veil of the reading of the old testament be taken away" from us, so that we may be able to perceive what is the meaning of his "lampstand and lamps" according to the spiritual understanding. Before the coming of my Lord Jesus Christ the sun did not rise upon the people of Israel, but it made use of "the light of a lamp". For among them the word of the law and the prophetic word was a "lamp" shut within narrow walls, which could not pour out its light upon the whole earth. For within Judea the knowledge of God was confined, as the prophet also says: "God is known in Judea". But when the "sun of righteousness", our Lord and Savior, rose, and the man was born of whom it is written: "behold a man, the East is his name", throughout the whole world the light of the knowledge of God was poured out. The word of the law, then, and the prophetic word was a "burning lamp", but it burned within the house and could not send its splendor beyond. And that the word of the law and of the prophets is called a "lamp", the Lord himself taught us, saying of John the Baptist: "he was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing for an hour to rejoice in his light". And elsewhere he says that "the law and the prophets were until John". And so John is the "burning lamp" in whom the "law" is enclosed "and the prophets". As long, then, as that people had "oil" which it "contributed for the light", the "lamp" was not extinguished. But when among them the oil of mercy, the oil of good works, failed, and no purity was found among them — for clean oil was required for the light — necessarily the "lamp" was extinguished. But why do we say that these things befell them, but are foreign to us? Rather, the Christian has a greater care for procuring oil. For see how the Lord in the gospels names, through a parable, "foolish virgins" who "do not carry oil in their vessels", and so foolish that, since oil for kindling their lamps was lacking to them, they were shut out from the marriage chambers, and to those who knocked, who had neglected the care of the oil, the bridegroom commanded that it be no longer opened. Yet I remember that some time ago, when we were expounding that verse of the hundred and eighteenth psalm in which it is written: "your law is a lamp to my feet, O Lord, and a light to my paths", we showed, according to our ability, the difference between the "lamp" and the "light". For we said that he assigned the "lamp" indeed to the "feet", that is, to the lower parts of the body, but gave the "light" to the "paths", which "paths" in another place are called "eternal paths". Since, then, according to a certain mystical meaning, this world is understood as the lower parts of creation, therefore the "lamp" of the law is recorded as kindled for those who are in this world as it were the feet of the whole creation. But the "light" will be eternal for those "paths" along which in the age to come each one will walk according to his merits. But concerning these things enough has been said in its own place according to our ability. Now therefore, since it is evening and night "until the consummation of the age" and until the new day of the age to come and of the new light shines forth, this "lamp" burns for each one of us, giving so much splendor of light as the abundance of oil has been supplied by the plenty of works. Finally, Job too in a certain place, when he was setting forth the good things of his works, added also this: "when", he says, "the lamp shone above my head". This "lamp", then, shines for each one of us, insofar as it has been kindled with the oil of good works.
