But if we act wickedly and our works are evil, we not only do not kindle but even extinguish this lamp for ourselves, and there is fulfilled in us that which Scripture says: "he who does evil walks in darkness, and he who hates his brother walks in darkness". For he has extinguished the "lamp" of charity and therefore "walks in darkness". Or does it not seem to you that he has extinguished the "lamp" who has extinguished the "light" of charity? "But he who loves his brother" continues in the light of charity and can say with confidence: "but I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God", and: "his sons are like young olive shoots around" his "table". "Oil", therefore, is commanded to be offered by the people, and not oil of any sort whatever, but "clean" oil, and not from any kinds of seeds, as is the custom in various regions, but pressed "from olives", in which a sign of peace is shown. For your works cannot be acceptable to God unless they are performed in peace; as the Apostle James also says: "but the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace". For this reason, I believe, the Lord also handed on to his disciples a faithful deposit, saying: "my peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you". From this "olive", then, let us press the oil of our works, from which a lamp can be kindled for the Lord, "that we may not walk in darkness". Let these things be said by us, insofar as concerns the "lamp of the lampstand" and its "oil".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But now let us see what is written also in what follows concerning the shewbread. "And you shall take", it says, "fine flour and make from it twelve loaves; of two tenths shall be one loaf; and you shall set them in two rows, six loaves in one row, upon the clean table before the Lord. And you shall put upon the row clean frankincense and salt, and the loaves shall be set as a memorial before the Lord; on the day of the sabbaths they shall always be set forth before the Lord by the children of Israel, an everlasting covenant. And it shall be Aaron's and his sons', and they shall eat them in a holy place; for they are the holy of holies. This shall be theirs of the things that are offered to the Lord, an everlasting statute". According to what is written, in the twelve loaves a "memorial before the Lord" seems to be made of the twelve tribes of Israel, and a command to be given that without ceasing these "twelve loaves be set forth in the sight of the Lord"; so that both the memory of the twelve tribes may always be held before him, whereby through these there may seem to be, as it were, a certain entreaty and supplication made for each of them. But such an intercession is small enough and slight. For how much does it avail toward propitiation, where the fruit of each tribe is to be considered through the loaf, and its works through the fruit? But if these things are referred to the greatness of the mystery, you will find that this "memorial" has the effect of an immense propitiation. If you return to that "bread which came down from heaven and gives life to this world", that bread of the presentation "whom God set forth as a propitiator through faith in his blood", and if you look to that "memorial" of which the Lord says: "do this in memory of me", you will find that this is the only "memorial" that makes God propitious to men. If, then, you recall more attentively the ecclesiastical mysteries, in the things which the law writes you will find preformed the image of the future truth. But of these things there is no need to discourse further, since it suffices to be understood by recollection alone. But we can also speak in another way. Every word of God is bread, but there is a difference among the loaves. For there is a certain word which can be brought forth for the common hearing and can teach the multitude concerning the works of mercy and of all beneficence; and this is the bread which will seem common. But there is another which contains hidden things and discourses concerning the faith of God or the knowledge of things. This bread is clean and made from "fine flour". This is "always to be placed in the sight of the Lord and to be set forth upon the clean table". This is set apart for the priests alone and bestowed on the sons of Aaron as an everlasting gift. But lest you suppose that we are relating these things devised by our own imaginings and have not observed them in the divine volumes, I will bring forth for you from the scriptures how among different men a difference of bread was maintained according to the merit of each one. It is related in Genesis that Abraham the patriarch received angels as guests, and likewise also Lot. But Abraham, who excelled in merits, is described as having set before them loaves made from "fine flour", which he also named — that is, hidden and secret ones. But Lot, because he did not have fine flour, set before his guests loaves made from meal; not that he was so poor that he did not have fine flour, he who is written to be not inferior to his uncle in riches, but the difference of the merits of both is designated by these tokens; that he indeed, to whom the mysteries were to be revealed by the Lord and to whom it was said: "I will not hide from my servant Abraham what I am about to do", who was to be instructed and taught concerning the hidden and secret things of God, that man is written to have had loaves "of fine flour"; but that other, to whom nothing of the sacrament was conveyed, but the account of present salvation and life, is written to have had common loaves made from "meal" alone. And so you too, if you have the knowledge of secret things, if you can discourse knowingly and carefully concerning the faith of God, concerning the mystery of Christ, concerning the unity of the Holy Spirit, you offer loaves "of fine flour" to the Lord; but if you employ common admonitions to the people and know only how to treat the moral topic, which pertains to all, know that you have offered common bread.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us now see what is the making of these shewbread loaves which are commanded to be "always placed before the Lord". "Of two tenths", it says, "let there be one loaf". He said "two tenths" indeed, but of what measure these "tenths" are he did not specify; although surely it would have been consistent, if he wished the quantity of the fine flour to be known, to name the measure itself of which he commanded "two tenths" to be taken. What, then, is this thing whose measure and amount could neither be specified nor named? The number ten is everywhere found to be perfect; for from it arises the reckoning and origin of every number. Fittingly, therefore, the author and origin of all things, God, is seen to be shown under this number. But if in the church I speak of the Father alone and utter the praises of him alone, I have made a loaf of one tenth. Or if I make a discourse concerning Christ alone and recount his passion and preach his resurrection, I have offered a "loaf" of one tenth. But if I say that the Father is always with the Son and "he does his works", or even if I say that "the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father" and "he who has seen the Son has seen also the Father", and that the Father and the Son are one, then "of two tenths" of clean fine flour I have offered one "loaf", a true loaf, "which gives life to this world". Heretics do not make "one loaf of two tenths", for they deny that the creator God is the Father of Christ, nor do they make the old and new testament "one loaf" and profess one spirit in both instruments. But we say that one and the same Holy Spirit is present in the law and the gospels, and in this way too "of two tenths" we offer "one loaf" of the presentation. Those, therefore, who separate Christ from the creator God his Father — the heretics — and the Jews, who receive the Father alone and do not receive Christ, his Word and Wisdom, do not make "one loaf of two tenths". But we cannot grasp or discover the name or the reckoning of the measure itself, that is, of the substance; yet, confessing the Father and the Son, we make "one loaf of two tenths", not so that one loaf is made of one tenth and another of the other, so that the "two tenths" themselves are separate, but so that these "two tenths" are one mass and "one loaf". How do "two tenths" become one mass? Because I do not separate the Son from the Father nor the Father from the Son: "for he who has seen me", he says, "has seen also the Father". The loaves, then, are made each "of two tenths and are set forth in two rows", that is, in two orders. For if there were one row, the discourse concerning the Father and the Son would be confused and intermingled. But now there is indeed "one loaf" — for there is one will and one substance — but there are "two rows", that is, the two properties of the persons. For we call the Father that one who is not the Son, and the Son this one who is not the Father. And in this way we preserve the "two tenths" in "one loaf" and profess "two rows before the Lord". But truly it belongs, so to speak, to some great baker and highly skilled craftsman to preserve these measures diligently and so to temper the discourse concerning the Father and the Son, to join where it is fitting and again to separate where it is proper, that neither the "two measures" are ever lacking nor that the "one loaf" ever fails to appear. "Twelve loaves", then, are commanded to be made "of" this "fine flour" according to the number of the tribes which were then of the carnal Israel. In which there seems to me to be contained the form of the whole rational nature; for the general orders of the rational creation are thought to be twelve, whose figure was in those twelve tribes. Among which there was one royal order, which is named "Judah". Another was the priestly order, and it is called "Levi". And there was another order neighboring on Judah, which is called "Benjamin", in which order both the temple of God and the altar were placed. Another order was "Issachar and Zebulun and Ephraim" and the others which the divine Scripture designates by name, whose meaning it is not the time now to explain. Yet there is a "loaf before the Lord" of each tribe or order. And although there may be some tribe which descends not from a freewoman but from a concubine of Israel, and which is in part free, in part servile, nevertheless for all a "loaf of two tenths is set forth before the Lord", and in all the "two tenths of fine flour" hold firm. And they are commanded to be "set forth upon the clean table". Who among us is there who has so "clean a table" that upon it "loaves" may be offered to the Lord? "If you sit down to dine at the table of a powerful man", says Solomon, "understand intelligently what is set before you". What, then, is the "table of the powerful man", if not the mind of him who said: "I can do all things in him who strengthens me, Christ", and: "when I am weak, then am I strong"? Upon the "clean table of this powerful man", that is, in his heart, in his mind, the "loaf" is offered to the Lord. If you sit down to dine at the "table" of this "powerful" Apostle, "understand intelligently what is set before you", that is, attend spiritually to the things that are said by him, so that you too may be able to do what is added; for he says: "knowing that you must prepare such things".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us see how these "twelve loaves" are set forth: "two rows", it says, "six loaves in one row". Do you suppose this division is idle? Why is it that the number twelve is again divided into six? For the number six has a certain kinship with this world; for in six days this visible world was made. Two orders, therefore, are held in this world, that is, two peoples, who guard the faith of the Father and the Son in one church as it were upon "one clean table".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And there shall be placed", it says, "upon the row clean frankincense". The kind of frankincense holds the form of prayers. It is fitting, therefore, to join to the loaves of faith the vigilance and purity of prayers. And prayer is pure, as the Apostle says: "lifting up pure hands without wrath and dispute". At the same time the sweetness of the odor also causes to be fulfilled that which is written: "let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight". If anyone, therefore, offers prayers indeed to God, but does not have a conscience clean from evil works, this man seems indeed to "place frankincense" upon the loaves, but not entirely "clean" frankincense. For if all frankincense were "clean", Scripture would surely not have added that "clean frankincense" be "placed before the Lord" upon the shewbread. For do not suppose that almighty God commanded this and sanctioned it by law, that frankincense be brought to him from Arabia. But this is the frankincense which God seeks to be offered to him by men, from which he takes "an odor of sweetness": prayers from a pure heart and a good conscience, in which God truly receives the fragrance of sweetness. "And the loaves", it says, "shall be for a memorial, set forth before the Lord. On the day of the sabbaths you shall set them forth". If it is not yet manifest to you that these "loaves" are the word of God, be confirmed now from these words. For what is it that makes for us a "memorial" of God? What is it that recalls us to the memory of righteousness and of all good if not the word of God? Therefore, then, it says that "they shall be for a memorial, set forth before the Lord". It adds also "on the day of the sabbaths", that is, in the rest of souls. And what greater rest is there for the faithful soul than the "memory" of God, than to dwell "in the sight of the Lord", than to remain in the faith of the Father and the Son, than to offer prayers to the Lord as an "odor of sweetness"?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "An everlasting covenant", it says, "it shall be for Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat them in a holy place". "Aaron and his sons" are "a chosen race, a priestly race", to whom this portion of the holy things is given by God — which we all are who believe in Christ. But I do not seek the "holy place" set on earth, but in the heart. For the rational soul is called a "holy place", for which reason also the Apostle says: "do not give place to the devil". My soul, then, is the place — if I act wickedly, of the devil; if well, of God. Finally also "the evil spirit", it says, "when it has gone out from a man, and has gone about arid places, and has not found rest, then it says: I will return to my place, whence I went out". The "holy place", then, is the pure soul. In which place we are commanded to eat the food of the word of God. For it is not fitting that an unholy soul should receive holy words, but when it has purified itself from every defilement of flesh and of morals, then, made a "holy place", it may take the food of that "bread which came down from heaven". Is not the "holy place" better understood thus than if we suppose that a structure of insensible stones is called a "holy place"? Whence in a similar manner this law too is set before you, that, when you receive the mystic bread, you eat it in a clean place, that is, that you do not receive the sacraments of the Lord's body in a soul contaminated and polluted with sins: "for whoever", it says, "eats the bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let each one prove himself, and then let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "For they are the holy of holies". You see how he did not say holy only, but "holy of holies", as if he said: this food is not the common food of all, nor of anyone unworthy, but it belongs to "the holy". How much more shall we also say this rightly and deservedly concerning the word of God: this discourse is not for all; not just anyone can hear the mystery of this word, but it belongs only to the holy, who are purified in mind, "who are clean of heart", who are "simple in soul", who are blameless in life, who are free in conscience — theirs it is to hear the discourse concerning this, to them can these mysteries be explained. "For to you it is given", he says, "to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to those", that is, who are not worthy, who are not such as to deserve it nor can be capable of the understanding of secret things, "to those it cannot be given": this priestly bread, which is the secret and mystic discourse, but in "parables", which is common to the crowd. "This shall be an everlasting statute". For everything that is mystic is an "everlasting statute". For these present and everywhere visible things are temporal and quickly come to an end: "for the fashion of this world passes away". But if "the fashion of this world passes away", without doubt the "fashion" of the letter also passes away, and those things remain which are eternal, which the spiritual sense contains. If, then, we have understood first how God speaks to Moses and Moses to the children of Israel, second also the meaning of the "clean lampstand" and of the "lamps" and its oil, third also that the "loaves" of the presentation are "made each of two tenths" according to the will of the Spirit: let us give our effort that we too may not be made unworthy of this so great and so sublime understanding, but that our soul may first become a "holy place", and that in a "holy place" we may take the holy mysteries through the grace of the Holy Spirit, by whom is sanctified everything that is holy. "To Him be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
A narrative has been read to us whose account, though it may seem plain, will nevertheless not easily disclose to us its inner sense unless we follow rather diligently its coherence according to the letter. The passage of Scripture, then, on which we must discourse, is this: "And there went out," it says, "the son of the Israelite woman, and this one was the son of an Egyptian among the sons of Israel; and they quarreled in the camp, he who was of the Israelite woman and a man who was an Israelite. And the son of the Israelite woman, naming the name, cursed; and they brought him to Moses; and the name of his mother was Salomith, the daughter of Dabri, of the tribe of Dan. And they put him into prison, that they might judge concerning him according to the command of the Lord. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Cast out him who cursed, outside the camp, and all who heard shall lay their hands upon his head, and the whole synagogue shall stone him." Let us see, then, first what the narrative we have set forth means, and, although it seems plain, let us nevertheless attempt to set it before our eyes still more evidently. Let us suppose, then, one man rejoicing in the nobility of the Israelite name from both father and mother, and another from the mother only and not also from the father, and as it were noble in part and in part not—not of the father, which would surely seem the better, but of the mother, which is the inferior. For if the father had been an Israelite and the mother an Egyptian, there would be something more; for this is what Manasseh and Ephraim had been. But now it is written that he is the son of an Israelite woman and of an Egyptian father. If, then, you have diligently followed these two men, the one wholly noble, the other in part, behold now these men "quarreling with one another"; in which quarrel he who appears to have been begotten of an Egyptian father and of an Israelite mother alone, "naming, cursed," and on this account he who had cursed was brought to Moses, but Moses, daring neither to acquit him nor to condemn him without God, "handed him over to custody" until he should receive an answer from God as to what He willed to be done with him. This is the coherence of the narrative; now let us see what spiritual meaning there is in it, which ought to build up the Church.

First of all the passage says that "there went out the son of the Israelite woman" and of an Egyptian father; and from where or to where he went out, it does not matter. For both are found placed within the camp, as the word of the Lord indicates, which says: "Lead out the man who cursed, forth outside the camp." If, then, "he is led out from the camp," he was necessarily in the camp. What, then, is the meaning that, when he had not yet gone out from the camp, the divine Scripture says of him: "and there went out the son of the Israelite woman"? I think the divine word wishes to teach us that he who sins is said to go out in a twofold way. For first he goes out from his good purpose and right judgment, he goes out from the way of righteousness, he goes out from the law of God. But afterward, when he has been convicted for his sin, he goes out also from the assembly and congregation of the saints. So that, if for example we should say: one of the faithful has sinned—this man, even if he is not yet cast out by the sentence of the bishop, yet already by the very sin which he has committed he has been cast out; and although he enters the church, nevertheless he has been cast out and is outside, separated from the fellowship and unanimity of the faithful. "There went out," then, the son of an Egyptian father and of an Israelite mother. He who is wholly outside the faith is entirely an Egyptian. But he who is among us and sins, on the one part, in which he believes God, seems to be of Israelite origin; but on that part in which he sins, he draws his lineage from the Egyptian. Two men, then, Scripture has set forth quarreling: the one wholly an Israelite, who indeed quarreled but did not sin; but the other, whose sin it designates, it indicates to be for the greatest part mixed with the Egyptian race, against whom the Israelite quarrels, and perhaps quarrels fittingly and reasonably. For in Exodus too an Israelite and an Egyptian quarrel, where the Israelite prevails and the Egyptian falls. Therefore I too today, if I defend the truth, if I fight for the faith of the Church against him who indeed in part believes Christ and receives the Scriptures, but does not receive their sense wholly nor faithfully, I quarrel against him who is indeed by his mother an Israelite, but by his father an Egyptian. If, then, anyone is both by the belief of faith and by the profession of the name a Christian and a Catholic, this man is on both parts an Israelite. But he who by profession indeed is a Christian, but in the understanding of the faith is a heretic and perverse, this man has indeed an Israelite mother, but an Egyptian father. How, then, does this come about? When someone reads the Scriptures and follows indeed the letter, but repudiates the spiritual understanding, this man has indeed an Israelite mother, that is, the letter, but because he follows not the spiritual sense but the carnal, to him there is an Egyptian father; and therefore he quarrels against the churchman, against the Catholic, against him who is on both parts an Israelite, who is both according to the letter an Israelite and according to the spirit an Israelite—because he himself is according to the letter indeed an Israelite, but according to the spirit an Egyptian. What, then, is the case with both quarreling? Necessarily he who follows the carnal sense, as one drawing his lineage from the Egyptian, "names the name and curses." For he names the name of God, and names it with a curse; for he denies that He is the creator of the world, he denies that He is the Father of Christ. But we, who are Israelites of both races and defend both the letter and the spirit in the holy Scriptures, quarrel also against those who seem to be Israelites of the middle part, and we say that neither according to the letter ought He to be cursed, nor according to the spiritual understanding to be blasphemed. For the "reviler," not only against God but also against his neighbor, is by the sentence of the Apostle Paul excluded from the kingdom of God. For see how the Apostle says: "Do not err: neither fornicators nor adulterers nor the effeminate nor abusers of themselves with men nor thieves nor the covetous nor revilers shall possess the kingdom of God." See among what crimes—among "adulterers," among "abusers of themselves with men," among "the covetous," whom elsewhere he calls "servants of idols"—he has also placed "revilers" and has excluded them together with those from the kingdom of God. Let them see, then, if there are any who by an almost daily habit accustom their mouth to this vice, what peril hangs over them. For thinking this to be a slight and easy sin, they do not easily guard against it; but let them consider how the Apostle excludes the "reviler" from the kingdom of God, and how God through Moses commands the "reviler" to be punished. Whence I too have greatly marveled that in this passage which we have in hand, Scripture has not openly designated that this man who draws his lineage from the Egyptian cursed God, but has only set down that "naming, he cursed," and has left it in the middle, whether it is to be suspected of God or of man. Whence it seems to me that for this reason it was unwilling to declare openly concerning God, lest it should seem to have given license concerning men, and therefore it kept silence both concerning God and concerning man, that on both accounts one might beware.

But since we have set forth the sentence of the Apostle, in which he says that revilers are to be excluded from the kingdom of God, this discourse demands some consolation, lest we should seem in every way to pronounce despair upon those who are carried away by an almost daily habit of reviling and neglect to set a guard, or a door, upon their mouth. Of the future promise there is not one mode nor a single kind; but, as the Lord Himself taught in the Gospel, when He calls "blessed" the "poor in spirit" and says that "theirs is the kingdom of heaven," and again calls "blessed" the "meek," yet promises them not the kingdoms of heaven but "the inheritance of the earth." He calls "the peacemakers" also "blessed," but not even to them did He give the kingdom of heaven, yet He declares them to be "sons of God." And when He promises different things to different persons, He calls all "blessed" who attain to the promises, yet He has not granted to all the kingdoms of heaven. It can happen, then, that someone may perhaps in his other works and acts be corrected and perfect, yet be tripped up in the vice of the mouth and the slip of speech; to him, even if according to the sentence of the Apostle the kingdoms of heaven are denied, yet the place of another blessedness is not cut off. Nevertheless, all the more, if anyone is perfect in other things, he ought to labor also in this, lest the vice of a depraved habit, tripping him up, snatch away from him "the kingdoms of heaven," which is the summit of all blessednesses—although the Lord has said: "In my Father's house are many mansions." We can still add also this, that the nature of sin is like the material which is consumed by fire, which the Apostle Paul says is built up by sinners, who "upon the foundation" of Christ "build wood, hay, stubble." In which it is manifestly shown that there are certain sins so slight that they are compared to "stubble," over which, when fire is brought, it cannot tarry long; but others are like "hay," which the fire likewise consumes not with difficulty, yet tarries somewhat longer than upon "stubble"; but others there are which are compared to "wood," in which, according to the quality of the crimes, the fire finds lasting and great fuel. Thus, then, each sin, according to its quality or quantity, pays its just penalties. Nevertheless, what need is there for the faithful and for those who have known God to think about the qualities of penalties? What need to place "wood," what "hay," what even "stubble" itself "upon the foundation" of Christ? Why do we not rather place "gold" or "silver" or "precious stones" upon the precious "foundation," where, when the fire comes, it may find nothing that it may consume? For if it comes to "stubble," from "stubble" it will render embers and ashes; but if it comes to "gold," it will render "gold" purer. Let these things be said by us for those who neglect to cut off the habit of a reviling mouth; who, even if they do not curse from the heart, even if they do not utter curses with an evil wish and mind, yet incur the uncleanness of lips, according to the word of Isaiah, and the defilements of the mouth. Yet this man, who, though of an Israelite mother, was nevertheless begotten of an Egyptian father, "went out" and "naming the name, cursed." Concerning whom I think that, unless he had gone out, he would neither have quarreled against the true Israelite nor "naming, have cursed." For "he went out" from the truth, "he went out" from the fear of God, from faith, from charity, as we said above, in what manner someone "goes out" from the camp of the church, even if by the voice of the bishop he is by no means cast out. Just as, on the contrary, it sometimes happens that someone is driven off and put out by an unjust judgment of those who preside over the church. But if he himself has not first "gone out," that is, if he has not so acted that he deserved to "go out," he is in no way harmed by the fact that he seems by an unjust judgment to have been expelled by men. And thus it happens that sometimes he who is put out is within, and he is outside who seems to be retained within. Do you wish me to show you another also who is said to have "gone out" though cast out by none? It is written of Cain that: "he went out from the face of God." Whither did "he go out from the face of God"? For where was "the face of God" not? But "he is said to have gone out" for the reason that he went out from the law of nature and, the first, infected with a brother's blood the earth that was ignorant of so great a crime. Yet there are also those who go out well and are blessed because they go out. I will show this too from the Scriptures. In Exodus it is written: "All," it says, "who sought the name of the Lord went out forth to Moses outside the camp." These went out well "outside the camp," because they followed Moses, that is, the law of God. And of others it is said: "Go out, my people, from the midst of them, and do not touch the unclean thing." "There went out," then, it says, "the son of the Israelite woman, and this one was the son of an Egyptian, among the sons of Israel; and they quarreled in the camp, he who was of the Israelite woman and a man who was an Israelite." See how great is the caution of the divine Scripture, if only you attend, if you inspect diligently: him who was born of an Israelite mother and of an Egyptian father, it did not call "a man," but him who was of both races an Israelite it named "a man." Do we think these things were written by chance? Do we think it was added by accident, that the one should not be called "a man" and the other should? These things are not fortuitous; there is a reason. For nothing in the words of God has been written without a profound reason. For that one, who was in part an Egyptian, in part an Israelite, did not yet deserve to be named "a man"; but this one, who was wholly an Israelite, that is, who saw God with his mind, this one is called "a man"—that inner man who was made "according to the image of God" and can "see God."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these things, now the matters which are recounted in what follows are not without a certain question, concerning which, though many have inquired, not many have been able to explain. But if you help me with your prayers, we too will attempt to bring forward into the midst what the Lord shall grant. "A man, a man," it says, "if he shall curse God, shall receive sin; but he who names the name of the Lord, let him die the death." What is this? He who "shall curse God" does not have the penalty of death, but "he who shall name the name of the Lord"? Is it not far more grievous to "curse God" than to "name" Him, although he is said to have named Him in vain? And how is it that he who "curses" only takes on sin, but he who "names" is punished "with death"? These, then, are the things which in this passage are wont to raise a question, which to those ignorant of the sense of the Scriptures seem to be said inconsequently and incongruously. For they think that he who curses the name of God ought to be punished at once; but that he "who shall name the name of the Lord," that is, shall name it superfluously and in vain, it should suffice that he "has received sin." But let us attempt to open the sequence of the passage with some such sense as this. That the sin is greater in which God is cursed than that in which He is named, we cannot doubt. It remains that we should show that it is far more grievous to "receive sin" and to have it with oneself than to be punished with death. Death, which is inflicted for the sake of penalty for sin, is a purgation of the sin itself for which it is commanded to be inflicted. The sin, then, is absolved through the penalty of death, nor does anything remain which the day of judgment and the penalty of eternal fire may find for this crime. But where someone "receives sin" and has it with himself and remains with it, and the penalty which is washed away does not pass by any punishment, it is with him even after death; and because he does not pay the temporal penalties here, there he pays the eternal punishments. You see, then, how much more grievous it is to "receive sin" than to be punished with death. For here death is given as vengeance, and with the "Lord, the just judge," "vengeance is not taken twice for the same thing," as the prophet said; but where the vengeance has not been paid, the sin remains to be extinguished by those eternal fires. And that these things are so, I can bring forward to you as witnesses from the divine volumes the patriarchs Reuben and Judah, speaking to their father Jacob, when they wished to take Benjamin with them and lead him to Egypt on account of the pledges which they had made with their brother Joseph. There, then, Reuben indeed speaks thus to his father: "Kill both my sons, unless I bring Benjamin back to you"; but Judah says: "I shall be a sinner against you, unless I bring him back to you." Jacob, then, their father, knowing that what Judah had promised, who had said "I shall be a sinner against you," was far more grievous than that of the one who had said "Kill my sons," did not entrust the son to Reuben, as to one who had chosen the lighter penalty, but handed him over to Judah, knowing that what he had chosen was more grievous. In this way, then, the divine Scripture has fittingly adapted to him who "shall curse God" that he "takes on sin," but to him who has offended more lightly that he "shall die the death." But do you also wish to learn from the Gospels that he who "shall have received in this life his evil things" does not there receive them again, but he who has not received them here, there all things are reserved for him? The example of "poor Lazarus" and of that rich man teaches us, to whom it is said "in the netherworld" by the patriarch Abraham: "Remember, son, that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise the evil things. But now you indeed are tormented, while this one is at rest." And men ignorant of the judgments of God, which are "a great abyss," are wont to complain against God and to say, why do wicked and unjust men, plunderers, impious, criminal, in this life suffer nothing adverse, but all things yield to them with prosperous successes—honors, riches, power, health too itself and the constitution of the body serve them; on the contrary, upon the innocent and pious and those who worship God innumerable troubles come, and they live abject, humble, despised, and under the buffets of the powerful, and sometimes even the diseases of the body themselves rule more savagely over them. But these things, as I said, are complained of by those ignorant of what the order is in the divine judgments. For the more grievously they wish those to be punished at whose power and iniquities they groan, the more necessary it is that the penalties be deferred, which, if they were not deferred, would surely be temporal and lighter, because they would receive their end with death; but now, because they are deferred, it is certain that they will be eternal and will be extended with the ages. On the contrary, therefore, if they should wish good things to be rendered to the just and innocent in the present age, those good things too would be temporal and to be concluded with a swift end; but the more they are deferred into the future, the more they will be perpetual and will know no end. This, then, is what this passage of Scripture, comprised in a few words, has taught us: that we may know that it is far more grievous to "receive sin" and to have it and carry it with oneself down to the netherworld than to pay the penalties of the deed in the present. And therefore, knowing these things to be expedient for the faithful, the Apostle Paul says of him who had sinned: "whom I have handed over," he says, "to Satan for the destruction of the flesh," that is, to have punished him with death. But what the fruit of this death is, he shows in what follows, saying: "that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ." You see, then, how openly the Apostle has set forth the usefulness of this death. For what he says, "I have handed over for the destruction of the flesh," that is, for the affliction of the body, which is wont to be paid out by penitents, and he named it a destruction of the flesh which nevertheless confers life on the spirit. Whence now too, if perhaps any of us recalls in himself the consciousness of some sin, if anyone knows himself to be liable to an offense, let him take refuge in penitence and take upon himself a voluntary destruction of the flesh, that, purged in the present life, our spirit may proceed clean and pure to Christ our Lord, "who is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Who is there who has grasped the mind of Christ so well that he knows the meaning of the seventh year of freedom of Hebrew slaves and the remission of debts and the intermission of the cultivation of the holy land? Over and above the feast of every seventh year is the feast called the jubilee. No one can ever come near divining its precise meaning or the true import of the prescriptions enjoined by it, except him who knows the Father's will and his disposition for every age according to "his incomprehensible judgments and unsearchable ways."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us rather quickly refer these things to ourselves, to whom the law of Christ, if we follow it, permits us to have neither possessions on earth nor houses in cities. And why do I speak of houses? It does not grant us to possess even several tunics, nor much money: for "having", he says, "food and clothing, let us be content with these". How then shall we observe the laws given concerning houses, whether set "within a walled city" or "in villages that have no walls"? We find in other places of Scripture that the divine word names a house with a certain greater mystery, as when it speaks of Jacob and sets it down as if for his praise: "for Jacob", it says, "was a simple man, dwelling in a house". And again I find it written concerning the midwives of the Hebrews: "and because", it says, "the midwives feared God, they made themselves houses". We see, then, that for the midwives the cause of making houses was the fear of God, while for Jacob simplicity and innocence gave the cause that he "dwelt in a house". Finally Esau, because he was evil, it is not written of him that he dwelt in a house, nor is it written of any other who did not have the fear of God that he built himself a house. What, then, this "house" is, and what kind of building it is, the Apostle Paul expounds more openly, when he says: "we have a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens". This, then, is the "house" which no one can build unless he fear God. This is the "house" which no one can construct or inhabit save in simplicity of mind and purity of heart. But since it is wont to happen that even one who has built well and has constructed for himself a heavenly house by acting well and living well and believing rightly, may incur the debt of some sin and be compelled by a most cruel usurer to sell it and to pour out his labors into another, the piety and clemency of the lawgiver comes to meet him, so that within a fixed time it may be redeemed. "If however your hand shall find", he says, "the price which you may restore". What kind of "price"? Gathered, without doubt, by the tears of repentance and found by the hands, that is, by the labor of good work. But that "year" can be understood which the Lord came to call "the acceptable year", in which he might release the broken into remission and grant salvation to those confessing their sins. But as to what he says, "a house in a walled city", rightly, as I judge, the "house" which is said to be "in heaven" is understood "in a walled city". For the wall of houses of this kind is the very firmament of heaven. But such a house only a rare few can have, those perhaps "who, walking upon the earth, have their conversation in the heavens" and of whom the Apostle says: "you are God's building". But the rest have houses "in villages that have no wall", yet there lies adjacent to them a fruitful field—those perhaps who prepare for themselves a dwelling "in the land of the living" and in that land which the Lord promises to "the meek", saying: "blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth by inheritance". These houses, then, if perchance some lapse should occur, as we expounded above, there is "always" the possibility of recovering—so that, to speak by way of example, if some mortal fault should find us, one that consists not in a mortal crime, not in blasphemy of the faith, which is girded by the wall of ecclesiastical and apostolic teaching, but rather in a fault of speech or of conduct; this is to have "sold the house" which is in the field or "in a village that has no wall". This sale, then, and a fault of this kind can always be repaired, nor is it ever forbidden you to bear repentance for things committed of this kind. For in graver crimes place for repentance is granted only once; but these common faults, which we frequently incur, always admit of repentance and are redeemed without intermission.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We see three distinct laws concerning the sale and redemption of houses given through Moses in Leviticus. Let us first treat their content according to the historical sense, so that afterward we may be able to ascend also to the spiritual sense. Some houses are "in walled cities", others "in villages or fields that have no walls". He says, then, that "if anyone sell a house in a walled city, let him have the opportunity of redeeming it for a full year, but after the year no power of recovering it is granted". "For it shall be", he says, "the settled possession of the buyer, if he who sold it has not been able to free it within the year". The second law is that "if the house which has been sold be in a village that has no wall, but a village to which a field lies adjacent, it shall be lawful for the seller both after the year and whenever he is able, to restore the price and recover the house which he had sold". The third law is that "if perchance the house be a Levite's or a priest's, wherever such a house shall be, whether in a walled city or in a village that has no wall, it shall always and at every time be lawful, that whenever the Levite or the priest is able, he may redeem his house"; nor do the divine ordinances ever permit a priestly or Levitical possession to be confirmed to another who is not of the same order. These, then, are the laws which that former people used, even according to this very thing which is set forth through the history, providing quite religiously and piously for the priestly or Levitical orders.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "But if this house be a priest's", he says, "or a Levite's, wherever it be, whether in a city or in a field, it always has redemption". In this place I seek the priestly sense and the Levitical understanding. For the hearer of these things ought not, if it can be, to be inferior to that very one who wrote and sanctioned these things. What is it, then, that the priest and the Levite "always" and wherever it be "has redemption" of his house? According to the spiritual understanding a priest is called a mind consecrated to God, and he is named a Levite who unceasingly stands beside God and ministers to his will. Perfection, therefore, in understanding and work, in faith and deeds, is to be taken as the priest and the Levite. And so, if it should ever happen to this perfect mind to sell the "house which it has not made with hands, eternal in the heavens", and to give it into the hands of another—as befell once the great patriarch David, when "from his roof" he "looked upon" the wife of Uriah the Hittite—straightway he redeems it, straightway he repairs it; for straightway he says: "I have sinned". Nay rather, we ought to look at something still more sublime in this sense: how the house of priests and Levites, that is, of perfect minds, always has its sins redeemed and is always purged. If ever we read the divine scriptures and review in them certain faults of the holy fathers, if according to the sentence of the Apostle Paul we say that "all these things happened to them in figure, but they were written for our admonition", in this way "their house is always redeemed", because for their faults purgation and satisfaction is always applied by the teachers who show from the divine scriptures that these were forms and images of things to come, not by which the sins of the saints were reproved, but by which it was shown that sinners and the impious are enrolled into the portion and fellowship of the saints. Never, then, is the priestly possession separated from the priest; even if it be taken away for a time, even if it be sold, it is "always redeemed", "always" repaired, as if he should say, "charity", which is "perfect", "endures all things, hopes all things, bears all things, charity never falls". So, then, also the possession and house of the saints "never falls", is never taken away, is never separated from their right. For how can a house be separated from priests which has been built "upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets, in which Christ Jesus himself is the cornerstone"? But that this house can sometimes be sold, that is, that a building of this kind may fall into sin, hear how the Apostle Paul speaks concerning such: "as a wise architect I laid the foundation", he says, "another builds upon it, but let each one see how he builds upon it. For no one can lay another foundation besides that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble". You see, then, that there can be "built upon the foundation of Christ wood, hay, stubble", that is, works of sin; and whoever "builds" these has without doubt "sold his house" to the worst buyer, the devil, from whom each of those who sin obtains the price of sin, the satisfaction of his desire. If perchance anyone should incur this—which God forbid—let him quickly redeem it, quickly repair it, while there is time for repairing, while there is place for repentance, praying in common that we be not defrauded of the habitation of the eternal house, but be held worthy "to be received into the eternal tabernacles", through Christ our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In bodily contests certain grades and distinctions of the several ranks are customarily observed, so that each one may be rewarded with the prize of victory according to the quality of the struggle. For instance, if someone should have a contest among boys, or among youths, or among men, what observance ought to be kept for each rank, what may be done and what may not be done, and what rule of the contest is to be guarded, and what palm of reward the victor deserves after these things—all this is nonetheless provided for by the very laws of the games. So now too Almighty God, appointing for mortals in this world a contest of observing His law, after He had handed down very many things to be observed and had prescribed what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fittingly, at the very end, in the book of Leviticus, in which it is laid down concerning each of the several observances, announces what reward he carries off who has fulfilled them and what penalty he undergoes who has not observed them. But if the law, according to what the Jews will have it and those who think the Scriptures are to be understood in their sense, is not "spiritual" but carnal, there is no doubt that, observed carnally, it also bestows carnal blessings on those who observe it. But if, as it seems to Paul the Apostle, "the law is spiritual", then without doubt it is to be observed spiritually, and from it a spiritual reward of blessings is to be hoped for. For it is of the whole consequence that "the spiritual law" gives spiritual blessings, and it is nonetheless of the same consequence that also the curses and condemnations of "the spiritual law" are not bodily.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us now see what is the opening of the blessings in Leviticus. "If", He says, "you walk in my precepts, and keep my commandments and do them". There are three things which He says: "one must walk in the precepts, one must keep the commandments and do the things which are commanded". Whence it seems to me that a precept is, for instance, when it is enjoined that he who has not kept the sabbath "be stoned by the whole synagogue", or "he who has cursed God, that he be destroyed with stones", and any such things that are enjoined. But that commandments are those by which it is enjoined, for instance, that tithes be offered to the Levites, or "to appear before the Lord three times in the year", or "not to appear empty in the sight of the Lord". "To keep" therefore is "the commandment" to understand or to attend to the things which are enjoined; but "to do" is "the commandment" to fulfill the things which are enjoined. Thus therefore I think it is to be understood, what He said: "if you walk in my precepts, and keep my commandments and do them".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But let us see what is the first blessing for those who have fulfilled the things which are commanded. "I will give", He says, "you rain in its season". Therefore let us first say to the Jews and to those who suppose these things are to be understood simply or bodily: if this "rain" is given as a reward for labors to those who "keep the commandments", how is it that also to those who do not keep the commandments one and the same "rain" is given in its seasons, and the whole world makes use of the common rains given by God? For "He rains upon the just and the unjust". But if "rain" is given "to the just and the unjust", it will not be an exceptional reward for those who have kept the commandments. See therefore that, even if the Jews do not acquiesce in the words of Jesus our Lord, yet you, who are reckoned by His name and are called a Christian, ought to believe Him when He says that His heavenly Father "rains" this common rain "upon the just and the unjust", and you ought not to think that He has set apart for "the just" an exceptional portion, this which He has appointed common even with "the unjust". Let us therefore seek in the Scriptures what is the "rain" which is given to the saints alone and concerning which "it is commanded to the clouds that they rain not this rain" upon the unjust. What then this "rain" is, Moses himself, the lawgiver of these things, teaches us. For he himself says in Deuteronomy: "Attend, O heaven, and I will speak, and let the earth hear the words from my mouth; let my utterance be awaited as rain". Are these my words? Do we by rhetorical arguments violently bend the sense of the divine law? Is it not Moses who says that what he speaks is "rain"? "Let my utterance", he says, "be awaited as rain, and let my words come down as dew, as a shower upon the grass, and as snow upon the hay". Attend diligently, O hearer, lest you think we do violence to the divine Scripture, when, teaching the church, we say that either waters or showers or other things which seem to be said bodily are to be understood spiritually. Hear Moses, how he now names the word of the law "rain", now calls it "dew", now "shower", now even says "snow". And just as Moses speaks various and diverse things, as though speaking out of the grace of the manifold wisdom of God, so also Isaiah, when he says: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken". But also each one of the prophets, when he has opened his mouth, brings down showers "upon the face of the earth", that is, upon the ears and hearts of the hearers. Knowing this, the Apostle Paul also said: "For the earth, drinking in the rain that comes often upon it and bearing herb fit for those by whom it is tilled, receives blessings from God; but that which brings forth thorns and thistles is reprobate and near to a curse, whose end is unto burning". Did the Apostle say these things about this earth? But neither does the earth receive blessings from God "when it has drunk in the showers" and produced fruit; nor, if after the rain "it has brought forth thorns and thistles", does it obtain curses from God. But our earth, that is, our heart, if it should receive "the rain that comes frequently upon it" of the doctrine of the law and should bring forth the fruit of works, receives blessings. But if it should have, not spiritual work, but "thorns and thistles", that is, the cares of the world, or the desires of pleasures and riches, it is "reprobate and near to a curse, whose end will be unto burning". Therefore each one of the hearers, when he comes together to hear, receives "the shower" of the word of God; and if indeed he has brought forth the fruit of a good work, he will obtain "blessing"; but if he has despised the word of God he has received, and has neglected what he has often heard, and has subjected himself to the care of worldly affairs and to lust, as one who has choked the word with "thorns", he will procure "a curse" instead of a blessing, and instead of the end of beatitude he will find "the end of burning". "I will give", therefore, He says, "you rain in season". Necessarily He added also "in season". For just as this earthly shower, if it come unseasonably, that is, when the harvest is being gathered, when the grain is threshed on the threshing-floors, will seem to hurt rather than to help, so also those to whom "the rain" of the word of God is committed to be ministered ought to observe this which the Scripture says, that they furnish it "in season", that is, that they not press the word of God upon one who is glutted and drunken, nor upon a mind occupied with other things, when it cannot be attentive, or when it is constricted by the languor of some vice, and the inner hearing is offered not to the teacher but to one's own disease. Prudently therefore let him conjecture where the mind can be at leisure, where the hearer is sober, where watchful, where attentive, and there let him minister "the rain in season"; so also "the faithful and prudent servant" in the Gospel is bidden "to give to his fellow-servants their measure of wheat in season". But in another way too we can understand this which is commanded, "the shower is to be given in season". Someone is a child and "a little one in the faith": he needs rain, but the "rain" of "milk"; for so says he who knew how to dispense "rains in season": "I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able". He has advanced after these things in the faith, "he has grown in age and wisdom": without doubt he has become fit to receive "more solid food". Someone is weak and, not according to the season but according to weakness, cannot receive the things that are robust; for instance, he cannot fully receive a discourse about chastity: one must have compassion and measure the doctrine according to the quality of his strength, and to such ones marriage is to be conceded. This is to feed "the weak one" with "vegetables" and to fit to measures of the soul of this kind, as it were, the thin "rain" of the word, like unto "dew". But there is another earth which can receive strong "showers", and even bear "rivers" of the word of God and carry rushing "torrents". For concerning such ones the prophet says in the Psalms: "and you will give them to drink of the torrent of your delight".

"I will give", therefore, He says, "you rain in its season, and the earth shall give its births". After the first blessing of rain, this is the second, in which it is said that "the earth", having received the rain, "gives its births". We find that Isaac also, blessing Jacob, says: "May the Lord give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, an abundance of grain and wine". Do you suppose that Isaac was giving in blessing to his son Jacob such grain as sinful men also have, and with which even the impious Pharaoh abounded? Was this the blessing of so great a patriarch? Do you wish that I still show you how others also, the unjust, have a multitude of grain? Behold that man in the Gospel, whose "field brought forth many fruits, who says": "I will pull down my barns and build greater ones, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; eat, drink, and be merry". Do we therefore believe such to be the goods which by divine blessings were handed over to the saints and to the faithful? Other fruits of the earth do I behold, and otherwise do I regard the multitude of "birth". For if my "earth" bring forth fruit, if it produce "its births" out of the Lord's blessing, my understanding will perceive and be able to explain what and of what kind is this "earth" which, having received the heavenly rain, brings forth the "births" of rational crops. Take a testimony from the Gospels, how "he who sows went out to sow, and some indeed fell along the way, but some upon the rock, some among thorns, but some upon the good earth". If therefore those things which "fell upon the good earth" have brought forth fruit, "the earth has given its fruit" and "its births", it has produced "a hundredfold and sixtyfold and thirtyfold".

"But also the trees", He says, "of the fields shall give their fruit". We have within our very selves also "the trees of the fields which produce their fruit". What are these "trees of the fields which produce their fruit"? Perhaps the hearer says: what is this word-hunter doing again? Why does he seek out words from everywhere, so as to escape the explanation of the reading? How will he teach that there are "trees" and shrubs within us? If you do not rashly disparage, you will now hear that: "a good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit". We have therefore trees within us, whether good or bad; and those which are good "cannot bear bad fruits", just as those which are "bad bear not good fruits". Do you wish that I set forth for you also the terms and appellations of the very trees which are within us? It is not a fig or an apple or a vine, but one tree is called justice, another prudence, another fortitude, another is named temperance. And if you will, learn yet a greater multitude of trees, with which perhaps the paradise of God will be thought more worthily planted. For there is there a tree of piety, and there is another tree of wisdom, and there is another of discipline, and there is another "of the knowledge of good and evil". But above all is "the tree of life". Does it not seem to you rather that the heavenly "Father", "the husbandman", cultivates trees of this kind in your soul and establishes plantings of this kind in your mind? Thus therefore says the Savior: "a bad tree cannot bear good fruits, nor a good one bad fruits". This is what He teaches: the tree of chastity is "good", it cannot bear the fruits of unchastity; the tree of justice is "good" and cannot bear the fruits of injustice. So also, on the contrary, if you should have the root of "a bad tree" planted in your mind, it cannot render "good fruits". For if there be in you a root of malice, it will not give "good fruits"; if there be within your heart a plant of folly, it will never bring forth the flower of wisdom; if it be a tree of injustice, if of iniquity, never can such trees rejoice in "good fruits". If therefore we keep the commandments of God, having received "the rain" of the word of God, of which we spoke above, the trees also which are planted in the fields of our soul and in the breadth of our heart will bring forth glad fruit of good sweetness. But do you wish that I show you from the Scriptures that these several virtues, which we mentioned above, are called trees or shrubs? I bring forward as witness the most wise Solomon, saying concerning wisdom: "it is a tree of life", he says, "to all who embrace it". If therefore "wisdom is a tree of life", without doubt there is also another tree of prudence, and another of knowledge, and another of justice. For it is not consequently said that of all the virtues wisdom alone deserved to be called "a tree of life", but that the other virtues by no means received the appellations of a like lot. "The trees", therefore, "of the field shall give their fruit". This, I believe, blessed David also felt concerning himself, when he said: "but I am like a fruitful olive in the house of God". From which he manifestly shows that a just and holy man is called a tree of olive.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And the threshing shall reach for you unto the vintage". If good seed has been sown in my soul and, having received "rain" from God, it has grown and come to the ear, of necessity the harvest also will follow; and if the harvest, then also "threshing" will follow, in which the grains are cleansed. For indeed the soul which germinates from the word of God and, watered by the heavenly "rain", produces its sprout unto harvest, it is necessary that the very harvest which it brings forth be cleansed on the floor, that is, that the meanings which the soul has begotten it bring forth into the midst, and confer them—the things which it perceives—either with the other teachers or even with the divine volumes themselves; so that, if there be anything in them empty and superfluous, if there be anything like chaff or awns, it may shake it out with the spirit of discernment blowing within it, and retain the pure grain, by which alone it can nourish its fellow-servants and "dispense the measure of wheat in season". "And there shall reach", He says, "for you the threshing unto the vintage". Since "bread", as the Scripture says, "strengthens the heart of man, and wine gladdens it", whatever things are said concerning continence, concerning observances and the keeping of the commandments, these can be seen as grain, out of which "bread" is made and "strengthens the hearts" of the hearers. But those things which pertain to knowledge and by the explanation of hidden things "gladden" the minds of the hearers will seem to be fitted to "wine" and the vintage. For gladness is bestowed on the heart when the things that are hidden and obscure are explained. — "And the vintage", He says, "shall reach unto the sowing". As if we should say: first I sowed the things which are of the law and, after the sowing was done, I prayed that "the Lord would give rain in season": the harvest was made. After this I do not remain idle, but again I sow; I take the prophetic Scripture and from it I sow the lands and the fallow-grounds of the hearers. After these things I sow also other things from the evangelical discourses. Diverse are the things that are sown; through the whole year we can sow; for we can also cast many seeds from the apostolic writings. There is always something to be sown; in the whole of our life there is no time of idleness. As long as we breathe, let us sow; only let it be that "we sow in the spirit, that of the spirit we may reap eternal life". — "And you shall eat your bread in fullness". Neither do I take this to be of bodily blessing, as though he who keeps the law of God obtains this common bread in abundance. For what? Do not the impious and the wicked eat bread not only in abundance, but even in delicacies? Rather therefore, if we look to Him who said: "I am the living bread, who came down from heaven; and he who eats this bread shall live forever", and if we advert that He who said these things was "the word" by which souls are fed, we understand of what bread it was said in the blessings from God: "and you shall eat your bread in fullness". Things similar to these Solomon also pronounces in the Proverbs, saying concerning the just man: "the just man eating shall fill his soul; but the souls of the impious shall be in want". If you take this according to the letter, that "the just man eating shall fill his soul, but the souls of the impious shall be in want", it will seem false. For rather the souls of the impious take food with avidity and are eager for "fullness"; but the just at times even hunger. In fine, Paul was just and said: "even unto this hour we both hunger and thirst and are naked and are buffeted". And again he says: "in hunger and thirst, in many fastings". And how does Solomon say that "the just man eating shall satisfy his soul"? But if you consider how "the just man" always and "without intermission" eats of "the living bread" and fills his soul and satisfies it with the heavenly food, which is the word of God and His wisdom, you will find how out of the blessing of God the just man "eats his bread in fullness". — "And you shall dwell secure upon your land". The unjust is never inwardly, but is always moved and "tossed and carried about with every wind of doctrine, in the deceit of men, unto the deception of error". But the just man, who keeps the law of God, "dwells secure upon his land". For firm is the understanding of him who says to God: "confirm me, O Lord, in your words". "Confirmed" therefore and "secure" and "rooted" he "dwells upon the land", "founded in the faith", because "his building is not set upon the sand" nor is his root "upon the rock", but "his house" indeed "is founded" upon the land, but his plant is rooted "in the depth of the land", that is, in the inmost parts of his soul.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Rightly therefore to a soul of this kind it is said in the blessings: "and you shall dwell secure upon your land; and I will give peace upon your land". What "peace does" God "give"? That which the world has? Christ denies that He gives this. For He says: "my peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you; not as this world gives peace, do I also give to you". He denies therefore that He gives "the peace of the world" to His disciples, because elsewhere too He says: "do you think that I came to send peace on the earth? I came not to send peace, but a sword". Do you wish then to see what "peace God gives upon our land"? If the land be that "good" one which "bears fruit a hundredfold or sixtyfold or thirtyfold", it will receive from God that "peace" which the Apostle speaks of: "but the peace of God, which surpasses every mind, shall guard your hearts and your understandings". This then is the "peace" which "God gives upon our land".

"And you shall sleep and there shall be none to terrify you". Solomon too in the Proverbs said: "for if you sit, you shall be without fear; and if you sleep, you shall gladly take sleep; and you shall not fear the terror coming upon you, nor the assaults of the impious coming upon you". These things he said concerning the just and wise man, and these things are said in the blessing: "you shall sleep, and there shall be none to terrify you". For if I become just, no one can terrify me; I fear nothing else, if I fear God; for "the just man", he says, "is confident as a lion", and therefore he does not fear the lion, the devil, nor "the dragon", Satan, nor "his angels", but says according to David: "I will not fear the nocturnal terror, the arrow flying by day, and the business walking in the darkness, the ruin and the noonday demon". He adds also this: "The Lord is my illumination and my Savior, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life, of whom shall I tremble?". And again: "if camps stand against me, my heart shall not fear". You see the constancy and virtue of the soul that keeps the commandments of God and has the confidence of an inborn liberty. After these things, "and I will exterminate", He says, "the evil beasts from your land". Those bodily beasts are neither evil nor good, but something in between; for they are dumb animals. But those evil beasts are spiritual, which the Apostle calls "spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places". And that is the evil beast of which the Scripture says: "but the serpent was wiser than all the beasts that are upon the earth". This itself, then, is that "evil beast" which God promises "He will exterminate from our land", if we keep His commandments. Do you wish to see also another evil beast? "Your adversary", he says, "the devil, as a roaring lion goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in the faith". But if you wish to learn yet more beasts, the prophet Isaiah will teach you, who, under "the vision" which he entitled "of the quadrupeds in the desert", speaks by the prophetic spirit certain such things concerning beasts: "in tribulation", he says, "and anguish, the lion and the lion's whelp; thence also the offspring of flying asps, who carried upon asses and camels their riches to a nation which shall not profit them". Can these things in any way be seen as said of bodily beasts, even by those who are exceedingly friends of the letter? For how can "the lion and the lion's whelp" or "the flying asps" "carry upon camels and asses their riches"? But evidently the prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit, enumerates the contrary powers of the most wicked demons, and designated that they place "the riches" of their deceptions upon souls stolid and perverse, which by a figure he compares to camels and asses. And that his soul might not be handed over to these beasts, fearing God he prayed, saying: "deliver not to the beasts the soul that confesses to you". — "And I will exterminate", He says, "the malignant beasts from your land, and war shall not pass through your land". Many are the "wars" which "pass through our land", if we do not keep the law of God nor observe His precepts. Let each one return to his own soul and shake himself out by inner recollection, and see how our land, that is, our flesh, is now pressed by the spirit of fornication, now by that of anger and fury, now is agitated by the darts of avarice, now is struck by the weapons of envy, now is bored through by the arrows of lust, and in whatever ways "the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh", it is always agitated by inner battles. But what shall I say of the wars of thoughts, which the enemy suggests to our heart, that he may strip us of the faith of Christ and of the hope of our calling? For when he has stirred up for us the afflictions of temptations and the troubles of the world, consequently he then suggests to the thought that it is superfluous and foolish to endure these things for Christ, that it is much better to lead a secure life and without persecutions. Knowing this, the Apostle Paul too said: "destroying thoughts and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of Christ". He therefore who "keeps the divine precepts and keeps His commandments and does them", does not suffer this war and these battles, but God takes them away "from" his "land" and does not permit them "to pass" through the soul of the just.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And you shall pursue your enemies". What "enemies", except "the devil" himself "and his angels" and the malignant spirits and "the unclean demons"? We shall pursue them not only that we may drive them away from ourselves, but also from others whom they assail, if we keep the divine precepts. "You shall pursue", He says, "your enemies, and they shall fall before you by death". If "God should crush Satan under our feet swiftly", "the enemies shall fall before us by death". By whose "death"? I think, by ours; for if we "mortify our members, which are upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness", if we inflict this death upon our members, "they shall fall before us". How "shall they fall before us"? If you be just, injustice has fallen "before" you; if you be chaste, lust has fallen; if you be pious, impiety has collapsed before you.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And five of you shall pursue a hundred, and a hundred of you shall pursue many thousands". Who are those "five" who can "pursue a hundred"? The number "five" is set both among the praiseworthy and among the culpable. There are "five wise virgins" and "five foolish". So therefore also the number of a hundred can be taken to either part. If then we be of the five praiseworthy, that is, of the five wise, we shall pursue a hundred foolish. For if we fight wisely and provably in the word of God, if we discourse prudently concerning the law of the Lord, we shall convince and put to flight a multitude of the unfaithful. For just as the number five indicates both the wise and the foolish, so also the number of a hundred indicates both the faithful and the unfaithful. For under the number of a hundred years Abraham is described as having believed God and been justified, and "the sinner who dies at a hundred years shall be accursed". And here a "hundred" unfaithful are put to flight by "five" wise, and again a "hundred" faithful, marked not so much by the number of a hundred as by perfection, "shall pursue many thousands" of the unfaithful. For the faithful teachers put to flight innumerable demons, lest by the ancient fraud they deceive the souls of believers. — "And your enemies shall fall before you by the sword". Who the "enemies" are, we said above; but by what "sword" they are said "to fall", let us inquire. The Apostle Paul teaches us what this sword is, when he says: "for the word of God is living and effective and more penetrating than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the joint of soul and spirit, of the members also and the marrows, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart". This is the "sword" by whose edge "our enemies shall fall". For it is the word of God which lays low "all enemies" and puts them "under His feet", "that the whole world may be made subject to God". Do you wish to learn still from another epistle of Paul that the sword is the word of God? Hear him, when he prepares arms for the soldiers of Christ, how he says: "and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God, through all prayer and supplication", most evidently pronouncing also through these things that by "the word of God", which is "the two-edged sword", "our enemies shall fall before us".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And I will look upon you and increase you". Full of beatitude is this very thing, if "God look upon" anyone. Do you wish to see, if "the Lord look upon" a man, how great is salvation? Peter had once almost perished and, by the devil breathing through the mouth of "the maidservant of the high priest", had been snatched from the consecration of the apostolic number; but when "Jesus only looked upon him", when He turned toward him the countenance of a placid face, at once, returning into himself and recalling his foot slipped from the precipice, "he wept", it says, "most bitterly", and thus, looked upon by God, by weeping he recovered his place, which by denying he had lost. — "I will look", therefore, He says, "upon you, and increase you". As if the sun should look upon a crop and bring forth its fruits—which surely, if it had not looked upon it, would have remained fruitless—so God, "looking upon" the crop of our heart and illuminating us with the rays of His word, "increases us" and multiplies us, that we may no longer be "little ones", but be made "great", just as "Isaac was made great", and Moses was made "great", and John "great". — "And I will establish my covenant with you". See how great blessings are promised, if we keep the commandments.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For we eat with blessing the old things, the prophetic words and the old things of the old things, the words of the law. And, when the new and evangelical words came, living according to the gospel, we bring forth the old things of the letter from before the new. He sets his tabernacle in us, fulfilling the promise which he spoke, "I will dwell among them and walk in them."
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 10.15

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "I will establish", He says, "my covenant with you. And you shall eat the old things and the old of the old, and you shall cast out the old from before the face of the new". How do we "cast out the old from before the face of the new"? "The old" things: "we had the law and the prophets"; but "the old of the old" are those things which were before the law, from the beginning, when the world was made. There came the new Gospels, there came also the Apostles. From before the face of these we cast out "the old things". How do we cast them out? We cast out the law according to the letter, that we may establish the law according to the spirit. We can also say in this manner: before the man came "from heaven" and the "heavenly man" was born, we were all "earthly" and "bore the image of the earthly"; but when there came "the new man, who was created according to God", we cast out "from before the face" of him "the old things", "putting off the old man and putting on the new", "who according to the interior man is renewed from day to day".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And I will set my tabernacle among you". If we have these things in us which were said above, if, the "old man" having been cast off, our heart has been renewed, God comes to us and dwells in us, He who said: "and I will set my tabernacle among you, and my soul shall not abominate you". "The soul of God" will not "abominate" us, if we observe the things which are written. Yet I should wish to inquire what is "the soul of God". Shall we perhaps suppose that God has a soul as a man has? It is absurd to think this of God. But I dare and say that the soul of God is Christ. For just as Christ is "the Word" of God and "the wisdom of God and the power of God", so also He is the soul of God. And in this manner it is said: "my soul shall not abominate you", that is, my Son, but "I will walk among you".

author: Origen of Alexandria
